pg007_n0011: Netball is a team sport where players use their hands to pass, and shoot the ball into the opponents’ goal to score goals.
pg007_n0012: It is played by male and female competitively and recreationally.
pg007_n0013: Engaging in netball provides employment opportunities, enhances physical health, and helps players develop essential life skills.
pg007_n0014: In this chapter, you will learn the concept, safety measures, skills, and rules of netball.
pg007_n0015: The competencies developed will enable you to analyse and play netball skillfully and confidently.
pg007_n0019: Netball is a positional skill-benched game
pg007_n0023: Netball is a team sport played by hands on a rectangular court with clearly defined areas.
pg007_n0024: A team consists of seven (7) players, each assigned with specific roles and position that restricts movement.
pg007_n0025: The players must pass the ball to their teammates within three (3) seconds of receiving it, aiming to move the ball and score towards their attacking goal.
pg007_n0026: The game is played in four quarters, each lasting for 15 minutes with four (4) minutes break between the first-second and third-fourth quarters, and an interval of 12 minutes at the half time.
pg007_n0028: A team scores when the Goal Shooter (GS) or Goal Attack (GA) successfully shoots the ball through the opponent’s hoop.
pg007_n0029: At the end of the match, the team with the highest number of goals is declared the winner.
pg007_n0030: If the game ends in a tie, extra time or other tie-breaking rules may be applied depending on the competition’s regulations.
pg007_n0031: Netball promotes teamwork, discipline, and strategic thinking while improving physical fitness, hand-eye coordination, and spatial awareness.
pg007_n0032: It is inclusive, allowing participation regardless of skill level, gender or ability, making it a valuable activity for recreation and competition.
pg008_n0005: Netball basic facilities comprise the court with goal posts and it is either played outdoors or indoors.
pg008_n0006: The equipment varies depending on the level of play, from recreational to professional level.
pg008_n0007: However, netballs, shoes and bibs are basic requirements.
pg008_n0011: Netball is played on a level and firm rectangular court with specific markings to ensure smooth gameplay.
pg008_n0012: The standard netball court measures 30.5 metres in length and 15.25 metres in width and is divided into three sections which are the attacking third, the centre third, and the defensive third.
pg008_n0013: The court features include a centre circle, two goal circles (each with a radius of 4.9 metres), the sidelines and goal lines as shown in Figure 1.1.

pg009_n0005: Survey a netball court at your school to identify all markings, and measure its playing area, then judge whether it is standard or not.
pg009_n0009: Netball goalposts are essential for scoring.
pg009_n0010: Each court has two goalposts, one at each end, positioned at the centre of the goal line within the goal circle.
pg009_n0011: The goalposts are between 65 mm to 100 mm in diameter and 3.05 m high, inserted into the ground and mounted with a ring at its upper end.
pg009_n0012: The ring is 15 mm thick and has a 150 mm length connection to the post.
pg009_n0013: The internal diameter of the ring is 380 mm fitted with a net.
pg009_n0014: The net is open at both ends measuring 380 mm to 457 mm in length, as shown in Figure 1.2.

pg009_n0033: The netball is spherical in shape, as shown in Figure 1.3 and made of leather, rubber or any other suitable synthetic material.
pg009_n0034: It measures 690 mm – 710 mm in circumference
pg010_n0004: The standard netball is size four (4) for players below 10 years old, and size five (5) for players above 10 years old.
pg010_n0010: Netball shoes are non-slip sports shoes that are designed to handle severe side-to-side movements that players make on the netball court, Figure 14.
pg010_n0011: They are made of rubber soles designed to provide stability, better grip, and easy pivots keeping the foot on the platform and protecting players from slipping.
pg010_im002: Pair of white netball shoes on a court, with one shoe upright to show the textured rubber sole.
pg010_n0017: In netball player bibs are used to identify each player’s position on the court.
pg010_n0018: They are sleeveless vests with bold letters printed on the front and back to indicate the player’s role, as shown in Figure 1.5.
pg010_n0019: Bibs are worn over the uniform to help teammates, opponents, and officials recognise players and their positions easily during the game.

pg011_n0012: To ensure safe play in netball, players must take precautions to protect themselves and others from injuries such as dislocations, fractures, or wounds.
pg011_n0013: Since netball involves quick movements, jumping, and sudden stops, it is important to observe the following safety measures before, during, and after the game:
pg011_n0019: Warm-up: Engage in stretching and light exercises to prepare muscles, reduce the risk of injury and improve performance;
pg011_n0022: First aid kit: Ensure that a first aid kit is available at the playing area in case of emergencies;
pg011_n0025: Inspect the playing area and the equipment: Inspect the netballs pressure and quality, remove any debris, wet spots, or unsafe objects from the court; and
pg011_n0028: Wear proper gear: Use appropriate netball shoes, uniforms, and protective gear if necessary.
pg011_n0034: Observe the rules: Adhere to netball rules to avoid fouls and ensure fair play;
pg011_n0037: Communicate with teammates: Prevent collisions by using verbal and non-verbal signals;
pg011_n0040: Be aware of your movements: Avoid sudden stops or dangerous landings that may cause injury; and
pg012_n0005: Respect opponents and officials: Avoid trash talk, aggressive and disrespectfully behaviour.
pg012_n0011: Cool down: Perform light stretching to relax muscles, reduce stiffness and slowly return to pre-exercise level;
pg012_n0014: Report injuries: Seek medical attention for any discomfort or injury sustained during the game; and
pg012_n0017: Rehydrate and rest: Drink enough water and allow the body to recover after physical exertion.
pg012_n0022: Describe the benefits of playing netball.
pg012_n0024: Identify the potential hazards in the netball court and suggest ways to make the court safer to play.
pg012_n0026: Skills and techniques in playing netball
pg012_n0028: The primary objective of netball is to score goals by shooting the ball through the opponent’s goal ring while preventing the opposing team from scoring.
pg012_n0029: To play netball effectively, players need to develop key skills and techniques that enhance their performance on the court.
pg012_n0030: Techniques are the parts that make up a whole skill.
pg012_n0031: The skills include passing, movement, shooting, positioning and defending, all of which contribute to the overall performance of the player, consequently, to the success of the team.
pg012_n0035: Passing is one of the most important skills in netball as players are not allowed to run with the ball.
pg012_n0036: Effective passing ensures smooth ball movement, maintains possession, and facilitates teamwork.
pg012_n0037: There are several types of passes that players can use to move the ball around the court, each serving a particular purpose depending on the situation.
pg012_n0038: The common types of passes include chest pass, bounce pass, overhead pass, and shoulder pass.
pg012_n0042: A chest pass is a two-handed pass delivered from the chest for a fast, accurate delivery over short distances.
pg012_n0043: It is most effective when defender pressure is low and is ideal for quick exchanges between teammates.
pg012_n0044: The ball is passed straight from the player’s chest to the teammate’s chest by pushing it forward with both hands.
pg013_n0003: speed and precision, making it perfect for short-range passes.
pg013_n0004: To practice chest pass, follow these steps:
pg013_n0008: Stand with legs shoulder-width apart, slightly bending your knees;
pg013_n0011: Hold the ball with two hands at chest height, as shown in Figure 1.6 (a), to ensure a strong and stable grip;
pg013_n0014: Spread your fingers around the side of the ball and point your thumbs towards the back, with your elbows bent, preparing to push it;
pg013_n0017: Push the ball forward by straightening your elbows, fingers, and thumbs, delivering the ball, and follow-through to ensure accuracy and power as shown in Figure 1.6 (b); and
pg013_n0020: Step forward after passing the ball by transferring your weight onto the front foot, helping to propel the ball and maintain balance.
pg013_im001_seg001_v1: Player standing with knees slightly bent, holding the ball at chest height with both hands, ready to make a chest pass; arrow points forward.
pg013_im001_seg002_v1: Player completes the chest pass by stepping forward and extending both arms as the ball travels ahead; arrow shows weight transfer onto the front foot.
pg013_n0033: Using various drills, practice a chest pass repetitively to master the skill.
pg013_n0037: A bounce pass is a passing technique where the ball is thrown down towards the ground, bouncing once before it reaches the intended receiver.
pg013_n0038: The pass is useful for evading defenders as it travels low to the ground and is harder to intercept.
pg013_n0039: The ball should bounce about two-thirds of the way to the target player, with a controlled bounce to ensure accuracy.
pg013_n0040: This pass is ideal for passing through tight spaces where
pg014_n0003: defenders are concentrated, allowing for smoother ball movement and reduced chances of interception.
pg014_n0004: A bounce pass can be performed with one or two hands from the front or the side of the body.
pg014_n0005: To practice bounce pass, follow these steps:
pg014_n0009: Stand with legs shoulder-width apart, slightly bending your knees;
pg014_n0012: Hold the ball with both hands or one hand at chest height, positioning your elbows out in front;
pg014_n0015: Spread your fingers on either side of the ball, with thumbs behind it and fingers pointing downward;
pg014_n0018: Step forward with your dominant foot as you release the ball at wrist height, pushing it forward toward the ground, as shown in Figure 1.7;
pg014_n0021: Aim for the ball to bounce just over halfway between you and the receiver; and
pg014_n0024: Follow through by extending your arms upon releasing the ball to ensure accuracy and keep the ball on the right path.
pg014_im001: Two netball players demonstrate a bounce pass, with arrows showing the ball thrown to the ground midway before rising to the receiving player.
pg014_n0030: Using various drills, practice a bounce pass repetitively to master the skill.
pg015_n0005: An overhead pass is a high pass thrown with both hands from above the head.
pg015_n0006: The ball is held above the head and thrown with a firm push of the arms; making it ideal for passing over an opponent’s head reaching teammates further in the court.
pg015_n0007: This pass is especially useful when a player is under pressure, as it helps cover more distance efficiently.
pg015_n0008: To practice the overhead pass, follow these steps:
pg015_n0012: Stand tall, facing the direction of the throw with knees slightly bent and feet hip-width apart;
pg015_n0015: Position hands on either side of the ball, with fingers spread out and pointing upward, and hold the ball over the head, as shown in Figure 1.8;
pg015_n0018: Bend arms to allow the ball to drop back slightly, ensuring elbows point forward before releasing;
pg015_n0021: Step forward with the dominant foot while releasing the ball to maximize power; and
pg015_n0024: Follow through with arms, wrists, and fingers for accuracy and control of the ball.
pg015_im001: Sequence of an overhead pass in netball: a player raises the ball above her head, steps forward and throws it in a high arc to a teammate who catches it with both hands.
pg015_n0033: Using various drills, practice an overhead pass repetitively to master the skill.
pg016_n0005: A shoulder pass is a strong, one-handed pass thrown from the shoulder.
pg016_n0006: The pass is ideal for long-distance passing when a quick, powerful throw is needed to reach a teammate far away.
pg016_n0007: The ball is held with one hand near the shoulder and pushed forward with force, making it best suited for longer, faster pass.
pg016_n0008: This pass requires good hand-eye coordination to ensure accuracy and effective ball movement across the court.
pg016_n0009: To practice the shoulder pass, follow these steps:
pg016_n0013: Hold the ball with your dominant hand just behind your head at the shoulder;
pg016_n0016: Bend your elbow at a 90-degree angle and use your other hand to support the ball;
pg016_n0019: Position your feet shoulder-width apart, with one foot in front of the other;
pg016_n0022: Remove your supporting hand and use your dominant arm to propel the ball toward your target as shown in Figure 1.9; and
pg016_n0025: Use your fingers to direct the ball’s path, following through with your arm for accuracy and control.
pg016_im001: Three-step sequence of a netball player executing a shoulder pass, holding the ball near the shoulder, stepping forward, and extending the throwing arm in follow-through.
pg016_n0033: Using various drills, practice a shoulder pass repetitively to master the skill.
pg016_n0037: Catching the ball means stopping the ball that is moving through the air and taking hold of it.
pg016_n0038: It is crucial for maintaining possession, keeping the game flowing, and setting up attacking plays.
pg016_n0039: A good catch allows players to quickly pass or shoot with accuracy.
pg017_n0005: This is the safest and most commonly used catching technique.
pg017_n0006: A player uses both hands to catch the ball, ensuring a firmer grip and better control.
pg017_n0007: A two-handed catch is often employed when the ball is coming at a high speed or rebounds.
pg017_n0008: Players extend their arms toward the ball, spreading their fingers wide, and absorb the impact by pulling the ball toward their chest.
pg017_n0009: This method provides better control, reduces the risk of fumbling, and ensures accuracy when transitioning to a pass or shot.
pg017_n0010: To practice the two-handed catch, follow these steps:
pg017_n0014: Keep the body well-balanced and focus your eyes on the ball to track its flight and anticipate its path;
pg017_n0017: Extend your arms toward the ball, spreading your fingers to form a shape that mirrors the spherical form of the ball;
pg017_n0020: Catch the ball firmly by bringing your palms and fingers together, ensuring a secure grip; and
pg017_n0023: Pull the ball back towards your chest after catching it to maintain control and prepare for the next move as shown in Figure 1.10.
pg017_im001: Netball player securing the ball with both hands and pulling it to the chest in a balanced two-handed catch position.
pg017_n0029: This technique is used when the ball is out of reach, such as during a high pass or a deflection.
pg017_n0030: It requires quick reflexes, strong hand-eye coordination, and grip strength to control the ball before securing it with both hands.
pg017_n0031: While riskier than a two-handed catch, it is useful in fast-paced situations where a player needs to react quickly.
pg017_n0032: To practice the one-handed catch, follow these steps:
pg017_n0036: Keep the body well-balanced and focus your eyes on the ball to track its flight path;
pg018_n0005: Extend your arm toward the ball, positioning your fingers to form the shape of the ball;
pg018_n0008: Catch the ball firmly with the palm and fingers of one hand, ensuring a strong grip as the ball makes contact as shown in Figure 1.11; and
pg018_n0011: Pull the ball back towards your body to secure it, using your other hand to assist.
pg018_im001: Netball player demonstrating a one-handed catch, reaching out with one arm to secure the ball while balancing with bent knees.
pg018_n0018: Using various drills, practice the two-handed and one-handed catch repetitively to master the skills.
pg018_n0022: Proper movement and footwork are essential for creating space, maintaining possession, and staying agile on the court.
pg018_n0023: Players must adhere to footwork rules to avoid violations and ensure efficient gameplay.
pg018_n0024: The key footwork techniques include pivoting, dodging, and landing.
pg018_n0028: Pivoting is the keeping of one foot planted while making a swivel movement that allows the player to move on a fixed axis to either pass or shoot.
pg018_n0029: It opens up space on the court by changing the direction of the game.
pg018_n0030: After receiving the ball, a player can pivot on one foot, allowing them to quickly change direction without losing possession.
pg018_n0031: This technique helps maintain control while setting up for a pass or shot.
pg018_n0032: To practice pivoting, follow these steps:
pg019_n0005: Receive the ball and come to a complete stop with one or two feet firmly planted on the ground;
pg019_n0008: Choose your pivot foot (the foot that will remain stationary) and shift your weight onto it;
pg019_n0011: Rotate on your pivot foot by turning your body in the direction you want to move, keeping the ball in control with your other hand;
pg019_n0014: Keep your body low and balanced, bending your knees slightly to maintain stability during the pivot;
pg019_n0017: Use your free foot to step in the direction you want to go once you have pivoted, ensuring a smooth and controlled change of direction as shown in Figure 1.12; and
pg019_n0020: Stay aware of your surroundings and prepare for the next pass or play after completing the pivot.
pg019_im001: Three-step netball pivot: a player stops with the ball, keeps one foot planted as the pivot foot, and rotates the body to the left or right while the other foot steps around, as shown by dashed directional arrows.
pg019_n0030: Using various drills, practice pivoting repetitively to master the skill.
pg019_n0034: Dodging is a quick lateral movement used to break free from defenders and create space for a pass or shot.
pg019_n0035: It requires agility and quick decision-making to escape the
pg020_n0004: To practice dodging, follow these steps:
pg020_n0008: Stay low with your knees bent and body balanced;
pg020_n0011: Push off quickly with your non-dominant foot to start the dodge;
pg020_n0014: Move sharply to one side to escape the defender as shown in Figure 1.13;
pg020_n0017: Sprint away to create space for a pass or shot; and
pg020_n0020: Be ready to change direction again if needed, stay unpredictable.
pg020_im001: Netball player dodging to the side with the ball while a defender crouches in front, ready to block.
pg020_n0025: Using various drills, practice dodging repetitively to master the skill.
pg020_n0029: Landing is the action of a player coming to a stop after receiving the ball, whether from a jump or a move across the court.
pg020_n0030: The player lands with either one foot or both feet.
pg020_n0031: Proper landing techniques are crucial for maintaining balance and preventing injury.
pg020_n0032: Bending the knees and landing softly ensures a stable position and reduces the risk of injuries or falls.
pg020_n0033: There are two techniques of landing which are one-foot landing and two-foot landing.
pg021_n0005: One-foot landing occurs when a player catches the ball while moving and lands with one foot.
pg021_n0006: The first foot to touch the ground is called the landing foot, while the second foot is the pivoting foot, the later can be used to step in any direction before passing or shooting, and allows for quick decision-making on the court.
pg021_n0007: To practice one-foot landing, follow these key steps:
pg021_n0011: Focus on the ball and anticipate the landing while in motion;
pg021_n0014: Land with one foot first to absorb impact and maintain control, as shown in Figure 1.14;
pg021_n0017: Keep your knees slightly bent to ensure stability and balance;
pg021_n0020: Use the second foot as a pivot to change direction for passing or shooting; and
pg021_n0023: Ensure quick ball distribution to keep the game flowing effectively.
pg021_im001: Netball player in motion preparing for a one-foot landing as she reaches to catch the ball.
pg021_im002: Netball player completing a one-foot landing, balancing on one leg with bent knees while holding the ball.
pg021_n0034: A two-foot landing occurs when a player catches the ball and lands on both feet simultaneously.
pg021_n0035: This technique provides greater balance and stability, allowing the player to decide which foot to use as the pivot foot before passing or shooting.
pg021_n0036: It is especially useful when receiving the ball under defensive pressure.
pg021_n0037: To practice two-foot landing, follow these key steps:
pg021_n0041: Keep your eyes on the ball and anticipate the landing while in motion;
pg021_n0044: Land with both feet at the same time to evenly distribute weight and maintain control;
pg021_n0047: Keep your knees slightly bent to absorb impact and ensure stability, as shown in Figure 1.15;
pg022_n0005: Choose either foot as the pivot to adjust positioning for passing or shooting; and
pg022_n0008: Stay balanced and make a quick decision to pass, pivot, or shoot effectively.
pg022_im001: Netball player catches the ball and lands on both feet together with knees bent in a balanced two-foot landing.
pg022_n0017: Using various drills, practice the one and two-foot landing repetitively to master the skills.
pg022_n0021: Shooting is the action of attempting to score a goal by throwing the ball through the opponent’s hoop from within the goal circle.
pg022_n0022: It is the way a team scores goals, it involves a one-handed shot, which requires a strong shooting arm and a supportive non-shooting hand.
pg022_n0023: Shooting comes from a combination of leg power and upper-body strength, allowing players to release the ball with a high arm and follow through with a wrist action.
pg022_n0024: Shooting is a crucial skill reserved only for a Goal Shooter (GS) and a Goal Attack (GA) and is only executed from inside the goal circle.
pg022_n0025: Shooting technique directly impacts ability of a team to score.
pg022_n0026: Mastering proper shooting techniques improves accuracy and increases the chances of making successful shots.
pg023_n0005: A stable, controlled shot aimed for accuracy, usually taken with both hands.
pg023_n0006: This technique involves standing still, focusing on the target, and shooting in a smooth, controlled motion to ensure precision and consistency.
pg023_n0007: To practice the set shot, follow these steps:
pg023_n0011: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and knees slightly bent for balance and stability;
pg023_n0014: Hold the ball with both hands in front of you, ensuring your shooting hand is under the ball and your non-shooting hand is on the side;
pg023_n0017: Focus on the target, aiming for the centre of the goal or the highest point of the net;
pg023_n0020: Push the ball upwards with a smooth motion, using your legs for power and extending your arms fully. as shown in Figure 1.16; and
pg023_n0023: Follow through by flicking your wrist towards the target, ensuring your shooting hand finishes in a relaxed position, pointing towards the hoop.
pg023_im001: Two-stage netball set shot: the player bends slightly with the ball held above her head, then extends upward and follows through as the ball arcs toward the hoop.
pg023_n0031: A jump shot is taken while jumping, which helps to avoid defenders and increases the shooting angle.
pg023_n0032: By leaping as they shoot, players can create space between themselves and the defenders, making the shot more difficult to block, and giving them a higher shooting trajectory.
pg023_n0033: To practice the jump shot, follow these steps:
pg024_n0005: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and knees slightly bent, ready to explode upwards;
pg024_n0008: Hold the ball with both hands in front of you, with your shooting hand under the ball and your non-shooting hand on the side for support;
pg024_n0011: Focus on the target and prepare to jump, aiming for the centre of the goal ring;
pg024_n0014: Jump upwards using your legs for power while simultaneously extending your arms to release the ball at the highest point of your jump, as shown in Figure 1.17; and
pg024_n0017: Follow through with a flick of your wrist, keeping your shooting hand relaxed and pointing towards the hoop to ensure accuracy.
pg024_im001: Two-step diagram of a netball jump shot: a player bends slightly with the ball raised above her head, then jumps straight up and releases it with arms fully extended as the ball arcs toward the hoop.
pg024_n0025: In netball, the lay-up shot is a close-range shooting technique typically used when a player is driving towards the hoop and needs to score quickly.
pg024_n0026: It is especially useful when close to the goalpost and can be performed while jumping off one foot, aiming for a smooth and accurate shot.
pg024_n0027: To practice the lay-up shot in netball, follow these steps:
pg024_n0031: Approach the goalpost at a controlled pace, with the ball in hand and a defender behind or to the side of you;
pg025_n0005: Take a step with your dominant foot and jump off your non-dominant foot, bringing the ball towards the goalpost, as shown in Figure 1.18;
pg025_n0008: Use your shooting hand to gently push the ball directly into the hoop, aiming for a soft and accurate shot;
pg025_n0011: Keep your body aligned while using your non-shooting hand for balance; and
pg025_n0014: Follow through the arms and fingers towards the direction of the ball.
pg025_im001: Netball player performing a lay-up shot, jumping off one foot with one knee raised and the ball lifted toward the hoop.
pg025_n0020: Using various drills, practice set shot, jump shot and layup shot repetitively to master the skills.
pg025_n0024: Defending means preventing the opposing team from scoring and forcing turnovers.
pg025_n0025: Defenders must use strategic positioning, quick reflexes, and strong anticipation skills to challenge opponents and disrupt their attacking plays.
pg025_n0026: Good defensive play requires focus, discipline, and teamwork to regain possession and create counterattacking opportunities.
pg025_n0027: The key techniques of defense include marking, intercepting and blocking.
pg026_n0005: Marking is a defensive strategy where a player follows and restricts the movement of an opponent to prevent them from receiving the ball or making a pass.
pg026_n0006: Marking helps restrict an opponent’s movement and passing options, as shown in Figure 1.19.
pg026_n0007: To mark effectively, a defender must stay close to their opponent while maintaining an arm’s length distance to apply pressure without committing a foul.
pg026_n0008: Tracking the attacker’s movements and positioning oneself strategically can limit their ability to receive passes or take a shot.
pg026_n0009: Additionally, good body positioning forces the opponent into less dangerous areas of the court, making it harder for them to contribute to the attack.
pg026_im001: Netball defender crouches with arms spread, marking a ball carrier near the goalpost at arm’s-length distance.
pg026_im002: Goal defence raises both arms wide to mark the goal attack holding the ball and block passing or shooting options.
pg026_n0019: Interception is the gaining of possession of the ball from the opposition team during a pass.
pg026_n0020: Intercepting requires anticipation and quick reactions to cut off passes before they reach the intended player, as shown in Figure 1.20.
pg026_n0021: A defender must read the game by observing the eyes and body movement of the opponent to predict where the ball will go.
pg026_n0022: Stepping into passing lanes at the right moment or timing a leap effectively increases the chances of a successful interception.
pg026_n0023: Once the ball is intercepted, maintaining balance is crucial for transitioning quickly into an attacking play.

pg027_n0007: Blocking shots is a defensive technique used by players to prevent an opposing player from scoring by intercepting or obstructing shots aimed for a goal.
pg027_n0008: It is a key defensive skill that challenges shooters and reduces their scoring accuracy.
pg027_n0009: A defender should stand with arms fully extended and hands open to make it difficult for the shooter to score, as shown in Figure 1.21 (a and b).
pg027_n0010: Timing the jump correctly is important to contest the shot without making a foul and conceding a penalty.
pg027_n0011: Additionally, maintaining a strong stance after blocking ensures the defender can quickly react to rebounds or loose balls.

pg028_n0017: In netball, each player has a specific position with defined roles and movement restrictions on the court.
pg028_n0018: Understanding positioning is crucial for effective teamwork, strategy, and gameplay.
pg028_n0019: The seven playing positions in a netball team are divided into attacking, defending, and midcourt roles.
pg028_n0020: Each position plays a vital role in maintaining team structure, ensuring smooth ball movement, and defending the opposing team.
pg028_n0023: These are the positions between the centre circle and the goal third of the attacking team including the goal circle.
pg028_n0024: It covers the area played by the Goal Shooter (GS), Goal Attack (GA) and Wing Attack (WA).
pg028_n0028: Goal Shooter (GS): Primarily responsible for scoring goals.
pg028_n0029: Positioned inside the goal circle, they work closely with the Goal Attack (GA) to create shooting opportunities;
pg028_n0032: Goal Attack (GA): Assists the Goal Shooter (GS) by feeding the ball into the goal circle and taking shots when necessary.
pg028_n0033: GA plays in the centre third, and attacking goal third including the goal circle; and
pg028_n0036: Wing Attack (WA): Plays a role to deliver the ball to the shooters (GS & GA).
pg028_n0037: Focuses on accurate passing, positioning, and creating space in the attacking third.
pg028_n0040: Centre (C): This is the position between defense and attack position.
pg028_n0041: The Centre dictates the speed of the play, breaks up opposing attacks and keeps possession of the ball.
pg028_n0042: They also link the play from defenders to attackers, often creating chances for forward players.
pg028_n0043: The centre moves across all thirds except the goal circles of both teams.
pg028_n0044: The centre starts and restarts the play after each time the goal is scored.
pg029_n0005: This is the position between the centre circle and the goal third of the defending team including the goal circle.
pg029_n0006: It covers the area played by the Wing Defense (WD), Goal Defense (GD) and Goal Keeper (GK).
pg029_n0007: Players playing in the defensive positions have the responsibility to prevent the opposing team from scoring.
pg029_n0011: Wing Defense (WD): Responsible for marking the opposing team’s Wing Attack and preventing them from feeding the ball into the shooting circle;
pg029_n0014: Goal Defense (GD): Marks the Goal Attack, preventing them from taking shots and intercepting passes into the goal circle.
pg029_n0015: They also assist in transitioning the ball to attack; and
pg029_n0018: Goal Keeper (GK): The last line of defense, responsible for marking the Goal Shooter and preventing goals.
pg029_n0019: They stay in the defensive third and inside the goal circle.

pg030_n0055: Rules and regulations for playing netball
pg030_n0057: The netball rules ensure fair play, safety, and consistency across all levels of competition.
pg030_n0058: The rules are updated periodically, however, they remain rooted in core values such as equal opportunity, fair play, and respect for opponents.
pg030_n0059: Below are the key rules governing the game:
pg030_n0063: A netball team consists of seven players on the court and each player has specific position that determines where they can move on the court.
pg030_n0064: Players must play within their designated areas to maintain the structure and prevent unfair advantages.
pg030_n0065: The player’s positions include Goal Shooter (GS), Goal Attack (GA), Wing Attack (WA), Centre (C), Wing Defense (WD), Goal Defense (GD), and Goal Keeper (GK).
pg030_n0069: A standard netball match is played over four quarters, each lasting for 15 minutes.
pg030_n0070: There are short breaks of not more than four minutes after the first and third quarters
pg031_n0003: and a longer halftime break of 12 minutes.
pg031_n0004: Teams change ends after each quarter.
pg031_n0005: If the game ends in a draw during knockout rounds or finals, extra time or a two-goals lead rule may apply to determine the winner.
pg031_n0009: Before the game begins the umpire toss coin where captains of both teams participate.
pg031_n0010: The game begins with a centre pass taken from the centre circle by the Centre (C) player of the team that won the toss.
pg031_n0011: The centre pass alternates between teams after each goal, ensuring fair opportunities for both teams to restart play.
pg031_n0012: Players must stay within their designated starting positions before the whistle is blown.
pg031_n0016: Netball players are not allowed to run with or dribble the ball.
pg031_n0017: Once a pass is received, the player must pass it within three seconds.
pg031_n0018: Additionally, players can pivot on one foot to adjust their position before passing but cannot take extra steps.
pg031_n0019: This rule promotes quick decision-making and continuous ball movement.
pg031_n0023: A team scores a goal when either the Goal Shooter (GS) or Goal Attack (GA) successfully shoots the ball through the opponent’s hoop.
pg031_n0024: There are two clear ways to score goals, through open play or by free shots as a result of a technical foul in a goal circle.
pg031_n0025: A goal is only scored from within the shooting circle.
pg031_n0026: If a player shoots from outside the goal circle, the goal does not count.
pg031_n0027: The team with the most goals at the end of the game wins.
pg031_n0031: Physical contact, such as pushing, hitting, or holding an opponent, is not allowed.
pg031_n0032: Any form of contact that interferes with movement of opponent results in a penalty pass to the opposing team.
pg031_n0033: If the contact happens inside the goal circle, the non-offending team may be given a penalty pass or shot.
pg031_n0035: Defenders must maintain a minimum distance of three feet (0.9 metres) from the player with the ball.
pg031_n0036: If a defender gets too close (within 3 feet or 0.9 metres), they commit an obstruction, giving the attacking team a penalty pass.
pg031_n0037: If the obstruction occurs inside the shooting circle against a shooter, it results in a penalty pass or shot, allowing the shooter a free attempt at the goal.
pg031_n0041: Each player in netball has specific areas in the court that is allowed to move within.
pg031_n0042: If steps outside the permitted zone, the player commits an offside violation, resulting
pg032_n0003: in a free pass for the opposing team.
pg032_n0004: This rule ensures team discipline and structure while preventing unfair advantages.
pg032_n0008: A player must not take more than one step while holding the ball.
pg032_n0009: If a player lands on one foot when catching the ball, can pivot but must release the ball before lifting the landing foot.
pg032_n0010: If a player lands on both feet simultaneously, may choose one foot to pivot while keeping the other grounded.
pg032_n0011: Taking extra steps results in a footwork infringement, causing possession to be handed to the opposing team.
pg032_n0015: When the ball goes out of court, the team that did not touch the ball last is awarded a throw-in which is taken from the point where the ball crossed the boundary line.
pg032_n0016: The player taking the throw-in must have at least one foot close to and touching the line, and must release the ball within three seconds.
pg032_n0017: A free pass is awarded for minor infractions, such as offside and over-a-third violations or footwork errors.
pg032_n0018: The player taking the pass must stand still before throwing the ball to a teammate.
pg032_n0022: A penalty in netball is a sanction awarded for serious rule infringements.
pg032_n0023: For instance, a penalty pass is given when a player commits a major foul, such as obstruction or contact.
pg032_n0024: Meanwhile, a sanction refers to the action taken by an umpire in response to an infringement committed by a player, team official, or bench player.
pg032_n0025: The penalised player must stand out of play until the pass is taken.
pg032_n0026: Additionally, if a player holds the ball for more than three seconds, the opposing team is awarded a free pass for a “held ball” violation.
pg032_n0027: Umpires may also issue warnings or suspensions for repeated rule-breaking or unsporting behaviour.

pg036_n0008: Field events is a sport focusing on jumping and throwing activities.
pg036_n0009: It is performed by male and female individuals for recreation or competition.
pg036_n0010: Engaging in field events provides employment opportunities, enhances physical health, and helps players to develop essential life skills.
pg036_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn the concept, safety measures, skills, and rules of field events.
pg036_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to analyze and perform the various field events skillfully and confidently.
pg036_n0020: Field events is a sport that encompasses athletic activities conducted on the field as opposed to track events.
pg036_n0021: The activities are classified into two categories: throwing events and jumping events.
pg036_n0022: The jumping events include long jump, triple jump, high jump, and pole vault while throwing events consist of the shot put, discus throw, and javelin throw.
pg036_n0023: These events can be organised as competitive sport or recreational activities, and are integral to major athletic competitions such as the Olympics, World Championships, and regional meets.
pg036_n0024: When organised as a competition, field events assess an athlete’s strength, technique, and coordination, highlighting their ability to propel themselves or an object across a measured distance.
pg037_n0005: Throwing in athletics are field events in which athletes propel an object as far as possible.
pg037_n0006: The sport requires strength, technique, and coordination.
pg037_n0007: The main types of throwing events include javelin throw, discus throw and shot put.
pg037_n0008: In organised throwing events, winners are awarded medals and other ancillary prizes including cash.
pg037_n0009: The known medals are gold medal for the first winner, silver for the second winner and bronze for the third winner.
pg037_n0013: Safety measures play a crucial role in throwing events, helping to prevent athletes and spectators from sustaining injuries during performance.
pg037_n0014: Both athletes and officials must prioritise safety by ensuring proper execution of movements and maintaining facilities and equipment.
pg037_n0015: The key safety precautions to be observed before, during and after throwing events include:
pg037_n0019: Perform warm-up exercises before, and cool-down exercises after workouts;
pg037_n0022: Ensure the throwing area is clean by removing any objects that could pose injury risks to athletes and spectators;
pg037_n0025: Ensure that protective barriers, such as throwing cages, are set to control throwing direction and prevent the implement from flying into athletes, officials or spectators that might cause injury;
pg037_n0028: Maintain all equipment and throwing implements in good condition, ensuring they meet the appropriate weight and size requirements based on the athletes’ age and physical maturity;
pg037_n0031: Prepare a fully equipped first aid kit, containing all necessary medical supplies for providing first aid during training and competitions;
pg037_n0034: Ensure that all athletes use proper movement techniques during training and competitions to minimize the risk of injury; and
pg037_n0037: Ensure your body stays hydrated by consuming appropriate fluids, including water to prevent dehydration.

pg038_n0005: The javelin throw is a field event in which athletes propel a javelin as far as possible in a designated direction.
pg038_n0006: This section covers the fundamental techniques, rules, and regulations of the javelin throw, helping you to develop the necessary skills for performing the javelin throw.
pg038_n0008: Facilities and equipment for javelin throw
pg038_n0010: The facilities and equipment in the javelin throw include a throwing area, measuring tape, flags, javelin, markers, wind indicators, and score and display boards.
pg038_n0014: A javelin throwing area consists of a runway, throwing arc, foul line and landing sector, Figure 2.1.
pg038_n0015: The runway has a length and width of 36.5 m and 4 m respectively.
pg038_n0016: The landing sector has an angle of 29° from the end of the runway and a width of 25 m.
pg038_im001: Diagram of a javelin throwing area showing a 36.5 m runway that is 4 m wide, leading to a 70 mm throwing arc and a landing sector about 100 m long, 25 m wide at the far end, with a 29° sector angle.
pg039_n0005: The javelin is a spear-shaped object constructed from metal, fibreglass, carbon fibre, or wood.
pg039_n0006: Its total length and weight range from 2.2 m to 2.7 m and 500 g to 800 g, respectively, depending on the gender and age of the athletes.
pg039_n0007: As illustrated in Figure 2.2, the primary parts of the javelin include the shaft, metal tip, and grip.
pg039_im001: Labeled diagram of a javelin showing the shaft, grip, metal head, and tip.
pg039_n0013: Go through internet and other relevant sources to identify length and weight of javelin according to age and sex of the athlete.
pg039_n0017: Throwing a javelin requires a combination of technical, physical, and mental skills, including gripping and throwing.
pg039_n0021: Gripping refers to the holding of a javelin during the throw.
pg039_n0022: The grip is crucial because it affects the control, stability, and power transferred to the javelin during the throw.
pg039_n0023: A proper grip ensures that the javelin is released smoothly and with the right amount of force and angle for maximum distance.
pg039_n0024: There are various gripping types including: American grip, Finnish grip and V-grip.
pg039_n0028: This is a gripping technique in which the index finger is placed on top at the edge of the cord, and the thumb beneath.
pg039_n0029: The middle and ring fingers support the javelin, Figure 2.3.
pg039_n0030: The javelin is held above the shoulder, ready for a sharp, whipping motion as it is thrown.
pg039_n0031: This grip allows for a more controlled release, often used to add spin or additional distance through wrist rotation.
pg040_im001: American grip on a javelin, with the fingers wrapped around the corded shaft and the thumb supporting underneath.
pg040_n0007: In this grip, the index finger is placed along the top of the javelin, and the thumb is underneath, creating a more secure grip.
pg040_n0008: The remaining fingers are wrapped around the shaft, Figure 2.4.
pg040_n0009: This grip is used when the javelin is raised slightly higher with the wrist cocked.
pg040_n0010: The grip produces a more powerful throw by generating more wrist snaps and control during the release.
pg040_im002: Finnish grip on a javelin, with the index finger extended along the top of the shaft, the thumb underneath, and the other fingers wrapped around the grip.
pg040_n0016: The V-grip is a gripping technique where the thrower holds the javelin between the index and middle fingers, forming a ‘V’ shape, as shown in Figure 2.5.
pg040_n0017: This grip provides a secure hold, allowing for better control and a balanced release, which helps to achieve greater distance.
pg040_im003: V-grip on a javelin, with the shaft held between the index and middle fingers while the remaining fingers and thumb support the grip.
pg041_n0005: Practice American grip, Finnish grip and V-grip repetitively and choose the best gripping type for you.
pg041_n0009: Throwing in javelin refers to the act of propelling the implement through the air to the landing sector.
pg041_n0010: A successful throw requires a combination of speed, technique, and strength.
pg041_n0011: It involves a sequence of coordinated movements, including a controlled approach run, a powerful impulse step, and an explosive throwing motion, followed by a proper follow-through to ensure maximum distance and accuracy.
pg041_n0012: The objective is to throw the javelin as far as possible while adhering to the official rules of the sport.
pg041_n0013: The following are the steps for throwing a javelin;
pg041_n0017: Hold the javelin at the grip (corded section) using one of the three techniques: Finish, American, or V-grip;
pg041_n0020: Stand tall with the javelin pointing slightly upward and begin running and increase speed while keeping the javelin steady;
pg041_n0023: Use crossover strides in the final steps to prepare for the throw, with the last two steps being longer;
pg041_n0026: Plant your front foot firmly while keeping your back foot slightly bent, rotating your hips and shoulders forward, and keeping the throwing arm extended back;
pg041_n0029: Launch the javelin using a fast arm whip motion, snapping the wrist at the release to create a smooth flight, Figure 2.6; and
pg041_n0032: Continue moving forward after the throw, maintaining balance while remaining in the throwing area until the javelin lands.
pg041_im001: Four-step sequence of a javelin throw showing the athlete releasing the javelin overhead, driving the body forward, and completing the follow-through.
pg042_n0005: Perform javelin throwing in walking and running stances.
pg042_n0007: Rules and regulations for javelin throw
pg042_n0009: The following are some of the rules for javelin throw:
pg042_n0013: The javelin must meet specific dimensions and weight requirements as per age and sex;
pg042_n0016: Athletes must hold the javelin by its corded grip and throw it over the shoulder or upper part of the throwing arm;
pg042_n0019: Throws must be executed within the designated throwing arc at the end of the runway;
pg042_n0022: The javelin’s metal head must strike the ground first within the marked sector lines;
pg042_n0025: The javelin must land within a landing sector for the throw to be considered valid;
pg042_n0028: Athletes have 30 seconds to complete their throws after their name is called; and
pg042_n0031: A throw is considered a foul if the athlete steps over the runway’s boundary lines, the javelin lands outside the sector lines, or if the throw is not completed within the allotted time.

pg042_n0043: Shot put is a field event that involves propelling a heavy, spherical metal ball using a pushing motion.
pg042_n0044: The throw begins from a position close to the chin or neck and requires a controlled, forceful movement.
pg042_n0045: The primary goal in the shot put is to achieve the maximum distance possible while staying within the designated throwing area.
pg042_n0046: The athlete who propels the shot the furthest from the starting point is declared the winner.
pg043_n0003: Facilities and equipment for shot put
pg043_n0005: Shot put requires specific facilities and equipment for performance and athletes’ safety.
pg043_n0006: It includes the shot put area, shot, carbonate powder such as magnesium and specialised gear for the athletes.
pg043_n0010: The shot put area includes a throwing circle, a stop board, and a landing sector as shown in Figure 2.7.
pg043_n0011: The throwing circle has a diameter of 2.135 m, while the stop-board stands 10 cm high.
pg043_n0012: The landing sector spans approximately 35 degrees from the centre of the throwing circle.
pg043_im001: Diagram of a shot put area showing a 2.135 m throwing circle with a 10 cm high stop board, foul line, 75 cm wide dividing line, 50 mm line marking, and two 25 m sector lines forming a 34.92 degree landing sector from the centre of the circle.
pg044_n0003: The equipment used in the shot put event includes the shot, spike, recording sheet, towel, broom, flags (white and red), stopwatch, tape measure, and stop board.
pg044_n0007: The shot is a heavy spherical object used in the shot put event, Figure 2.8.
pg044_n0008: The object is made of metal such as iron or brass and varies in weight depending on the competition category.
pg044_n0009: While men’s shots are as heavy as 7.26 kg, women’s shots are 4 kg.
pg044_n0010: Notwithstanding, youth and junior weight categories are lighter depending on the age group.
pg044_im001: Metal shot used in the shot put event
pg044_n0016: The main objective of putting the shot is to propel the it as far as possible.
pg044_n0017: Achieving this requires the thrower to possess essential skills for throwing the shot over long distances.
pg044_n0018: These fundamental skills include gripping the shot, shot placement, and putting the shot.
pg044_n0022: This is the action of holding the shot.
pg044_n0024: To grip the shot properly, follow these steps:
pg044_n0028: Rest the shot on the base of the fingers as shown in Figure 2.9;
pg044_n0031: Position the thumb and little fingers opposite the index, middle and ring fingers slightly separate; and
pg044_n0034: Keep the shot on the base of the fingers, it should not touch the palm to allow for better control and a smooth pushing action.
pg045_im001: Hand gripping a shot put with the ball resting on the base of the fingers and supported by the thumb.
pg045_n0007: Placement is the positioning of the shot near the shot putter’s chin.
pg045_n0008: An athlete positions the shot under the jawline, close to the neck.
pg045_n0009: The following steps will help you execute a shot placement:
pg045_n0013: Rest the shot comfortably at the base of the fingers;
pg045_n0016: Press the shot against the hollow base of the neck, just beneath the jaw;
pg045_n0019: Keep your palm facing upward and your thumb pointing downward; and
pg045_n0022: Keep your elbow high, at shoulder level, and parallel to the ground, as shown in Figure 2.10
pg045_im002: Athlete positioning the shot beneath the jaw close to the neck, with the elbow raised at shoulder level.
pg046_n0005: Practice shot gripping and placement repetitively until you master the skills.
pg046_n0009: Putting the shot refers to the pushing of a heavy metal ball from the shoulder using one hand.
pg046_n0010: There are two fundamental techniques for putting the shot: the linear technique and the rotational technique.
pg046_n0014: The linear technique is also known as glide technique, involves the shot putter moving in a straight line from the starting position to the centre of the circle.
pg046_n0015: The following are the steps for putting shot by linear technique:
pg046_n0019: Stand at the back of the circle with your back facing the throwing direction;
pg046_n0022: Squat slightly with shot placed against the neck supported by fingers;
pg046_n0025: Shift your weight onto the rear leg while torso relaxed;
pg046_n0028: Drive back with your rear leg, pushing off the toe, keeping hips low and rear leg land approximately in the centre pointing slightly to the front.
pg046_n0031: As rear leg land in the centre, place the front leg at the back of the circle, slightly open to the front.
pg046_n0034: Turn hips and shoulders toward the throwing sector upon reaching the front of the circle;
pg046_n0037: Push the shot explosively forward and upward while engaging the core as shown in Figure 2.11; and
pg046_n0040: Quickly bring the rear leg forward to prevent fouling and remain inside the circle until the shot lands.
pg046_im001: Sequence of a shot put athlete performing the linear glide technique: crouched start at the back of the circle, shot held against the neck, glide forward, upward release of the shot, and balanced recovery inside the circle.
pg046_n0047: Figure 2.11: Putting the shot by liner technique
pg047_n0006: Practice putting the shot using linear technique repetitively until you master it.
pg047_n0010: The rotational technique (also called spin) is a method of putting a shot where the athlete spins inside the circle to generate more speed and power, allowing for a longer throw.
pg047_n0011: The following are the steps for putting the shot by rotational technique.
pg047_n0015: Stand facing the back of the circle with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and the shot placed against the neck with proper hand positioning;
pg047_n0018: Initiate a spinning motion by turning on the ball of the non-throwing foot, rotating the body across the circle;
pg047_n0021: Land at the front of the circle with hips and shoulders squared generating force for the push by the rear leg;
pg047_n0024: Thrust the shot forward with an upward angle using full body rotation to increase distance; and
pg047_n0027: Quickly bring the rear leg forward to prevent fouling and remain inside the circle until the shot lands, Figure 2.12.
pg047_im001: Sequence of an athlete performing the rotational shot put technique: crouched start, spinning across the circle, driving upward to release the shot, and bringing the rear leg through to balance after the throw.
pg047_n0036: Figure 2.12: Putting the shot by rotational technique
pg047_n0041: Practice putting the shot using rotational technique repetitively until you master it.
pg047_n0043: Basic rules and regulations for shot put
pg047_n0045: The following are some of the rules for shot put:
pg047_n0049: The shot shall be put from the shoulder with one hand.
pg047_n0050: At the time an athlete takes a stance in a circle to commence a put, the shot shall not touch the neck;
pg048_n0005: The stop board shall be white and made of wood or suitable materials in the shape of an arc so that the inner surface aligns with the inner edge of the rim;
pg048_n0008: The stop board shall measure 11.2 cm wide, with a chord of 123 cm for the arc of the same radius as the circle and 10 cm high from the level of the inside of the circle adjacent to the stop board;
pg048_n0011: The shot shall be solid iron, brass or any metal not softer than brass or a shell of such metal filled with lead or other solid materials; and
pg048_n0014: The shot shall conform to the following specifications in weight and diameter as shown in Table 2.1.

pg048_n0071: Discus throw is a field event in which an athlete throws a heavy, plate-shaped implement (the discus) from within a marked circle to as far a distance as possible.
pg048_n0072: The winner is a thrower who throws a discus to the longest distance starting from the throwing circle.
pg048_n0076: Discus throwing requires facilities such as the throwing area and measurement tools.
pg048_n0077: It also requires some equipment including the discus, shoes, chalk, stopwatch, flags (white and red), and recording sheet.
pg049_n0005: The throwing area for discus consists of the throwing circle, cage and landing zone, also called the sector area.
pg049_n0006: The throwing circle is an area where players take a start and complete the throw.
pg049_n0007: The diameter of the throwing circle is 2.5 m.
pg049_n0008: The cage is a U-shaped netted or metal fenced to prevent errant throws from injuring officials, spectators and other athletes.
pg049_n0009: The landing zone, is an area marked by two lines forming an angle of 34.92 degrees from the centre of the circle, where the discus lands, Figure 2.13.
pg049_im001: Diagram of a discus throwing area showing a 2.5 m diameter throwing circle, 50 mm white boundary lines, a 34.92 degree landing sector, a 6 m cage opening, 5 m side fencing, and a minimum 3 m protective cage around the circle.
pg049_n0015: The major discus throwing equipment is a discus.
pg049_n0016: It is a plate-like implement made from various materials such as rubber, wood and metals.
pg049_n0017: The diameter and weight of the discus for women and men are 18 cm and 1 kg, and 22 cm and 2 kg, respectively.
pg049_n0018: The shape of the discus is circular often paired with a case that protects it from damage, Figure 2.14.
pg050_im001: Red discus with a silver metal rim and central plate.
pg050_n0005: Other supporting equipment includes a tape measure for measuring the length of the discus throw; flags used to signal a valid or invalid throw, and a recording sheet for keeping scores and other details of the thrower.
pg050_n0009: The discus throwers aim to throw the discus effectively as far as possible.
pg050_n0010: The following are the fundamental skills for discus throw.
pg050_n0014: Gripping the discus is the act of holding the implement in a proper position.
pg050_n0015: Gripping influences the way the discus is released and the direction in which it is thrown.
pg050_n0016: The following are steps for gripping the discus:
pg050_n0020: Hold the discus on your non-throwing hand for support;
pg050_n0023: Place your throwing hand on top of the discus;
pg050_n0026: Spread evenly your fingers on the rim of the discus;
pg050_n0029: Hold the discus properly at the first joint of your fingers resting the first knuckle over the rim;
pg050_n0032: Place your fingertips firmly over the discus ensuring most of the pressure being applied by the fingers, not the palm; and
pg050_n0035: Keep your wrist straight and relaxed as shown in Figure 2.15 (a, b and c).
pg050_im002_seg001_v1: Front view of a hand supporting a discus from below, with the fingers spread along the rim.
pg050_im002_seg002_v1: Back view of a hand gripping the discus, with the fingers spread around the rim and the thumb resting across the face.
pg050_im002_seg003_v1: Side view of a hand holding the discus vertically at the fingertips with the wrist straight.
pg051_n0004: Practice gripping the discus repetitively until you master the skill.
pg051_n0008: Throwing the discus is the propelling of the implement in the proper direction with correct body movements.
pg051_n0009: It starts from the discus thrower’s stance to the release of the discus.
pg051_n0010: The following steps will help you throw the discus:
pg051_n0014: Place the discus in your throwing hand with your fingers spread evenly along the rim;
pg051_n0017: Stand at the back of the throwing circle with your feet shoulder-width apart, facing away from the direction of the throw;
pg051_n0020: Rotate your upper body while extending the discus arm backwards, keeping your non-throwing arm extended forward for balance;
pg051_n0023: Turn your body by shifting weight onto your dominant leg, engaging your core to generate rotational momentum while staying low and balanced;
pg051_n0026: Plant your non-dominant foot first as you near the front of the circle, pulling your throwing hand back, ready to release;
pg051_n0029: Extend your throwing arm forward while rotating your wrist for a smooth spin, aiming for a high, flat trajectory for maximum distance, Figure 2.16; and
pg051_n0032: Continue the motion forward after release to maintain balance, keeping your eyes on the discus, and stay in the circle until the discus lands.
pg051_im001: Sequence of a discus thrower demonstrating the throwing technique: starting with the discus arm extended back, turning and stepping through the circle, rotating the body to release the discus, and finishing with a balanced follow-through.
pg051_n0044: Practice throwing the discus repetitively until you master the skill.
pg052_n0006: Rules and regulations for discus throw
pg052_n0008: The following are some rules and regulations for discus throw:
pg052_n0012: Men’s and women’s discus shall be 2 kg and 22 cm, and 1 kg and 18 cm in weight and diameter respectively;
pg052_n0015: The thrower shall commence throw from a stationary position within the circle and may place the discus inside the circle or outside the circle;
pg052_n0018: The thrower shall not leave the circle till the discus has landed in the sector;
pg052_n0021: The chief judge shall control the whole event supported by two judges; one for checking legal throws, the other judge shall act as a recorder, in-charge of throwers and standards; and
pg052_n0024: All discus throws shall be within the cage enclosure for the safety of the participants.
pg052_n0028: Practice discus throws repetitively until you master the skill adhering to its rules and regulations.

pg052_n0037: Jumping in athletics involves athletes propelling themselves off the ground to achieve a maximum distance or height.
pg052_n0038: There are four main jumping events in athletics: long jump, triple jump, high jump, and pole vault.
pg052_n0039: These events are categorised into horizontal jumps, which focus on covering distance, and vertical jumps, which focus on height.
pg052_n0043: Jumping events require athletes and officials to follow essential safety precautions before and during competitions.
pg052_n0048: Ensuring all equipment used are appropriate and in good condition;
pg053_n0005: Wearing clean, properly fitted footwear and attire;
pg053_n0008: Inspecting the landing and run-up areas before the event and removing any objects that could pose a risk of injury to jumpers;
pg053_n0011: Performing warm-up exercises before the event and cool-down exercises afterwards; and
pg053_n0014: Preparing a first aid kit with all necessary medical supplies.
pg053_n0018: Horizontal jumps require the athlete to jump as far as possible from a take-off board into a sandpit.
pg053_n0019: Horizontal jumping events include long jump and triple jump.
pg053_n0023: A long jump is a horizontal jumping event in which an athlete attempts to cover the greatest distance possible from the take-off board to the landing point.
pg053_n0027: The long jump requires a long jump facility, also called a long jump area and a variety of equipment such as measuring tapes, marking devices, and maintenance tools.
pg053_n0028: Proper facility setup and the right equipment contribute to accurate measurements, athlete’s consistency, and overall event efficiency.
pg053_n0032: The jumping area for the long jump consists of three key components: the runway, take-off board, and landing area as shown in Figure 2.17.
pg053_im001: Diagram of a long jump area showing the runway leading to the take-off board, a red foul line at the board, and the landing area beyond it.
pg053_n0038: The runway must be at least 40 metres long and 1.22 m wide.
pg053_n0039: It is measured from the start of the runway to the take-off board and is marked with white lines or broken lines measuring 0.05 m wide, 0.10 m long, and spaced 0.50 m apart.
pg054_n0005: The take-off board is a white rectangular board measuring 1.22 m in length, 0.20 m in width, and at most 0.10 m in depth.
pg054_n0006: It must be level with the surface of the runway to ensure a smooth transition for athletes.
pg054_n0010: The landing area is about 7 m to 9 m long, depending on the distance from the take-off board.
pg054_n0011: It is 2.75 m wide, with an optimal setup being 8 m in length and positioned 1m from the take-off board.
pg054_n0012: The runway centre must align with the centre of the landing area.
pg054_n0016: There are various equipment required for long jump performance, as shown in Table 2.2.
pg054_im001: Plasticine indicator board for marking foul jumps in long jump.
pg054_n0030: Used to indicate foul jumps in major competitions.
pg054_im002: Reel tape measure used to measure long jump distance.
pg054_im003: Rake used to level the sand in the long jump landing area.
pg054_n0042: Level the sand in the landing area after each attempt.
pg055_im001: Broom used to clear sand from the runway.
pg055_im002: Shovel used to maintain and move sand in the landing area.
pg055_n0014: Helps to maintain and move sand in the landing area
pg055_im003: Orange markers used to mark different points in the long jump area.
pg055_n0020: Used to mark the different points of the long jump area
pg055_im004: Red, white, and yellow flags used to signal jump validity and warnings.
pg055_n0026: Red and white flags are used to signal the validity of a jump while yellow flag are used for warning.
pg055_im005: Take-off board marking the designated take-off point.
pg056_n0003: Other equipment includes a stopwatch, wind gauge and wind sock, spike, hand-brush, recording sheet, bucket/hose/watering cane.
pg056_n0005: Fundamental skills in the long jump
pg056_n0007: To achieve maximum jumping distance, an athlete must have the fundamental skills of the long jump.
pg056_n0008: Since it is a speed-based event, jumpers must be proficient in four fundamental skills, which are approach run, take-off, flight, and landing.
pg056_n0012: The approach run is vital for building momentum and ensuring precise placement on the take-off board.
pg056_n0013: A well-coordinated approach run helps jumpers gain speed while maintaining control and accuracy for take-off.
pg056_n0014: The following steps will help you practice the approach run:
pg056_n0018: From the long jump-starting position, start your run with your take-off foot forward and build up speed gradually as shown in Figure 2.18;
pg056_n0021: Maintain your head in a natural position;
pg056_n0024: Look forward all the time while keeping your back flat;
pg056_n0027: Extend your take-off leg and place the thigh of the non-take-off foot in a good position; and
pg056_n0030: Ensure the last two strides are long enough to prepare you for take-off.
pg056_im001: Long jumper in a forward-leaning sprint position during the approach run, with one knee lifted and arms driving.
pg056_n0036: The take-off begins in the later phase of the approach run.
pg056_n0037: During the last two strides of the approach run, the athlete sinks and raises their hips into the take-off point.
pg056_n0038: The following steps will help you execute a take-off:
pg057_n0005: Drive forcefully through the ankle, knee, and hip to propel upwards and forward;
pg057_n0008: Make sure the take-off foot strikes the take-off board on the midline during take-off, Figure 2.19;
pg057_n0011: Ensure the heel of the take-off foot strikes first to allow a rolling action onto the ball and then the toes of the foot to give maximum vertical lift;
pg057_n0014: Strongly push the take-off foot using your toes; and
pg057_n0017: Increase the vertical acceleration by arms and the non-take-off leg.
pg057_im001: Long jumper in the take-off phase, pushing off one foot with the opposite knee lifted high and one arm reaching upward.
pg057_n0023: The flight occurs after the take-off.
pg057_n0024: It is a body transfer from the take-off point to the landing point maintaining balance, maximising distance, and preparing for a smooth landing.
pg057_n0025: Since the athlete cannot generate additional momentum in the air, the goal is to control body posture and minimise forward rotation to achieve an optimal landing position.
pg057_n0026: The following steps will help you execute a flight:
pg057_n0030: Raise the non-take-off leg to a horizontal position during take-off;
pg057_n0033: Keep hands above shoulder level, Figure 2.20;
pg057_n0036: Keep your trunk in an upright position to facilitate the up movement of your leg during landing; and
pg057_n0039: Maintain the perfect alignment between your head, back and hips.
pg058_im001_crop_v1: Two views of a long jumper in flight, showing balanced airborne body positions with arms raised to control movement before landing.
pg058_n0007: The flight is essential for maintaining control and maximising distance.
pg058_n0008: There are three main techniques that athletes use to stay balanced in the air and prepare for landing.
pg058_n0009: These techniques are the stride, hang and the hitch-kick.
pg058_n0013: The stride technique involves maintaining the take-off position until landing, where the take-off leg joins the free leg to achieve a proper landing position, as shown in Figure 2.21.
pg058_n0014: The athlete raises the take-off leg and remains in the air until the non-take-off leg joins, allowing for a controlled and effective landing.
pg058_im002: Sequence of the long jump stride technique, from take-off with one knee lifted, through running-style flight in the air, to legs extended forward for landing in the sand.
pg058_n0028: This is a flight technique where the athlete remains hanging in the air before landing.
pg058_n0029: The following steps will help you execute an efficient flight:
pg059_n0005: Push off forcefully from the take-off board;
pg059_n0008: Extend and bring back the leading leg that was initially bent and pushed upwards to join the take-off leg;
pg059_n0011: Thrust both legs to the rear of the body in the extended positions;
pg059_n0014: Circle the arm downward, backward and then upward and forward, Figure 2.22;
pg059_n0017: Flex your leg and thrust it forward and as they extend for landing, move the arms circle forward; and
pg059_n0020: As you land in the sand, flex your leg at the knees and move the upper body forward and over the feet.
pg059_im001: Sequence of the long jump hang technique, showing the athlete running up, taking off, hanging in the air with arms raised and legs extended back, then bringing the legs forward to land in the sand.
pg059_n0035: The hitch-kick technique is a flight style used to maintain balance, counteract forward rotation, and maximise jump distance.
pg059_n0036: This technique involves a cyclical leg motion in the air, providing greater control and efficiency during the flight phase, Figure 2.23.
pg059_n0037: The following steps will help you execute a hitch-kick technique:
pg059_n0041: Drive up powerfully at take-off after a fast run-up;
pg059_n0044: Stretch the front leg forward as if you are running in the air;
pg059_n0047: Swing the extended leg backward while keeping it straight;
pg059_n0050: Flex and bring forward both legs for the landing; and
pg059_n0053: Rotate the arms forward and then backwards, balancing the action of the legs and assisting in thrusting forward during landing.
pg060_im001: Sequence of a long jumper performing the hitch-kick technique, moving from take-off through running-style leg action in the air to forward landing in the sand.
pg060_n0018: Landing involves taking heels as far away as possible from the take-off board.
pg060_n0019: Proper landing maximises distance and ensures a safe, controlled finish.
pg060_n0020: A well-executed landing helps athletes avoid losing distance by falling backwards or placing their hands behind them in the sand as shown in Figure 2.24.
pg060_n0021: The following steps will help you practice landing:
pg060_n0025: Keep the body upright and head looking forward;
pg060_n0028: Move arms down and backward to assist the upward movement of the legs; and
pg060_n0031: Keep arms in a forward position until landing is complete.
pg060_im002: Step-by-step long jump landing technique showing the athlete bringing the arms down and back, extending the legs forward, and finishing in a controlled seated landing without falling backward.
pg060_n0041: The long jump event follows specific rules and regulations to ensure fair competition.
pg060_n0042: The following are some of the rules:
pg060_n0046: Athletes must take off from the take-off board without stepping beyond its front edge;
pg061_n0005: The jump is measured from the nearest mark made in the sand by any body part from the front edge of the take-off board;
pg061_n0008: If the athlete takes off before the take-off board, then the jump shall be measured from the break in the sand to the front edge of the take-off board;
pg061_n0011: The athlete must land within the designated landing pit;
pg061_n0014: A valid attempt must be completed within 30 seconds after being called to jump;
pg061_n0017: In standard competitions, each athlete is given three to six attempts, depending on the level of competition;
pg061_n0020: If there is a tie, the athlete with the second-best jump is ranked higher; and
pg061_n0023: After landing, the jumper must exit the pit from the front or sides to avoid shortening the measured distance.
pg061_n0029: Construct a long jump area and mark the key parts.
pg061_n0032: Practice the various flight techniques employed in the long jump.
