pg061_n0044: The triple jump is one of the jumping events whereby the athletes attempt to leap as far as possible from the take-off point after three successive jumps called hop, step and jump.
pg061_n0045: The three jump rhythms are either right-right-left or left-left-right.
pg061_n0049: The equipment required for the triple jump is the same as those described in the long jump.
pg061_n0050: The triple jump requires a jumping area and a variety of equipment such as tape measures, marking devices, and maintenance tools.
pg061_n0051: Proper facility setup and the right equipment contribute to accurate measurements, athlete’s consistency, and overall event efficiency.
pg062_n0005: The triple jump area consists of a run-way, take-off board and landing area, Figure 2.26.
pg062_n0009: This is a space set for an athlete to prepare for jumping.
pg062_n0010: The length and width of the runway are 40 m and 1.22 m respectively, and are marked with white lines which are 5 cm wide.
pg062_n0014: The take-off board is placed 13 m from the landing area.
pg062_n0015: The distance between take-off board and the landing area ranges from 9 m to 13 m based on the age and gender of the athlete.
pg062_n0019: The length and width of the landing area are 10 m and 2.74 m – 3.0 m respectively.
pg062_n0020: The landing area is filled with soft damp sand.
pg062_im001: Top view of a triple jump area showing a long runway with marked take-off boards leading to a rectangular sand landing pit.
pg062_n0022: Figure 2.25: Jumping area in the triple jump
pg062_n0026: Mastery of triple jump skills enables athletes to achieve maximum jumping distance.
pg062_n0027: The fundamental skills for performing triple jump are the approach run, take-off, three successive jumps, flight and landing.
pg062_n0028: These skills are usually expressed as triple jump phases.
pg062_n0032: The main objective of the approach run is to create the greatest amount of speed for successful jump.
pg062_n0033: The optimal run-up distance and speed depend on the athlete’s strength and technique.
pg062_n0034: Use the following steps for executing the approach run:
pg062_n0038: From the starting position, run fast beginning with take-off foot forward, Figure 2.26;
pg063_n0005: Keep your head upright in a natural position, look forward all the time;
pg063_n0008: Stretch your take-off leg forward and raise the other knee slightly to prepare for the hop; and
pg063_n0011: Land your take-off leg on the ground ready for the take-off.
pg063_im001: Athlete in mid-stride during the triple jump approach run, leaning forward with one knee lifted and arms driving.
pg063_n0013: Figure 2.26: The approach run in triple jump
pg063_n0017: The take-off occurs during the final phase of the approach run.
pg063_n0018: Follow these steps to execute a successful take-off:
pg063_n0022: Slightly bend your take-off leg and strike the board with a quick, firm motion;
pg063_n0025: Propel your body forward by extending your free leg;
pg063_n0028: Place your take-off foot flat on the take-off board;
pg063_n0031: Swing your free leg’s thigh horizontally; and
pg063_n0034: Bend the knee at a sharp angle, Figure 2.27.
pg063_im002: Front view of a triple jumper taking off from the board with one foot planted and the opposite knee bent sharply upward.
pg064_n0005: The three successive jumps are hop, step and jump.
pg064_n0006: These jumps occur in a specific order after the athlete takes off from the take-off board.
pg064_n0010: In the first jump, the athlete takes off from one foot at the take-off board and lands on the same foot on the runway.
pg064_n0011: Follow these steps to execute the hop effectively:
pg064_n0015: Actively plant the take-off foot on the ground before initiating take-off;
pg064_n0018: Drive the take-off leg forward and upward;
pg064_n0021: Swing the free leg’s thigh parallel to the ground;
pg064_n0024: Extend the free leg fully while reaching and executing a pawing action during landing;
pg064_n0027: Bring up the take-off leg toward your buttock, then move it forward and downward;
pg064_n0030: Maintain an upright trunk, keep your head still, and focus your eyes forward; and
pg064_n0033: Push backward slightly with your foot during landing to stay stable and prepare for the next jump, Figure 2.28.
pg064_im001: Six-position sequence of an athlete performing the hop phase of the triple jump, showing take-off from one foot, forward leg drive, upright body posture, and landing on the same foot to prepare for the next phase.
pg064_n0045: In this stage, the athlete lands on the opposite foot on the runway.
pg064_n0046: Follow these steps to execute the step effectively:
pg064_n0050: Extend your ankle, knee, and hip to generate a quick take-off;
pg064_n0053: Maintain the take-off position to prepare for the jump;
pg064_n0056: Keep the free leg’s thigh parallel to the ground, then extend the foot forward until it is nearly fully stretched from the hip;
pg065_n0004: (iv) Land with the free leg approximately in front of your centre of gravity;
pg065_n0006: (v) Swing both arms backwards, keeping them close to the body during the second half of the flight; and
pg065_n0008: (vi) Maintain an upright upper body and keep your eyes looking forward, Figure 2.29.
pg065_im001: Sequence of the step phase in triple jump, showing the athlete driving one knee forward, swinging the arms, landing with the free leg in front of the body, and maintaining an upright posture.
pg065_n0022: The jump is the final stage of the triple jump, following the hop and step.
pg065_n0023: Follow these steps to execute the jump effectively:
pg065_n0026: (i) Swing up quickly the take-off foot to the horizontal position;
pg065_n0028: (ii) Stretch the body with arms above the shoulders; and
pg065_n0030: (iii) Bring the arms forward and down while legs forward and up to prepare for the landing, Figure 2.30.
pg065_im002: Sequence of the jump phase in triple jump, showing the athlete taking off, lifting the take-off leg to horizontal, extending the body with the arms up, then bringing the arms and legs forward to prepare for landing.
pg065_n0043: The flight is the airborne stage that carries the athlete from the jump stage to landing.
pg065_n0044: The key objective is to adopt a position in the air that allows for an efficient transfer
pg066_n0004: While on the flight, the athlete can adopt the stride, hang, or hitch-kick jumping styles.
pg066_n0005: Follow these steps to execute the flight effectively:
pg066_n0009: Fully extend both legs forward as you jump;
pg066_n0012: Raise your arms high above your head, allowing them to swing downward before landing in the sandpit;
pg066_n0015: Maintain a low take-off angle; and
pg066_n0018: Keep your trunk upright to support the upward movement of your legs, Figure 2.31.
pg066_im001: Triple jumper in the flight phase above the sandpit, arms stretched overhead and one leg extended forward, with a distance scale marked from 14 to 17 metres beside the runway.
pg066_n0024: Landing in the triple jump is crucial for maximising the distance and ensuring a smooth finish.
pg066_n0025: Follow these steps to execute an effective landing:
pg066_n0029: Swing your arms downward and backward to aid an upward movement;
pg066_n0032: Then keep your arms in a forward position until the landing is complete, Figure 2.32;
pg066_n0035: Bend your knees slightly to absorb the impact of landing; and
pg066_n0038: Keep your body leaning forward slightly throughout the landing.
pg067_im001_seg003_v1: Triple jump landing phase a: athlete descending with arms stretched overhead and knees bent, preparing to land.
pg067_im001_seg002_v1: Triple jump landing phase b: athlete in mid-air with legs extended forward and arms reaching toward the feet.
pg067_im001_seg001_v1: Triple jump landing phase c: athlete landing in the sandpit in a deep squat with arms forward and sand kicking up at the feet.
pg067_n0012: Rules and regulations for triple jump
pg067_n0014: To ensure fairness and safety in triple jump competitions, athletes must follow specific rules and regulations.
pg067_n0015: Some of the rules that guide triple jump events are as follows:
pg067_n0018: 1. The triple jump consists of a hop, step, and jump, in that order;
pg067_n0020: 2. The hop lands on the same foot as take-off, and the step lands on the opposite foot, followed by the jump into the sandpit;
pg067_n0024: 4. The take-off foot must be on or before the take-off board;
pg067_n0026: 5. Markers are allowed beside the runway, but not on it or in the landing area;
pg067_n0028: 6. An attempt is invalid if the athlete:
pg067_n0033: (b) Takes off outside the board’s edges.
pg067_n0035: (c) Performs a somersault during the jump.
pg067_n0037: (d) Touches the runway or ground outside the landing area before landing.
pg067_n0039: (e) Loses control and lands outside the sandpit or too close to the take-off line
pg067_n0041: 7. The distance jumped shall be measured from the nearest imprint in the sand to the take-off board;
pg067_n0043: 8. If take-off is before the board, measurement shall be taken from the board’s front edge;
pg067_n0045: 9. The longest valid jump determines the winner; and
pg067_n0047: 10. Ties are broken by the next best jump.
pg068_n0004: Practice triple jump repetitively until you master the skills.

pg068_n0019: Vertical jumps include the high jump and pole vault.
pg068_n0020: These jumps require the athlete to jump as high as possible from the ground into a landing surface normally cushioned with sawdust, rice hull or mattresses.
pg068_n0024: The high jump is one of the field events where athletes attempt to jump high as much as possible to clear the bar.
pg068_n0025: Each jumper has three trials to clear the bar.
pg068_n0026: Depending on the event, the bar is raised for 3.8 or 5.1 cm for the next height after all jumpers have tried to clear the prior reading.
pg068_n0027: Only those who cleared the previous height qualify for the new height.
pg068_n0028: This process continues until the last jumper misses to clear the bar after making three trials.
pg068_n0032: High jump requires facilities and equipment such as the jumping area, and a variety of equipment including tape measures, marking devices and maintenance tools.
pg068_n0036: The jumping area is comprised of the semi-circular runway with a radius of either 15 m or 20 m and a landing area, Figure 2.33.
pg068_n0037: The runway allows an approach run for 15 m from any angle within a 180-degree arc.
pg068_n0038: The runway should have a similar level to the court.
pg069_im001: Plan view of a high jump jumping area with a semicircular runway marked in concentric arcs, a central runway approach, and a landing mat between two uprights. Labels show a 20 m minimum runway, 25 m radius, level area 10 m by 1 m, landing mat 6.0 m by 4.0 m, and widths of 3.0 m and 4.0 m near the approach.
pg069_n0003: Figure 2.33: Jumping area in high jump
pg069_n0005: Moreover, the length and width of the landing area are about 5 m and 3 m respectively.
pg069_n0006: The landing area can be covered by landing mats or other suitable materials or a pit cushioned by mattresses, sawdust or rice hull.
pg069_n0007: It is rectangular as shown in Figure 2.34.
pg069_im002: Front view of a high jump landing area with a large rectangular landing mat and two vertical uprights supporting a horizontal crossbar above it.
pg069_n0009: Figure 2.34: Landing area in high jump
pg069_n0013: The common equipment for the high jump is stands, a crossbar, landing bags, a measuring stick or tape, markers, flags, bloom, and restraining straps.
pg069_n0017: A stand comprises two vertical bars with an adjustable bracket for holding the crossbar, Figure 2.35.

pg071_n0005: The high jump requires a combination of physical, technical, and mental skills.
pg071_n0006: The skills include the approach run, the take-off, flight, bar clearance and landing.
pg071_n0010: The high jump approach run follows a J-shaped runway, as shown in Figure 2.36, consisting of a straight path for acceleration and a curved path for take-off preparation.
pg071_n0011: The goal is to build momentum and establish the correct take-off position.
pg071_n0012: The key steps for an effective approach run are:
pg071_n0016: Place the take-off foot forward and shift body weight slightly forward for a powerful start;
pg071_n0019: Take strong strides while swinging arms alternately with the legs to generate momentum;
pg071_n0022: Keep your head up and eyes on the turning point as you approach the curve;
pg071_n0025: As you move into the curve, lean your body slightly inward to turn smoothly;
pg071_n0028: In the last three strides, lower your hips and make the second-last stride a bit longer; and
pg071_n0031: Ensure a quick, explosive push-off for a take off.
pg071_im001: J-shaped high jump approach run showing a straight section into a curved path with alternating footprints leading to the take-off point beside the bar.
pg071_n0037: Take off is a transition of an athlete from approach run into the flight.
pg071_n0038: For a safe landing, the take-off point should be executed correctly to establish the ideal flight
pg072_n0003: path and ensure a safe landing.
pg072_n0004: It should be near the middle of the crossbar for proper height and clearance.
pg072_n0005: Follow these steps for a successful take-off:
pg072_n0009: Position the take-off foot correctly by placing it on the designated take-off mark, pointing toward the landing area, as shown in Figure 2.37;
pg072_n0012: Ensure proper foot placement on first contact: The take-off foot should land 2-3 foot lengths ahead of the hips and trunk, forming a 20 – 40-degree angle with the crossbar;
pg072_n0015: Lean away from the crossbar: Push the free leg forcefully upward while positioning your body in a “six o’clock” posture (legs down, upper body upright);
pg072_n0018: Stretch your arms upward: Keep your head upright while fully extending the take-off leg and foot;
pg072_n0021: Drive the non-take-off leg high: Raise the thigh to a horizontal position while swinging the arms upward to head level; and
pg072_n0024: Extend the body into vertical alignment: Ensure the lower body follows naturally into a fully extended take-off position for maximum height and stability.
pg072_im001: Three-stage high jump take-off: the athlete approaches, plants the take-off foot, then drives both arms upward and lifts the lead knee toward the crossbar beside the landing mat.
pg073_n0005: The flight occurs after take-off when the body is airborne, aiming to clear the bar.
pg073_n0006: Proper body positioning and control are crucial for a successful jump.
pg073_n0007: Follow these steps for an effective flight:
pg073_n0011: Raise your hips while keeping your head up to maintain balance and height;
pg073_n0014: Extend your arms to assist in body control and clearance;
pg073_n0017: Fully stretch the take-off leg as it passes over the bar; and
pg073_n0020: Drop the shoulders while lifting the hips to create an arching motion, allowing smooth clearance, Figure 2.38.
pg073_im001: Sequence of a high jump flight: the athlete runs in a curved approach, takes off, lifts one knee, then arches the back and hips to clear the crossbar before descending toward the landing mat.
pg073_n0030: In this phase, the athlete jumps up trying to pass over the crossbar, as shown in Figure 2.39, without dropping it.
pg073_n0031: The following steps will help you practice clearing the bar successfully:
pg073_n0035: Drive the knee up till the shoulder reaches the bar;
pg073_n0038: Extend the hips, lay body back towards the bar;
pg073_n0041: Flex the knee and drop below the bar;
pg073_n0044: Lift the hips while clearing the bar; and
pg073_n0047: When the hips clear the bar, pull the chin towards the chest and extend the legs to prevent heels from touching the bar.
pg074_im001: Sequence of a high jumper clearing the bar in the Fosbury flop style, showing take-off, back-first arch over the bar, hip clearance, and legs lifting through before landing on the mat.
pg074_n0007: Figure 2.39: Bar clearance in high jump
pg074_n0009: Bar clearance technique in high jump
pg074_n0011: There are five techniques jumpers employ in clearing the bar in the high jump.
pg074_n0012: The techniques include straddle, western roll, eastern cut-off with or without trunk layout, scissors and Fosbury flop.
pg074_n0013: However, this section will cover scissors and Fosbury flop.
pg074_n0017: This is the technique where the athlete clears the bar in a scissor shape mode.
pg074_n0018: In clearing the bar using this style, the jumper lands with feet first.
pg074_n0019: The following steps will help you practice the scissor bar clearance technique:
pg074_n0026: Accelerate for the last few strides;
pg074_n0029: Drive your leg near to and over the bar first;
pg074_n0032: Keep your hips up while running tall;
pg074_n0035: Lift your legs in a scissors motion over the bar;
pg074_n0038: Kick the leg close to the bar up in front of your body first, then follow the second leg; and
pg074_n0041: Land on your feet on the mat, Figure 2.40.
pg075_im001: Four sequential positions of an athlete performing the scissor high jump, taking off beside the upright, swinging one leg over the bar first, then the other, and leaning the torso across to clear the bar.
pg075_n0007: Figure 2.40: Scissor clearance in high jump
pg075_n0011: This is a bar clearance technique where the athlete runs from a straight line first and then twists the body on take-off and goes up head first with the back on the bar.
pg075_n0012: The following steps will help you practice Fosbury flop bar clearance:
pg075_n0016: From J-shaped run-up, run tall while keeping your hips high;
pg075_n0019: Plant the take-off foot (foot opposite to the side of the curve during the approach run);
pg075_n0022: Drive your knees high on take-off while keeping your head up;
pg075_n0025: Swing your arms high to propel your body up;
pg075_n0028: Jump up high rather than into the bar;
pg075_n0031: When crossing the bar, arch your back and pull your hips towards the sky;
pg075_n0034: Tuck your heels under the bar to lift your hips up; and
pg075_n0037: Land on the mat with your upper back or shoulders, Figure 2.41.

pg076_n0010: Rules and regulations for high jump
pg076_n0012: Rules are essential for maintaining standards and fairness in the events as well as safety of the athletes before and during events.
pg076_n0013: These are some rules that guide jumping events:
pg076_n0017: The jump: The athlete shall take-off using only one leg, and the jumping height is decided by the chief judge;
pg076_n0020: Jumping area: The runway shall be 15 m long and 16 m wide with a level take-off placed between the upright spaced 4 m in the midway of the runway.
pg076_n0021: The crossbar shall be cylindrical and hollow with tapered ends placed on the uprights.
pg076_n0022: The landing area shall not be smaller than 6 m x 4 m wide and 0.7 m high;
pg076_n0025: Officials: There will be the chief judge, landing judge, crossbar judge, recorder judge, scoreboard judge, clock judge and judge in charge of athlete;
pg076_n0028: Athlete’s trial: The athlete shall be entitled to three trials of bar clearance;
pg076_n0031: A foul: an attempt is failed if:
pg076_n0035: The jumper knocks the bar off its support.
pg076_n0038: The jumper fails to take off on one foot.
pg076_n0041: The jumper steps outside the take-off area before or after the jump.
pg076_n0044: The athlete exceeds the time limit for the attempt.
pg076_n0047: The jumper misses all three attempts at a given height.
pg077_n0006: Jump-off: The athlete concerned must jump at every height until the decision is reached, each athlete shall have one jump at each height, and the jump-off shall start at the next height.

pg080_n0007: Swimming is a sport in which an individual move through water using different strokes, just like aquatic animals.
pg080_n0008: Whether for fun, fitness, or competition, swimming is an essential survival, and sport related skill that benefits people of all gender and ages.
pg080_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn the concept, safety measures, fundamental skills, and rules of swimming.
pg080_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to swim efficiently and confidently.
pg080_n0014: Swimming is not just being in water
pg080_n0018: Swimming is a competitive aquatic sport that involves individual athletes or teams racing against each other through water using different strokes over varying distances.
pg080_n0019: The swimmers compete in freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly, and medley.
pg080_n0020: Competitive swimming takes place in pools or open waters, requiring endurance, speed, technique, and strategic planning.
pg080_n0021: It is featured in events like the Olympics, World Championships, and collegiate competitions.
pg080_n0022: As a recreational activity, swimming is a lifelong skill that enhances physical fitness, improves cardiovascular health, and builds endurance.
pg080_n0023: Additionally, swimming is essential for safety in water, as it equips individuals with skills needed to survive and respond effectively in water-related emergencies.
pg080_n0024: Furthermore, therapeutic swimming can offer a supportive environment for individuals to strengthen muscles, improve mobility, and manage pain.
pg081_n0005: Swimming requires designated facilities and equipment for training and competition.
pg081_n0006: These facilities and equipment provide an avenue for a smooth and enjoyable experience for swimmers of all levels.
pg081_n0010: The essential swimming facilities include swimming pools and open waters.
pg081_n0014: A swimming pool is a man-made structure designed to hold water for swimming, diving, and other recreational and competitive water-based activities, Figure 3.1.
pg081_n0015: It provides a structured and controlled environment that ensures safety, accessibility, and efficiency for swimmers of all levels.
pg081_n0016: Swimming pools are classified according to their intended use.
pg081_n0017: Recreational pools, typically located in homes, hotels, and resorts, are designed for leisure.
pg081_n0018: Training pools, found in schools and sports facilities, are used to develop swimming skills.
pg081_n0019: Competitive pools are built to meet national and international standards and are used for professional swimming competitions.
pg081_n0021: Competitive pools are further classified into short course pools (25 m), used for national and club-level competitions and long course (Olympic-size) pools (50 m), designated for international tournaments such as the Olympics and World Championships.
pg081_n0022: A swimming pool has depth variations to accommodate different skill levels, lane markings for guidance during swimming, starting blocks for competitive race starts, as well as filtration and chlorination systems that maintain water quality and hygiene.
pg081_n0023: These elements collectively contribute to an optimal swimming environment, facilitating both skill development and professional performance.
pg081_im001: Competitive swimming pool with multiple marked lanes separated by yellow lane ropes.
pg082_n0005: Open waters refer to natural aquatic environments such as lakes, rivers, seas, and oceans, which serve as venues for recreational swimming, endurance training, and competitive events, Figure 3.2.
pg082_n0006: Unlike swimming pools, open waters do not have artificial boundaries, making them more challenging due to varying water conditions such as currents, tides, and temperature fluctuations.
pg082_n0007: Open water swimming is commonly used in triathlons, long-distance races, and lifesaving training, requiring swimmers to develop advanced skills in navigation, endurance, and safety awareness.
pg082_im001: Open water beside a green hilly shoreline under a blue sky with clouds.
pg082_n0013: Swimming equipment refers to the tools used in training, recreation, and competitions to ensure safety, enhance performance, and improve technique.
pg082_n0014: The equipment includes swimsuits, goggles, swim caps, kickboards, pull buoys, fins, hand paddles, and earplugs.
pg082_n0018: A swimsuit is a clothing designed to be worn while swimming or participating in water-based activities.
pg082_n0019: A proper swimsuit should provide comfort, flexibility, and ease of movement in the water.
pg082_n0020: It is typically made of materials like polyester, which provides a snug fit and minimizes drag.
pg082_n0021: Streamlined swimsuits are used to reduce water resistance, enhancing speed and efficiency in the water, Figure 3.3.

pg083_im001_seg002_v1_crop_v1: Female one-piece swimsuit with a blue patterned design and narrow shoulder straps.
pg083_n0009: Goggles are protective eyewear designed to protect the eyes from water, chlorine, salt, and other irritants during swimming.
pg083_n0010: They also provide clear vision, allowing swimmers to maintain focus, especially during long swims or races.
pg083_n0011: Goggles are typically made from soft and adjustable materials like rubber seals to ensure a watertight fit around the eyes, Figure 3.4.
pg083_im002: Two pairs of swimming goggles: a small round-lens pair and a larger wide-lens pair with adjustable straps.
pg083_n0016: A swim cap is a close-fitting, flexible head covering worn while swimming, Figure 3.5.
pg083_n0017: The cap helps to protect hair, and reduce drag, which can slow down performance.
pg083_n0018: It is made of materials that offer a snug fit that protects the hair from chlorine damage.
pg083_n0019: In competitive swimming, the swim cap also serves to streamline the swimmer’s head and reduce drag, allowing for faster speed in the water.
pg084_im001: Side view of a swimmer’s head wearing a dark blue swim cap that covers the hair and ears.
pg084_n0007: The kickboard is a buoyant tool used during training to support the swimmer’s upper body, allowing them to focus on improving their leg movements, Figure 3.6.
pg084_n0008: Kickboards are commonly used for practicing kicking techniques.
pg084_n0009: They allow swimmers to isolate their leg movements and strengthen their lower body without worrying about balance in the water.
pg084_im002: Orange rectangular kickboard with rounded corners and two hand holes near one end.
pg084_n0015: A pull buoy is a buoyant device placed between the swimmer’s legs, typically at the thighs or ankles, to help maintain buoyancy and stability while focusing on arm movements, Figure 3.7.
pg084_n0016: It isolates the upper body, allowing swimmers to concentrate on improving their stroke technique, strength, and endurance without the added effort of kicking.
pg085_im001: Blue striped pull buoy used to support the legs during swimming practice.
pg085_n0007: Fins are devices worn on the feet to enhance speed and improve kicking technique, Figure 3.8.
pg085_n0008: Fins help increase propulsion through the water, allowing swimmers to develop more powerful kicks while reducing fatigue.
pg085_n0009: They also help improve leg strength and flexibility, making them an essential tool for training kick mechanics.
pg085_im002: Pair of swim fins with blue foot pockets and long yellow blades.
pg085_n0015: Hand paddles are flat, rigid plastic devices worn on the hands during swimming to increase resistance and strengthen arm strokes, Figure 3.9.
pg085_n0016: By increasing surface area, they provide more resistance, helping swimmers to build arm strength and improve stroke technique.
pg085_n0017: Hand paddles are especially useful for swimmers working on speed, and endurance in swimming strokes.
pg086_im001: Swimming hand paddles, with one paddle strapped onto a swimmer’s hand and a second paddle beside it.
pg086_n0007: Earplugs are devices inserted into the ears to prevent water from entering the ear canal during swimming, Figure 3.10.
pg086_n0008: They are commonly used by swimmers to reduce the risk of ear infections, such as ear fungus, and to enhance comfort during swimming.
pg086_n0009: Earplugs are of various types depending on the swimmer’s preference and need.
pg086_n0010: They are especially useful during long training sessions or for individuals with sensitive ears.

pg087_n0010: Swimming is an enjoyable and beneficial activity, but it requires adherence to safety measures to prevent accidents, injuries, or drowning.
pg087_n0011: Observe the following precautionary measures to ensure a safe and enjoyable swimming experience.
pg087_n0015: Performing light stretching and warm-up exercises before entering the water helps prevent muscle cramps, enhance flexibility, and reduce the risk of injuries while swimming.
pg087_n0019: Always swim in areas that are supervised by lifeguards, such as designated swimming pools or marked sections of open waters.
pg087_n0020: Avoid swimming in unknown or restricted areas such as areas with strong currents or deep waters.
pg087_n0024: Swimmers should be aware of their skill level before taking part in swimming.
pg087_n0028: Children and inexperienced swimmers should always be supervised.
pg087_n0030: (e) Observe pool and open water rules
pg087_n0032: Follow all posted signs and safety rules in swimming facilities.
pg087_n0033: For example, avoiding to: run on slippery surfaces, dive into shallow water, or engage in rough play that may lead to injuries.
pg087_n0037: Wearing appropriate swimming gear such as swimsuits, goggles, and swim caps ensures comfort and safety in swimming.
pg087_n0038: Beginners should use flotation devices like kickboards or life jackets for added safety.
pg088_n0005: Be cautious of tides, waves, aquatic animals, and underwater currents when swimming in open waters, as they can be dangerous even for experienced swimmers.
pg088_n0006: Always check weather forecasts and the water temperature before swimming in natural waters.
pg088_n0010: Always swim with a companion or in a group to ensure safety in case of an emergency, never swim without the presence of another person.
pg088_n0014: Swimming is a physically demanding activity, and dehydration can lead to fatigue.
pg088_n0015: Swimmers should drink enough water before and after swimming and take breaks when feeling exhausted.
pg088_n0019: Swimmers should be familiar with basic water rescue techniques and CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) for emergency rescues.
pg088_n0020: Learning how to recognize drowning signs and how to assist a struggling swimmer can help save lives.

pg088_n0029: Swimming is a fundamental life skill that enhances physical fitness, safety, and recreational enjoyment.
pg088_n0030: To become a proficient swimmer, one must develop essential swimming skills and master proper techniques.
pg088_n0031: These skills enable swimmers to move efficiently in the water, conserve energy, and maintain safety while swimming.
pg088_n0035: Before mastering swimming strokes, learners must first develop basic swimming skills that form the foundation for effective movement in water.
pg088_n0036: These skills help swimmers build confidence, maintain control, and ensure safety while swimming.
pg088_n0037: The key essential swimming skills include:
pg089_n0005: Floating is the ability to stay partially on the surface of water without sinking.
pg089_n0006: It is a fundamental swimming skill that helps swimmers conserve energy, rest, and remain calm in the water.
pg089_n0007: Mastering floating improves water confidence and safety, especially in deep water or emergencies.
pg089_n0008: There are two main types of floating:
pg089_n0012: The back float is an essential skill that allows swimmers to stay on the water surface while breathing freely.
pg089_n0013: For performing back float, follow these steps:
pg089_n0017: Lie on your back with the body fully extended and relaxed, Figure 3.11;
pg089_n0020: Spread your arms slightly away from the body or stretch out for better balance;
pg089_n0023: Legs remain straight and slightly apart or bent at the knees if needed for comfort;
pg089_n0026: Tilt your head slightly backwards, with the ears submerged, allowing the face to stay above water; and
pg089_n0029: Breathe normally and remain as still as possible to maintain buoyancy.
pg089_im001: Swimmer practising a back float with flotation aids under both arms, body relaxed on the water with arms spread and legs slightly apart.
pg089_im002: Swimmer performing a back float without equipment, lying flat on the water with face up, ears in the water, and body fully extended.
pg089_n0039: The front float is a skill that helps swimmers prepare for various strokes and learn to balance in water.
pg089_n0040: For performing front float, follow these steps:
pg089_n0044: Extend your body face-down in the water, keeping the arms and legs stretched out;
pg089_n0047: Take a deep breath before submerging, allowing the body to stay buoyant;
pg090_n0005: Extend your arms forward or position at the sides for balance, Figure 3.12;
pg090_n0008: Keep your legs straight and relaxed to avoid unnecessary movement; and
pg090_n0011: When ready to stand up or change position, lift your head, bend your knees, and push down with your hands to return to an upright position.
pg090_im001: Learner performing a front float with equipment, lying face down in the water with arms extended forward and flotation aids supporting the body.
pg090_im002: Learner performing a front float without equipment, floating face down in a straight horizontal position with arms resting along the sides.
pg090_n0021: Proper breathing control is essential for swimming efficiency, endurance, and relaxation in the water.
pg090_n0022: It allows swimmers to maintain a steady rhythm, reduce fatigue, and improve overall performance.
pg090_n0023: Without proper breathing techniques, swimmers may struggle with coordination and get tired quickly.
pg090_n0024: To develop effective breathing control, swimmers must focus on three key aspects:
pg090_n0030: Before entering the water, swimmers should take a deep breath, filling their lungs with enough air to enhance buoyancy and oxygen supply;
pg090_n0033: Deep inhalation should be done through the nose or mouth; and
pg090_n0036: Holding the breath momentarily before exhaling helps maintain stability and prevents panic while underwater.
pg090_n0042: Exhale gradually through the nose or mouth while the face is submerged;
pg090_n0045: Controlled exhalation prevents water from entering the airway and ensures a smooth breathing cycle;
pg090_n0048: In front crawl and backstroke, swimmers typically exhale through the nose to keep water from entering it.
pg090_n0049: In breaststroke and butterfly, they exhale through both the nose and mouth; and
pg091_n0005: A steady and complete exhalation makes it easier to take the next breath efficiently.
pg091_n0010: Each swimming stroke has a specific breathing pattern that must be synchronised with arm movements to maintain momentum;
pg091_n0013: In front crawl, swimmers turn their heads to the side during the arm recovery phase to inhale before exhaling underwater;
pg091_n0016: In breaststroke and butterfly, swimmers lift their head above water at the right moment to take a quick breath before submerging again; and
pg091_n0019: Proper timing ensures that breathing does not interrupt the swimming stroke or slow down movement.
pg091_n0022: Using various drills, practice the following breathing control:
pg091_n0034: Treading water is the ability to stay upright in deep water without sinking.
pg091_n0035: This skill is essential for resting, survival, and maintaining stability in situations where a swimmer needs to stay in one place, such as waiting for rescue or observing the surroundings.
pg091_n0036: Unlike swimming strokes that focus on forward movement, treading water allows the swimmer to remain stationary while keeping the head above water.
pg091_n0038: To tread water effectively, swimmers must use sculling arm movements to create lift, Figure 3.13.
pg091_n0039: The arms should move in a continuous circular motion, pushing water down and outward to generate buoyancy.
pg091_n0040: This motion helps keep the swimmer afloat without excessive use of energy.
pg091_n0041: The hands should remain relaxed, and small, controlled movements are preferred over forceful splashes.
pg091_n0042: Additionally, swimmers need to use effective kicking techniques to maintain balance.
pg091_n0043: There are three common kicks used for treading water:
pg091_n0048: Rapid, alternating leg movements up and down similar to those used in front crawl;
pg091_n0052: A wide sweeping kick similar to the one used in breaststroke; and
pg092_n0003: (iii) Eggbeater kick: A continuous, alternating circular motion of the legs, commonly used in water polo for stability and efficiency.

pg092_im002: Underwater view of a swimmer treading water with arms out to the sides and bent legs moving in an eggbeater kick.

pg092_n0013: Then, choose one of the following kicking techniques to practice with drills until you can perform it confidently:
pg092_n0023: Kicking is a fundamental swimming skill that generates propulsion and helps maintain body position in the water.
pg092_n0024: Effective kicking improves speed, balance, and efficiency in different swimming strokes.
pg092_n0025: Each stroke requires a specific kicking technique to maximize movement and maintain coordination with the arms and breathing.
pg092_n0029: Flutter kick is one of the most commonly used kicking techniques in swimming.
pg092_n0030: It consists of small, rapid, alternating leg movements.
pg092_n0031: This kick is used in front crawl and backstroke to propel the swimmer forward while keeping the body aligned, Figure 3.14.
pg092_n0032: The movement originates from the hips rather than the knees, with the legs remaining straight but slightly flexible.
pg092_n0033: To execute an efficient flutter kick, swimmers
pg093_n0003: should keep their feet close together and make quick, continuous motions to reduce drag and maintain speed.
pg093_im001: Alternating up-and-down flutter kick underwater, with arrows showing one leg rising as the other presses downward.
pg093_im002: Legs extended close together just below the water surface, showing the streamlined position for a flutter kick.
pg093_n0014: Use a kickboard to practice flutter kicks repeatedly while keeping your body straight and legs relaxed until you master the skill.
pg093_n0018: Frog kick is a wide-sweeping movement of the leg that powers the breaststroke.
pg093_n0019: In this kick, the swimmer bends their knees outward while bringing their feet toward their body, then pushes the legs outward and backward in a circular motion before bringing them back together, Figure 3.15.
pg093_n0020: The frog kick provides strong propulsion with each cycle and is most effective when synchronised with the arm movements of the breaststroke.
pg093_n0021: Proper execution requires a controlled, smooth motion rather than forceful splashes.
pg093_im003_crop_v1: Breaststroke frog kick with knees bent outward and feet turned out, preparing to sweep the legs backward and together.
pg094_n0005: Use kickboards to practice frog kicks repetitively to master the skill.
pg094_n0009: The dolphin kick is a powerful, wave-like motion used in the butterfly stroke and underwater swimming.
pg094_n0010: It involves keeping the legs together and generating movement from the hips, creating a fluid undulating motion similar to the movement of a dolphin’s tail, Figure 3.16.
pg094_n0011: This kick requires strong core engagement and flexibility to produce a continuous wave that moves through the body.
pg094_n0012: The dolphin kick is useful for explosive starts and turns in competitive swimming.
pg094_im001: Swimmer demonstrating the dolphin kick, with arms extended forward and arrows showing the wave-like undulating motion from the chest and hips through the legs and pointed feet underwater.
pg094_n0018: Use kickboards to practice dolphin kicks repetitively to master the skill.
pg094_n0022: Arm movements play a crucial role in determining the swimmers’ speed, direction and overall efficiency in the water.
pg094_n0023: Proper arm techniques help generate propulsion, reduce resistance and maintain balance.
pg094_n0024: Each stroke requires specific arm movements that must be synchronised with breathing and kicking for smooth and effective swimming.
pg094_n0025: The principles for arm movements include:
pg094_n0026: Keep the fingers together to maximize water resistance
pg094_n0028: When the fingers are slightly spread apart, water can pass through the gaps, reducing efficiency.
pg094_n0029: By keeping the fingers close together and cupped slightly, swimmers create a larger surface area to push against the water, generating more force with each stroke, Figure 3.17.
pg094_n0030: This technique is important in front crawl, breaststroke, backstroke and butterfly, where continuous propulsion is necessary.
pg095_im001: Open hand held upright with the fingers straight and close together to show correct finger alignment.
pg095_n0005: Use a high elbow position for strong, efficient strokes
pg095_n0007: In strokes like front crawl and butterfly, a high elbow catch allows swimmers to pull more water and generate forward movement with minimal resistance.
pg095_n0008: In executing swimming strokes, keeping the elbow high during the recovery phase helps maintain a smooth, circular motion.
pg095_n0009: A proper elbow position enhances stroke power and reduces drag, allowing the swimmer to move more efficiently through the water, Figure 3.18.
pg095_im002: Swimmer in the water demonstrating a high elbow position, with the elbow bent and hand dropping below it during the stroke.
pg095_n0013: Coordinate arm movements with kicking and breathing
pg095_n0015: Each swimming stroke has a specific timing pattern that synchronizes arm strokes with leg kicks and breathing cycles.
pg095_n0016: In front crawl and backstroke, one arm enters the water as the other recovers, while the legs continuously flutter kick.
pg096_n0003: and butterfly, both arms move together in a circular motion, requiring precise timing with kicks and breaths.
pg096_n0004: A well-coordinated technique ensures smooth movement, reduces fatigue, and enhances overall swimming performance.
pg096_n0009: Using various drills practice arm movements repetitively based on the three principles until you master the skill.

pg096_n0026: Swimming strokes refer to the different techniques used to propel the body through water.
pg096_n0027: Each stroke has unique arm movements, leg kicks, and breathing patterns that require coordination for efficient swimming.
pg096_n0028: Mastering these strokes allows swimmers to swim effectively while conserving energy.
pg096_n0029: The four main competitive swimming strokes are front crawl, backstroke, breaststroke, and butterfly.
pg096_n0033: Front crawl is a swimming stroke which involves flutter kicks with an alternating arm motion in a prone position, where one arm pulls through the water from above the head to the hip while the other recovers above the water.
pg096_n0034: The stroke is considered the fastest and most commonly used stroke in freestyle swimming races.
pg096_n0035: It is favoured for its efficiency, and speed, making it the preferred stroke for long-distance swimming and racing.
pg096_n0036: The following steps will help you practice front crawl:
pg096_n0040: Lie in water face-down, keeping the body streamlined to minimize resistance;
pg096_n0043: Move your arms in an alternating windmill motion.
pg096_n0044: One arm extends forward and enters the water, while the other pulls back beneath the body to generate propulsion;
pg096_n0047: Move your legs continuously in a flutter kick to maintain balance, stability, and forward momentum while reducing drag; and
pg096_n0050: Turn the head to the side after a set number of strokes and take in air, usually every two or three strokes, inhale quickly through the mouth while one arm
pg097_n0003: is recovering above the water and exhale while the face is submerged, Figure 3.19.
pg097_im001: Swimmer demonstrating front crawl technique with one arm extended forward, the other pulling through the water, and legs performing a flutter kick, with arrows showing the movement pattern.
pg097_n0008: Practice front crawl repetitively to master the skill.
pg097_n0012: Backstroke is a swimming style performed on the swimmer’s back with a flutter kick and alternating arms motion where one arm pulls through the water from above the head to the hip while the other recovers above the water.
pg097_n0013: It allows for unrestricted breathing since the face remains above water, making it a preferred stroke for beginners and a crucial technique in competitive swimming.
pg097_n0014: Proper coordination of arm movements, leg kicks, and body positioning ensures smooth and efficient swimming.
pg097_n0015: The following steps will help you practice backstroke:
pg097_n0019: Lie in water face-up, keeping the body streamlined to minimize resistance;
pg097_n0022: Move your arms in an alternating windmill motion.
pg097_n0023: One arm extends forward and enters the water, while the other pulls back beneath the body to generate propulsion;
pg097_n0026: Move your legs continuously in a flutter kick to maintain balance, stability, and forward momentum while reducing drag; and
pg097_n0029: Breath naturally free as your face is up, maintaining proper head positioning to avoid excessive movement that could slow you down.
pg097_n0030: Keeping the head still and looking upwards helps in maintaining balance and direction.
pg097_n0033: Use lane markers or ceiling patterns to help you maintain direction without trying to turn.
pg097_n0034: A streamlined body position, with the hips and legs kept near the water’s surface, minimizes drag and improves speed, Figure 3.20.
pg098_im001: Backstroke execution showing a swimmer floating on the back with alternating arm rotation and flutter kicks.
pg098_n0006: Practice backstroke repetitively to master the skill.
pg098_n0010: This is a swimming stroke executed in a prone position by coordinating a kick where the legs are brought forward with the knees together and the feet are turned outward and whipped back with a glide and a backward sweeping movement of the arms.
pg098_n0011: Breaststroke is one of the oldest and most widely practiced swimming strokes.
pg098_n0012: It is characterized by controlled, powerful movements that emphasize efficiency rather than speed.
pg098_n0013: This stroke requires precise coordination between the arms, legs, and breathing to maintain a smooth, rhythmic motion.
pg098_n0014: The following steps will help you practice breaststroke:
pg098_n0018: Push the feet off the wall with face down, body straight extending arms forward, hands together, and head in line with your body;
pg098_n0021: Move the arms in a circular, scooping motion in front of the body by extending your arms forward, then pulling them outward and back toward the chest in a sweeping motion, creating propulsion.
pg098_n0022: Keep the hands close together at the start of the stroke to reduce drag;
pg098_n0025: Perform a frog kick by bending the knees, pushing the feet outward in a circular motion, and bringing them back together; and
pg098_n0028: Breath during each stroke cycle, as you lift the head above the water when pulling the arms back.
pg098_n0029: After inhaling, exhale it out while submerging again, ensuring a smooth transition between strokes.
pg098_n0030: Proper timing of breathing helps maintain momentum and prevents fatigue, Figure 3.21.
pg099_im001: Swimmer demonstrating breaststroke execution in the water, with arms sweeping forward and legs bent for a frog kick.
pg099_n0006: Practice breaststroke repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg099_n0010: Butterfly stroke is a swimming style where both arms move symmetrically and simultaneously in a windmill motion while both legs kick together in a fluid wave-like motion.
pg099_n0011: In this movement, the swimmer’s body undulates to help propel forward while breathing occurs during the arm recovery as the head lifts.
pg099_n0012: It is one of the most powerful and physically demanding swimming strokes, requiring a high level of strength, endurance and coordination.
pg099_n0013: It is recognized for its unique wave-like motion and simultaneous arm movements, making it the second-fastest stroke after the front crawl.
pg099_n0014: The following steps will help you practice the butterfly stroke:
pg099_n0018: Dive or push from the wall with face down, body in wave-like motion;
pg099_n0021: Move your arms together in a sweeping motion over the water before pulling downwards for propulsion.
pg099_n0022: Start the strokes with both arms extended forward, then push outward and downward through the water before recovering back over the surface in a smooth, circular motion.
pg099_n0023: The arms generate most of the forward movement in the butterfly;
pg099_n0026: Perform a dolphin kick, moving both feet together in a wave-like motion.
pg099_n0027: This kick originates from the hips, with the legs and feet following in a fluid, undulating movement.
pg099_n0028: The dolphin kick provides continuous propulsion and helps maintain body position; and
pg099_n0031: Breath as you lift the head forward during the arm recovery phase.
pg099_n0032: Inhale quickly before the face returns to the water and then exhale while submerged.
pg100_n0003: Proper timing is crucial to avoid disrupting the stroke’s rhythm.
pg100_n0004: Many swimmers breathe every stroke cycle or every two cycles, depending on their endurance.
pg100_n0006: The butterfly stroke relies on a continuous wave-like motion that flows through the entire body.
pg100_n0007: Swimmers must coordinate arm movements, leg kicks and breathing to maintain speed and efficiency, Figure 3.22.
pg100_n0008: A streamlined body position helps reduce drag and enhances momentum.
pg100_im001: Butterfly stroke execution showing the swimmer’s arms extended forward, chest pressing down, hips rising, and legs performing a dolphin kick in a wave-like body motion.
pg100_n0013: Practice butterfly stroke repetitively to master the skill.
pg100_n0017: Swimming competitions are organised in different distances, strokes and formats.
pg100_n0018: Based on strokes, the races include freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly and medley.
pg100_n0022: Freestyle refers to a swimming race where swimmers are allowed to use any stroke they prefer.
pg100_n0023: However, in most freestyle swimming events, swimmers use front crawl, consequently, front crawl is sometimes misconceived as freestyle stroke.
pg100_n0024: Below are key rules governing freestyle swimming race:
pg100_n0032: Swimmers must begin the race by diving into the pool from the starting block;
pg100_n0035: The race starts with the sound of the whistle or a starting signal; and
pg100_n0038: To complete the race, a swimmer must touch the wall at the end of the final lap with any part of the body.
pg101_n0009: Swimmers may use any stroke, but the front crawl is the most commonly used stroke; and
pg101_n0012: Any forward motion is allowed as long as it does not violate other competition rules.
pg101_n0019: In races with multiple laps, swimmers must touch the wall before turning; and
pg101_n0022: Flip turns (tumble turns) are commonly used for faster transitions.
pg101_n0029: Swimmers can breathe as often as they want, usually turning their heads to the side; and
pg101_n0032: The head may be submerged, but swimmers must surface within 15 m after the start and each turn.
pg101_n0039: A swimmer who moves before the starting signal may be disqualified for a false start;
pg101_n0042: Swimmers who fail to remain in their designated lanes and interfere with others are disqualified;
pg101_n0045: Failure to touch the wall at the end of a lap or the finish also results in disqualification; and
pg101_n0048: Staying underwater beyond 15 metres after the start or a turn.
pg101_n0051: Practice competing using freestyle swimming while adhering to its rules.
pg101_n0055: Backstroke swimming requires the swimmer to swim using the backstroke throughout the race.
pg101_n0056: Below are the key rules governing backstroke swimming race:
pg101_n0064: Swimmers start in the water, holding onto the wall or the starting block grips;
pg101_n0067: After the start signal, swimmers push off the wall while remaining on their back; and
pg102_n0004: (iii) Swimmers can stay underwater for up to 15 metres after the start but must surface before passing that mark.
pg102_n0010: (i) Swimmers must remain on their back throughout the race, except when performing a turn;
pg102_n0012: (ii) Any arm movement is allowed, but alternating arm strokes and a continuous flutter kick are typically used; and
pg102_n0014: (iii) The swimmer’s body must be positioned flat on the back; though slight body rotation is allowed.
pg102_n0020: (i) Swimmers must touch the wall with any part of their body when turning;
pg102_n0022: (ii) A swimmer is allowed to rotate onto their stomach during the turn but must complete the turn quickly; and
pg102_n0024: (iii) After pushing off from the wall, swimmers may remain underwater for up to 15 metres before surfacing.
pg102_n0030: (i) The race ends when a swimmer touches the wall while still on their back; and
pg102_n0032: (ii) Swimmers cannot turn onto their front before touching the wall.
pg102_n0036: A swimmer may be disqualified for:
pg102_n0039: (i) Not remaining on their back (except during the turn);
pg102_n0041: (ii) Performing an illegal turn or failing to touch the wall;
pg102_n0043: (iii) Staying underwater beyond 15 metres after the start or a turn; and
pg102_n0045: (iv) False starting (leaving before the start signal).
pg102_n0048: Practice a backstroke swimming race while adhering to its rules.
pg102_n0052: Breaststroke swimming requires the swimmer to swim using breaststroke throughout the race.
pg102_n0053: Below are the key rules governing breaststroke swimming race:
pg102_n0060: (i) The race begins with a dive start from the starting block;
pg102_n0062: (ii) After diving, swimmers are allowed one arm pull and one leg kick underwater before surfacing; and
pg103_n0003: (iii) The head must break the water’s surface before completing the second arm stroke.
pg103_n0008: (i) Swimmers must stay on their stomachs at all times; turning onto their backs is not allowed;
pg103_n0010: (ii) Both arms must move at the same time in a circular, scooping motion;
pg103_n0012: (iii) The legs must perform a frog kick (breaststroke kick) where the feet turn outward and sweep back together;
pg103_n0014: (iv) Alternating or flutter kicks are not allowed and can lead to disqualification; and
pg103_n0016: (v) After each stroke, the head must break the water surface.
pg103_n0021: (i) Both hands must touch the wall simultaneously at each turn;
pg103_n0023: (ii) A swimmer can briefly dive underwater after pushing off but must surface before starting the second arm stroke; and
pg103_n0025: (iii) A single pull and kick are allowed after pushing off the wall before resuming normal strokes.
pg103_n0030: (i) Swimmers must touch the wall with both hands at the same time at the finish; and
pg103_n0032: (ii) The body must remain in a prone (face-down) position when finishing the race.
pg103_n0036: A swimmer may be disqualified for:
pg103_n0039: (i) Using a wrong kick, such as a flutter or dolphin kick;
pg103_n0041: (ii) Failing to touch the wall with both hands simultaneously at turns and finish;
pg103_n0043: (iii) Performing asynchronous arm movements (arms must move together);
pg103_n0045: (iv) Failing to break the surface of the water after the second stroke; and
pg103_n0047: (v) Turning onto the back at any point during the race.
pg103_n0051: Practice a breaststroke swimming race while adhering to its rules.
pg104_n0005: The butterfly swimming requires the swimmer to swim using butterfly stroke throughout the race.
pg104_n0006: Below are the key rules governing butterfly swimming race:
pg104_n0014: The race begins with a dive start from the starting block; and
pg104_n0017: After entering the water, swimmers are allowed one arm pull and up to two dolphin kicks underwater before surfacing.
pg104_n0020: Swimmers must break the surface of the water before completing the second arm stroke.
pg104_n0027: Swimmers must stay on their stomach (face-down position) throughout the race.
pg104_n0028: Turning onto the back is not allowed;
pg104_n0031: The arms must move simultaneously and symmetrically in an overwater recovery motion;
pg104_n0034: The legs must perform a dolphin kick, where both feet move together in a wave-like motion; and
pg104_n0037: Any form of flutter or breaststroke kicking is not allowed.
pg104_n0044: Swimmers may breathe at any time, but they must lift their head forward while keeping their body streamlined; and
pg104_n0047: The head must remain facing forward or downward when not taking a breath.
pg104_n0054: Both hands must touch the wall simultaneously at each turn;
pg104_n0057: After turning, swimmers may perform one arm pull and up to two dolphin kicks underwater before resurfacing; and
pg104_n0060: The swimmer must resume a regular stroke pattern before reaching 15 m from the wall.
pg104_n0067: The race ends when a swimmer touches the wall with both hands simultaneously; and
pg104_n0070: The body must remain in a prone (face-down) position when finishing.
pg104_n0075: A swimmer may be disqualified for:
pg104_n0079: Failing to touch the wall with both hands simultaneously at turns and finish;
pg104_n0082: Performing different arm movements or leg kicks other than that of a butterfly;
pg105_n0004: (iii) Failing to break the water’s surface within 15 metres after the start or a turn; and
pg105_n0006: (iv) Turning onto the back at any point during the race.
pg105_n0009: Practice a butterfly swimming race while adhering to its rules.
pg105_n0013: Medley refers to a race that involves multiple strokes, either performed by one swimmer (individual medley) or by a team (medley relay).
pg105_n0014: The rules that govern medley are the same which govern the various strokes used in the race.
pg105_n0015: In these races, a swimmer starts with butterfly, then backstroke, breaststroke and lastly front crawl.
pg105_n0016: In a medley relay, four swimmers each swim one stroke in the following order: backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly, and finally front crawl.

pg109_n0008: Gymnastics is a sport that involves a variety of physical exercises and routines performed on different apparatuses.
pg109_n0009: It is practiced by both males and females for competitive and recreational purposes.
pg109_n0010: Participating in gymnastics promotes physical health, creates employment opportunities, and helps individuals to develop essential life skills.
pg109_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn the concept, safety measures, skills and rules in gymnastics.
pg109_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to analyse and perform a variety of gymnastics activities with confidence and proficiency.
pg109_n0016: Gymnastics is more than physical skills
pg109_n0020: Gymnastics is both a competitive and developmental sport that involves performing a variety of movements using apparatuses such as floor, balance beam, vault, rings, parallel bars, and pommel horse.
pg109_n0021: Its main goal is to develop and showcase refined motor skills, physical control, and aesthetic movement.
pg109_n0022: The sport is typically divided into several distinct categories, including artistic gymnastics, rhythmic gymnastics, trampoline, acrobatic gymnastics, and aerobic gymnastics, each with its own technical requirements and performance standards.
pg109_n0023: Gymnastics plays a crucial role in the holistic development of individuals, particularly during early childhood and adolescence.
pg109_n0024: It contributes significantly to the enhancement of fundamental movement patterns, spatial awareness, muscular development, and self-discipline.
pg109_n0025: It also, supports cognitive and emotional growth through goal setting, perseverance, and striving for excellence.
pg109_n0026: Gymnastics serves as an essential component of physical
pg110_n0003: literacy and provides a comprehensive framework for lifelong fitness and motor skill development.
pg110_n0007: To ensure safety practice and competition, gymnasts must take a range of precautionary measures to protect themselves and others from injuries.
pg110_n0008: The measures are grouped into three main categories; namely safety gear, safe practices and competition and healthy gymnastics.
pg110_n0012: Using the right equipment is essential for injury prevention and optimal performance.
pg110_n0013: Gymnastics gear falls into the following categories:
pg110_n0017: Apparel: This includes properly fitted clothing such as leotards, grips, and wrist guards that allow freedom of movement while minimising risk;
pg110_n0020: Protective equipment: Gymnastics shoes, knee, elbow and ankle supports, and mouth guards help reduce the impact of falls and repetitive strain;
pg110_n0023: Safety equipment: Items like mats, padding, spring floors, spotting blocks, and other training aids provide cushioning and support during practice; and
pg110_n0026: Gymnast-specific gear: These are personalised items that enhance comfort and performance, such as headbands, hair ties, and compression wear.
pg110_n0030: Safety during gymnastic training and competition is maintained through adhering to guidelines, correct execution of techniques/skills, and proactive measures to prevent injuries.
pg110_n0031: For safe gymnastic practices and competition perform the following key safety practices:
pg110_n0035: Beginning with proper warm-up and ending with cool-down exercises;
pg110_n0038: Progressing from simple to complex skills to build confidence and reduce the risk of injury;
pg110_n0041: Training under qualified supervision and using spotting techniques;
pg110_n0044: Staying hydrated, following a nutritious diet, and ensuring adequate rest and recovery; and
pg110_n0047: Complying with rules and regulations, medically prepared, demonstrating sportsmanship, and maintaining mental readiness.
pg110_n0051: Healthy gymnastics focuses on sustaining physical and mental well-being alongside skill development.
pg110_n0052: It involves the practices that promote safety including:
pg111_n0005: Maintaining overall fitness and avoiding overtraining;
pg111_n0008: Practicing techniques that promote injury prevention;
pg111_n0011: Supporting mental health and maintaining a balanced training schedule; and
pg111_n0014: Encouraging enjoyment of the sport as a foundation for long-term participation and performance.

pg111_n0023: These typically consist of a gymnasium with padded flooring or spring floors.
pg111_n0024: Common equipment includes landing mats, gripping powder, balance beams, uneven bars, parallel and horizontal bars, vaults, gloves, pommel horse, rings and personal kit.

pg113_n0038: The routine of gymnastics activity depends on a mastery of various skills, which contribute to a skillful and confident performance in gymnastics.
pg113_n0039: The basic skills in gymnastics include handstand, splits, bridge, cartwheel and back and forward rolls.
pg113_n0040: The following are explanations of basic skills in gymnastics:
pg113_n0043: A forward roll is a gymnastics skill where the gymnast rolls forward on the floor by bending their body into a rounded shape, using momentum to move smoothly
pg114_n0003: over the back and return to a standing position.
pg114_n0004: It helps to develop body awareness, coordination and confidences in rolling movements, serving foundation for more gymnastic skills.
pg114_n0005: To perform forward roll, do the following:
pg114_n0009: Stand up straight with your arms raised;
pg114_n0012: Bend your knees and place your hands on the floor in front of you;
pg114_n0015: Bend your head forward, bringing your chin to your chest;
pg114_n0018: Roll forward over your back smoothly as shown in Figure 4.1; and
pg114_n0021: Finish by landing on your feet and standing up.
pg114_im001: Sequence of a gymnast performing a forward roll: squatting with hands on the floor, tucking the head, rolling over the shoulders and back, and finishing in a balanced squat.
pg114_n0031: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a forward roll, and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg114_n0035: A backward roll is a gymnastic skill where a gymnast rolls backward over their shoulders and returns to a standing or seated position.
pg114_n0036: It helps develop core strength, coordination, and body control, making it an essential skill for advanced moves like back handsprings and back tucks.
pg114_n0037: The following steps will help you practice backward rolls:
pg114_n0041: Stand, then squat with feet together keeping arms raised and chin inserted towards the chest to protect the neck;
pg114_n0044: Sit down and roll onto your back, bending your knees toward your chest;
pg114_n0047: Place hands by your ears, palms facing upward and push them against the floor to lift the back over the head;
pg114_n0050: Roll onto feet and stand up smoothly keeping arms raised for balance, Figure 4.2; and
pg114_n0053: Repeat the practice several times to perfect the skill.
pg115_im001: Five-step sequence of a gymnast performing a backward roll: standing upright, bending into a squat, tucking the knees and rolling backward, bringing the legs over the head, and pushing with the hands to finish on hands and feet.
pg115_n0013: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a backward roll, and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg115_n0017: Handstand gymnastics refers to the skill of balancing the body in an inverted position, supported by the hands.
pg115_n0018: It is a fundamental movement in gymnastics that requires strength, balance, flexibility, agility, coordination, and control.
pg115_n0019: Handstands are used in various gymnastics disciplines, including artistic gymnastics, acrobatics, and tumbling.
pg115_n0020: The following steps will help you practice the handstand:
pg115_n0024: Begin by kicking up against a wall for support and keep it for a while repeatedly;
pg115_n0027: Balance your body on the hands as you free your feet from the wall.
pg115_n0028: To start with, you may have someone to help you stabilise;
pg115_n0034: After being stable, start it by putting feet together, arms raised overhead with core engaged;
pg115_n0037: Step one foot forward and lean placing your hands shoulder-width apart on the ground;
pg115_n0040: Swing your back leg up first, followed by the other leg, use momentum, but stay controlled;
pg115_n0043: As your legs are high up, keep your body tight and straight squeezing your core, glutes and legs to stay balanced, Figure 4.3; and
pg115_n0046: If you feel like falling forward, tuck and roll out, if falling back, return one leg down first to land safely.
pg116_im001: Four-step sequence of a gymnast performing a handstand, progressing from a bent starting stance to hands on the floor, one leg kicking up, and a straight vertical handstand.
pg116_n0010: Search on the internet how a handstand is used in gymnastics, then practice it.

pg116_n0025: A cartwheel is a fundamental gymnastics skill where a gymnast moves sideways in a hand-hand-foot-foot motion, resembling the spokes of a turning wheel.
pg116_n0026: It helps to develop coordination, balance, flexibility, agility, strength, body control, and serves as a foundation for more advanced tumbling skills.
pg116_n0027: The following steps will help you practice the cartwheel:
pg116_n0031: Start by placing one foot in front and the other behind, with your front knee bent;
pg116_n0034: Step forward with your stronger foot and lift your arms straight up by your ears.
pg116_n0035: Your back leg should be straight and extended;
pg116_n0038: As you lean forward, place your first hand on the floor and quickly place your second hand in line with the first;
pg117_n0005: Kick your back leg up, followed by the front leg passing your body through a handstand position briefly;
pg117_n0008: Land with one foot at a time, finishing in a lunge facing the opposite direction, Figure 4.4; and
pg117_n0011: Repeat it to perfect the movement.
pg117_im001: Three stages of a cartwheel: entering with one leg kicked up, passing through an inverted handstand with legs straddled, and landing on the opposite foot facing the other direction.
pg117_n0021: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute two-hand cartwheel and one-hand cartwheel, and practice them repeatedly until you master the skills.
pg117_n0025: Split gymnastics refers to any movement, skill, or position in gymnastics that involves splitting the legs apart in opposite directions.
pg117_n0026: Splits are fundamental for flexibility and are used in various routines, including floor exercises, balance beams, and bars.
pg117_n0027: The types of splits include front splits (right or left), middle splits (straddle splits), over splits, standing splits and split leaps or jumps.
pg117_n0028: The following steps will help you practice the basic front split:
pg117_n0032: Step one leg forward into a deep lunge, keeping the back leg extended with an upright chest for 20 – 30 seconds on each side;
pg117_n0035: From the lunge position, straighten the front leg and try to reach the toes keeping your back straight for 20 – 30 seconds;
pg117_n0038: Sit down and press the soles of your feet together, gently push your knees toward the floor and hold for a while;
pg118_n0005: Sit with your legs straight in front and reach for your toes keeping your back flat and hold for a while;
pg118_n0008: From a lunge position, slowly extend your front leg straight while keeping your back knee on the ground, and hold it for 20 – 30 seconds before switching legs, Figure 4.5;
pg118_n0011: Start with a deep lunge and slowly slide your front foot forward while your hands are anchored on the ground for 20 – 30 seconds; and
pg118_n0014: Repeat the practice regularly to improve the basic cast skill.
pg118_im001: Gymnast performing a front split on a mat, with one leg extended forward, the other backward, and hands on the floor for support.
pg118_n0023: Go through the internet and other sources to find out steps for practising the various cast skills and practice it.
pg118_n0027: A split leap is a gymnastics skill where a gymnast jumps into the air and extends both legs into a split position while maintaining height, flexibility, and control.
pg118_n0028: The following steps will help you practice split leap:
pg118_n0032: Start in a lunge position with one foot forward, arms lifted and chest tall;
pg118_n0035: Push off the back leg explosively while swing the front leg upward to initiate the split;
pg118_n0038: Extend both legs into a full split, keeping toes pointed and back upright, Figure 4.6; and
pg119_n0003: (iv) Land lightly on the opposite foot with knees bent and controlled arms.
pg119_im001: Three stages of a split leap: starting upright with one leg swinging forward and arms raised, extending into a full split in the air with arms out, then landing lightly on the opposite foot with arms raised.
pg119_n0015: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a split leap and practice it.
pg119_n0019: The bridge is a gymnastics skill that involves arching the back while supporting the body with the hands and feet on the ground.
pg119_n0020: It helps develop flexibility, strength, and control, especially in the spine, shoulders, and wrists.
pg119_n0021: For progressive learning in bridge gymnastics, start with the basic bridge position, followed by the wall bridge before performing the full bridge.
pg119_n0022: The following steps will help you practice the bridge:
pg119_n0028: Lie on your back, bending the knees while keeping your feet flat and hip-width apart;
pg119_n0031: Place your hands flat on the ground near your ears, fingers pointing toward your shoulders;
pg119_n0034: Push through your hands and feet to lift your body off the ground;
pg119_n0037: Hold for a few seconds, then lower down slowly; and
pg119_n0040: Repeat it to acquire a comfortable positioning.
pg120_n0007: Stand close to a wall and reach back with your hands;
pg120_n0010: Slowly walk your hands down the wall until you are in a deep backbend; and
pg120_n0013: Hold for a few seconds, then carefully walk back up.
pg120_n0019: Lie on your back, bend your knees, and place your hands near your shoulders;
pg120_n0022: Push up through your arms and legs, lifting your body into an arch, Figure 4.7;
pg120_n0025: Try to straighten your arms and keep your shoulders over your wrists; and
pg120_n0028: Hold for 5–10 seconds and then lower down with control.
pg120_im001: A gymnast performs a bridge on a mat, with hands and feet planted on the floor and the body arched upward.
pg120_n0034: A round-off is a gymnastics skill with a powerful, two-foot landing that generates momentum for tumbling moves.
pg120_n0035: It is commonly used as a setup for back handsprings, flips, and other advanced skills.
pg120_n0036: The following steps will help you practice round-off:
pg120_n0040: Stand one foot forward, arms straight up by your ears, body upright;
pg120_n0043: Reach forward and place the first hand on the ground while the second hand turns inward to help square the body;
pg120_n0046: Kick your legs over while keeping them straight, and start turning your hips to face forward as your legs pass over, Figure 4.8; and
pg120_n0049: Pull your legs together in the air to land simultaneously while pushing off your hands to generate power for the next move.
pg121_im001: Five-step sequence of a gymnast performing a round-off: starting with arms raised, placing hands on the floor, passing through a handstand position, rebounding forward, and landing with knees bent and arms extended.
pg121_n0012: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a round-off and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg121_n0016: A turn on one foot in gymnastics is a skill where a gymnast rotates on a single foot while maintaining balance and control.
pg121_n0017: Turns are commonly performed on the floor and balance beam and are essential for artistic and rhythmic gymnastics.
pg121_n0018: The following steps will help you practice turns on one foot:
pg121_n0022: Stand tall with arms in a controlled position and shift your weight onto the supporting foot.
pg121_n0025: Lift the free foot to the knee of the standing leg while keeping the toes pointed and the body tight;
pg121_n0028: Push up onto the ball of the foot and rotate smoothly using core control and spotting technique, Figure 4.9; and
pg121_n0031: Lower the foot gently and finish with arms stretched out in a balanced position.
pg121_im002_crop_v1: Five-step sequence of a gymnast turning on one foot: beginning in a lunge with arms out, lifting one foot to the knee with arms overhead, rotating upright on the supporting foot, and finishing balanced with the free leg extended.
pg122_n0006: Search from the internet and other sources on how to execute a turn on one foot and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
