pg122_n0016: Gymnastics routines are planned sequences of movements performed by a gymnast on the apparatus.
pg122_n0017: Each routine is designed to develop the gymnast’s strength, flexibility, coordination, control, balance, and artistic expression.
pg122_n0018: The type of equipment used determines the nature of the movements, the skills performed, and the judging criteria.
pg122_n0019: The gymnastics routines include floor routines and equipment based routines.
pg122_n0023: A floor routine is a choreographed sequence of acrobatic and dance elements performed on a floor in gymnastics.
pg122_n0024: Both men and women compete in the floor exercise, but the structure of their routines differs slightly.
pg122_n0025: The following are some floor routines.
pg122_n0029: A headstand is a basic inverted balance skill where a gymnast supports their body weight on their head and hands while keeping their body straight and controlled.
pg122_n0030: It is often used as a beginner skill to develop balance, strength, and body control before progressing to more advanced inversions like handstands.
pg122_n0031: The following steps will help you practice headstand:
pg122_n0034: (i) Kneel and place your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor;
pg122_n0036: (ii) Create a triangle base with your head and hands for stability;
pg122_n0038: (iii) Lift your knees to slowly raise your hips, bringing your legs close to your body;
pg122_n0040: (iv) Engage core and lift legs extending your legs upward in a straight line while keeping control, Figure 4.10; and
pg123_n0002: (v) Hold and balance to maintain a straight body position and keep your weight evenly distributed.
pg123_im001: Gymnast performing a straight headstand with forearms and head on the floor, legs together and extended vertically upward.
pg123_n0008: Practice headstand with knee on arms exercise, and headstand on wall exercises.
pg123_n0012: A standing scale is a gymnastics balance skill where a gymnast stands on one leg and extends the other leg in a controlled position.
pg123_n0013: It helps to develop flexibility, balance, and body control and is commonly seen in artistic gymnastics.
pg123_n0014: Depending on positioning, there are front scales, side scales, and back scales.
pg123_n0015: The following steps will help you practice standing scale:
pg123_n0019: Stand tall with feet together, core engaged, keeping the standing leg straight and strong;
pg123_n0022: Lift the other leg extending it forward, sideways, or backward while maintaining control, Figure 4.11;
pg123_n0025: Engage core and hold keeping your back straight, and arms extended for balance; and
pg123_n0028: Lower the leg smoothly returning to a standing position with control.
pg124_im001_seg001_v1: Standing scale with one leg supporting, torso leaning forward, both arms extended in front, and the other leg stretched straight behind.
pg124_im001_seg002_v1: Side standing scale balance on one foot, with one arm raised upward, the other lowered, and the free leg extended sideways.
pg124_im001_seg003_v1: Standing scale variation with the body leaning slightly backward and one leg lifted straight forward while the arms rest by the sides.
pg124_im001_seg004_v1: Standing scale on one foot with the other leg raised straight up in front, one arm reaching toward the leg and the other extended sideways.
pg124_im001_seg005_v1: Standing scale with one leg lifted vertically to the side, one arm stretched outward and the other hand behind the head.
pg124_im001_seg006_v1: Standing scale with the raised leg bent backward and held by both hands behind the body while balancing on one foot.
pg124_n0018: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute standing scale and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg124_n0022: A V-sit is a strength and balance exercise where a gymnast supports the body on the hands while keeping the legs extended in a “V” shape.
pg124_n0023: It develops core strength, flexibility, and body control and is often used in training, conditioning, and some competitive gymnastics routines.
pg124_n0024: There are various V-sit including tucked V-sit, L-sit and V-sit press.
pg124_n0025: The following steps will help you practice a V-sit:
pg124_n0029: Sit on the floor keeping your legs straight in front of you;
pg124_n0032: Place hands on the floor positioning them slightly behind your hips for support;
pg124_n0035: Engage your core tighten and abdominal muscles;
pg124_n0038: Lift your legs raise them off the ground while keeping them straight;
pg125_n0005: Hold the V position keeping your back slightly leaned back for balance, Figure 4.12; and
pg125_n0008: Control the lowering slowly and bring your legs back down to finish.
pg125_im001: Gymnast performing a V-sit, balancing on the hands with the torso slightly leaned back and both legs together extended straight upward.
pg125_n0015: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a V-sit and practice it.
pg125_n0019: A straddle planche is an advanced strength and balance skill where a gymnast holds the body parallel to the ground, supported only by the hands, with the legs spread apart in a straddle position.
pg125_n0020: It requires core strength, shoulder stability, and balance and is often seen in men’s gymnastics, calisthenics, and breakdancing.
pg125_n0021: The following steps will help you practice straddle planche:
pg125_n0025: Place your hands on the floor, shoulder-width apart;
pg125_n0028: Lean forward shifting weight onto your arms while engaging your core and shoulders;
pg125_n0031: Straighten your arms completely keeping elbows locked to maintain stability;
pg125_n0034: Extend legs into a straddle opening legs wide while keeping them parallel to the floor, Figure 4.13; and
pg125_n0037: Hold the position to maintain control, keeping your body straight and strong.
pg126_im001: Gymnast performing a straddle planche on parallettes, supporting the body with straight arms while holding the torso nearly horizontal and the legs split.
pg126_n0007: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a straddle planche hold and practice it.
pg126_n0011: A split press to handstand is a skill where a gymnast lifts into a handstand from a split position on the floor without using momentum.
pg126_n0012: It requires flexibility, core strength, and controlled balance and is commonly used in floor, beam, and parallel bar routines.
pg126_n0013: The following steps will help you practice split press handstand:
pg126_n0017: Sit on the floor in a front split (one leg forward, one leg back);
pg126_n0020: Place hands on the floor positioning them near the front leg for support;
pg126_n0023: Engage core and push through arms activating your core, shoulders, and arms to begin lifting;
pg126_n0026: Lift hips and rear leg first followed by the front leg;
pg126_n0029: Press into a controlled handstand slowly bringing both legs together overhead while maintaining balance; and
pg126_n0032: Hold the handstand keeping core tight, arms straight, and body aligned, Figure 4.14.
pg127_im001_seg001_v1_crop_v1: Gymnast in a front split, arms straight with hands on the floor beside the hips and chest lifted, preparing for a split press to handstand.
pg127_im001_seg002_v1_crop_v1: Gymnast raising the hips into a pike-like position with both hands on the floor and legs split, transitioning into a split press to handstand.
pg127_im001_seg003_v1: Gymnast holding an L-sit on straight arms with both legs extended forward off the floor.
pg127_im001_seg004_v1: Gymnast balancing on the hands in a tucked press position, knees close to the chest with both legs extended forward.
pg127_n0015: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a split press to handstand with one leg and practice it.
pg127_n0019: Equipment-based routines are planned movements that gymnasts perform using special gym tools like the beam, bars, rings, or vault.
pg127_n0020: Each routine shows the gymnast’s strength, balance, and skills on that equipment.
pg127_n0021: The equipment based routines includes Griping, mounts, dismounts, Cast, swing, hangs, and holdings.
pg127_n0025: Gripping refers to how a gymnast holds onto an apparatus.
pg127_n0026: Proper gripping is crucial for control, safety, and performance in various skills and routines.
pg127_n0027: The various types of grips include the neutral grip, false grip, and above-the-ring grip.
pg127_n0031: A neutral grip is when the palms face each other while gripping an apparatus.
pg127_n0032: This grip is commonly used on parallel bars, rings, rope climbing and in some conditioning exercises to provide a natural wrist position and greater stability.
pg127_n0033: The following steps will help you practice a neutral grip on rings:
pg128_n0005: Hold the ring with your palm facing each other while your thumbs wrap around it, Figure 4.15;
pg128_n0008: Keep your wrists neutral, not flexed or extended; and
pg128_n0011: Engage your shoulder to maintain stability.
pg128_im001: Hands demonstrating a neutral grip on gymnastic rings, with palms facing each other and thumbs wrapped around the rings.
pg128_n0016: Go through reliable sources to find out how neutral grip is executed in parallel bars, and uneven bars, then practice it.
pg128_n0020: A false grip is a specialised grip used primarily on rings and sometimes on the high bar.
pg128_n0021: It involves positioning the wrist above the rings or bar, allowing gymnasts to transition smoothly into strength moves like muscle-ups, iron crosses, and levers.
pg128_n0022: The following steps will help you practice false grip on a ring:
pg128_n0026: Place your hands on the rings with the inside of your wrist resting directly on top, Figure 4.16;
pg128_n0029: Grip firmly while keeping the wrist bent so that your body weight is supported by the wrist, not just the fingers; and
pg128_n0032: Engage the forearms and shoulders to maintain control and avoid slipping.
pg129_im001: False grip on a gymnastics ring, with the hand wrapped incorrectly around the ring.
pg129_n0008: Go through reliable sources to find out how false grip is executed on the parallel bars and uneven bars, then, practice it.
pg129_n0012: In gymnastics, the above-the-ring grip refers to a hand position where the gymnast supports bodyweight above the rings, rather than hanging below them.
pg129_n0013: This grip is commonly used in support positions and advanced strength skills on the still rings.
pg129_n0014: The following steps will help you practice the above ring grip on a ring:
pg129_n0018: Grip the rings with the palms facing downward, Figure 4.17;
pg129_n0021: Keep the wrists and forearms above the rings, providing stability; and
pg129_n0024: Engaged shoulders, wrists, and core to maintain control.
pg129_im002: Above-the-ring grip on a gymnastics ring, with the wrist and forearm positioned above the ring for support.
pg130_n0004: Search from the internet and other reliable sources on how to execute above the ring grip and practice it.

pg130_n0012: A mount in gymnastics is the way a gymnast gets onto an apparatus at the start of their routine.
pg130_n0013: It serves as the first skill and sets the tone for the rest of the performance.
pg130_n0014: Mounts can be simple or complex, depending on the gymnast’s skill level and apparatus being used.
pg130_n0015: There are various forms of mounts including a balance beam mounts, uneven bar mounts, parallel bar mounts, and pommel horse mounts.
pg130_n0019: Balance beam mounts are the techniques or movements gymnasts use to get onto the balance beam at the beginning of a routine.
pg130_n0020: A balance beam mounts require more precision because the beam is narrow.
pg130_n0021: The following steps will help you practice a balance beam mount progressively:
pg130_n0025: Stand at the end of the beam;
pg130_n0028: Place your hands on the beam and lift your body, landing with your stomach on the beam; and
pg130_n0031: Push up into a sitting position or swing your legs into a straddle sit, Figure 4.18.
pg130_im001: Gymnast mounting a balance beam with both hands on the beam, one foot planted, and the other leg raised overhead.
pg130_n0033: Figure 4.18: Mounting on a beam balance
pg131_n0005: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a jump to beam balance mount and practice it.
pg131_n0009: Mounting the uneven bars refers to how a gymnast gets onto the bars to begin their routine.
pg131_n0010: The following steps will help you practice mounting on uneven bars:
pg131_n0017: Jump up and grip the bar, Figure 4.19;
pg131_n0020: Extend legs into a glide swing;
pg131_n0023: Pull feet to the bar and push into front support;
pg131_n0026: For high bar: jump and straddle legs to catch the bar in mid-air; and
pg131_im001: Gymnast mounting the uneven bars, upside down with both hands gripping the low bar and legs extended vertically above it.
pg131_n0035: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a mounting on uneven bars and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg132_n0005: Mounting the parallel bars is the act of getting onto the apparatus to start a routine.
pg132_n0006: The following steps will help you practice mounting on parallel bars:
pg132_n0010: Jump and grab the bars with both hands;
pg132_n0013: Swing your legs forward while pulling up;
pg132_n0016: Land in a straight-arm support position and exit; Then:
pg132_n0019: Place hands on the bars and jump up;
pg132_n0022: Lean forward while pushing into a handstand, Figure 4.20; and
pg132_n0025: Hold the handstand briefly before transitioning into the routine.
pg132_im001: Gymnast mounting the parallel bars, pushing up on straight arms with legs raised forward above the bars.
pg132_n0031: Search from the internet and other sources on how to execute a swing-up mount on the parallel bars and practice it.
pg132_n0035: What physical skills are necessary for a gymnast to perform successfully on the uneven bars?
pg132_n0039: Mounting the pommel horse is the way a gymnast gets onto the pommel horse to begin their routine.
pg132_n0040: The following steps will help you practice mounting on pommel horse:
pg133_n0010: Jump up and place one leg over while holding the handles;
pg133_n0013: Swing legs to start a scissor motion and exit; Then:
pg133_n0019: Jump and glide onto the pommel horse while holding the handles; and
pg133_n0022: Immediately begin your routine with leg swings, Figure 4.21.
pg133_im001: Gymnast mounting a pommel horse with both hands on the body of the horse and legs extended together above the handles.

pg133_n0041: A dismount is the skill in a gymnastics routine where the gymnast leaves the apparatus and lands on the floor in a controlled manner.
pg133_n0042: It is one of the most essential elements of a routine because it shows control, difficulty, and precision.
pg133_n0043: There are various types of dismounts grouped by the apparatus used.
pg133_n0044: It includes balance beam dismounts, uneven bars dismount, parallel bars dismount, and pommel horse dismounts.
pg133_n0045: Others are the ring dismounts and vault dismounts.
pg133_n0046: The following steps will help you practice the various dismounts:
pg134_n0005: Dismounting the balance beam is the way a gymnast skillfully leaves the balance beam at the end of their routine.
pg134_n0006: The following steps will help you practice dismounting from balance beam:
pg134_n0010: Stand at the end of the beam, facing forward;
pg134_n0013: Push off with your legs, jumping into the air.
pg134_n0014: Keep your body straight or tucked depending on the style, Figure 4.22;
pg134_n0017: Land with both feet with slightly bent knees; and
pg134_n0020: Hold the landing position with arms up for stability.
pg134_im001: Gymnast performing a backward-arching dismount above the balance beam.
pg134_n0026: Cartwheel dismount is a type of dismount from the balance beam where the gymnast performs a cartwheel at the end of the beam as a transition to leave the apparatus.
pg134_n0027: The following steps will help you practice cartwheel dismounting from a balance beam:
pg134_n0031: Place hands on the beam as you prepare to move into the cartwheel or round-off;
pg134_n0034: Perform a cartwheel or round-off (a round-off helps with more rotation and power); and
pg134_n0037: As you complete the cartwheel or round-off, push off with your hands and land with your feet on the floor, Figure 4.23.
pg135_im001: Gymnast performing a cartwheel dismount on a mat, with both hands on the surface, one leg extended upward and the other leg reaching toward the landing.
pg135_n0007: Search from the internet and other sources on how to execute a cartwheel dismount and practice it repeatedly until you master the skill.
pg135_n0011: A scissor dismount is a way of finishing a pommel horse routine by using a scissor movement to exit the apparatus with control and style.
pg135_n0012: The following steps will help you practice scissor dismounting from a pommel horse:
pg135_n0016: Start swinging your legs in a controlled scissor motion;
pg135_n0019: Swing your body and legs into a controlled dismount with one final powerful leg swing, Figure 4.24; and
pg135_n0022: Focus on landing cleanly and maintaining balance.
pg136_im001: Gymnast performing a scissor dismount from a pommel horse, supporting his body on one handle as his legs split and swing off to the side.
pg136_n0007: A swing-off dismount is a type of gymnastics dismount in which the gymnast uses a swinging motion to build momentum and then releases the apparatus to land on the floor.
pg136_n0008: The following steps will help you practice swing-off dismounting from a pommel horse:
pg136_n0012: Swing both legs and push off the pommel horse with momentum, Figure 4.25; and
pg136_n0015: As you leave the pommel horse, rotate and land cleanly with soft knees.
pg136_im002: Gymnast demonstrating a pommel horse swing-off dismount, body stretched sideways with legs together and one hand pushing off the horse.
pg137_n0004: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a pommel horse dismount with a hop and practice it.
pg137_n0008: The vault itself is the dismount from the vaulting table.
pg137_n0009: After completing the vault, ensure that you land properly to show control.
pg137_n0010: The following steps will help you practice it:
pg137_n0014: Push off the vaulting table with force, using your arms to propel yourself into the air;
pg137_n0017: Perform any required flips or twists (depending on the vault style); and
pg137_n0020: Spot your landing area then land with both feet simultaneously, keeping your knees slightly bent to absorb the impact, Figure 4.26.
pg137_im001: Gymnast arching forward above a vaulting table while performing a vault dismount.
pg137_n0025: Search from internet and other sources on how to execute a simple tuck-jump vault dismount and practice it.
pg138_n0003: Dismount at the rear end of the swing
pg138_n0005: A dismount at the rear end of the swing refers to a technique where a gymnast performs their dismount while at the farthest point of the swing typically just before their body starts to swing back toward the bar.
pg138_n0006: This is a common dismount technique for the uneven bars.
pg138_n0007: The following steps will help you practice the dismount at the rear end of the swing:
pg138_n0011: Begin by swinging your body back and forth with controlled momentum;
pg138_n0014: Extend your legs and engage your core as you approach the rear end to prepare for the dismount;
pg138_n0017: Ensure you reach the maximum height of the swing when you are at the rear end, with your hips above the bar;
pg138_n0020: Extended your legs, and slightly arche your body, ready for the release;
pg138_n0023: Push off the bar at the rear end of the swing, with your arms while tucking your knees or keeping them extended depending on the type of dismount you are doing;
pg138_n0026: Release the bar at the peak of the swing, initiating your rotation (backflip, twist, etc.) while keeping your body tight and controlled, Figure 4.27; and
pg138_n0029: Spot the landing early as you finish the rotation and focus on landing with both feet at the same time with knees bent.

pg139_n0009: The skin-the-cat dismount is a movement in gymnastics, commonly performed on rings or a horizontal bar.
pg139_n0010: It involves rotating the body backwards through the arms while hanging, passing through an inverted position, and then returning to a hang or dismounting completely.
pg139_n0011: The following steps will help you practice skin-the-cat dismount:
pg139_n0015: Hang from a bar or ring with an overhand grip;
pg139_n0018: Tuck your legs and rotate backwards, bringing your feet through your arms and over your head;
pg139_n0021: Pass through a controlled upside-down position;
pg139_n0024: Continue the rotation, lowering your legs back down toward the ground, Figure 4.28; and
pg139_n0027: You can let go and land on your feet instead of returning to a hang.

pg140_n0012: Cast is a fundamental skill performed on the uneven bars or the parallel bars and high bars.
pg140_n0013: It involves lifting the body from a front support position to a higher position, often in preparation for more advanced skills.
pg140_n0014: There are four main types of cast:
pg140_n0018: Basic cast: The gymnast pushes away from the bar and lifts their body upward from a front support position;
pg140_n0021: Cast to handstand: The gymnast continues the movement until they reach a fully extended handstand;
pg140_n0024: Straddle cast: Performed by spreading the legs apart (straddle) while lifting into a handstand; and
pg140_n0027: Cast to kip: A movement that creates momentum to move into a kip, a common bar skill used in routines.
pg140_n0029: The cast helps develop shoulder, arm, and core strength leading to more advanced bar skills like giants and releases.
pg140_n0030: The skill is used in transitions and as a connecting element in a bar routine.
pg140_n0031: Practicing a basic cast in gymnastics, especially on uneven bars or parallel bars, requires proper technique, strength, and body control.
pg140_n0032: The following steps will help you practice cast:
pg140_n0036: Begin in a front support position on the bar (arms straight, body tight, and hips against the bar);
pg140_n0039: Your hands should grip the bar firmly with straight arms and shoulders slightly over the bar;
pg140_n0042: Lean forward slightly and push through your shoulders, creating momentum;
pg140_n0045: Engage your core and glutes to keep your body straight;
pg140_n0048: Swing your legs slightly backwards and then kick them forward while squeezing your core.

pg141_n0008: Keep your body tight and avoid arching your back while pushing down on the bar to extend your cast higher, figure 4.29;
pg141_n0011: As your body reaches the highest point of the cast, control the descent by keeping your muscles engaged and land back in the front support position with control; and
pg141_n0014: Repeat multiple times, gradually increasing the height of your cast.

pg141_n0032: In gymnastics, hangs refers to the position where a gymnast holds onto the bar or rings with their body suspended in the air.
pg141_n0033: Hangs are fundamental for building muscles in
pg142_n0004: There are various hangs including straight arm hang, flexed arm hang, pike arm hangs and inverted hang.
pg142_n0008: Straight arm hang refers to a position where a gymnast hangs from a bar with arms fully extended and their body in a straight or slightly hollowed position.
pg142_n0009: This is a fundamental position used in various swings, releases, and transitions.
pg142_n0010: The following steps will help you practice straight arm hang:
pg142_n0014: Find a suitable bar, a high bar for men, and an uneven bar for women, ensure it is high enough relative to your height;
pg142_n0017: Grip the bar using an overhand grip with hands shoulder-width apart, fingers wrapped securely around, and thumbs under the bar for better grip;
pg142_n0020: Keep your arms fully extended but not locked engaging your shoulders and lats, and maintain a slightly hollow body position;
pg142_n0023: Keep your legs together and slightly in front of your body, fingers pointed; and
pg142_n0026: Hold for 10-30 seconds to develop grip and shoulder endurance and gradually increase your time as you get stronger, Figure 4.30.
pg142_im001: Gymnast performing a straight arm hang on the upper bar, with both hands gripping overhead, arms fully extended, body straight, and legs together.
pg143_n0005: A flexed arm hang is an upper-body strength exercise where you hang from a bar with your chin above the bar and arms flexed.
pg143_n0006: It is commonly used in gymnastics to measure upper body endurance and grip strength.
pg143_n0007: The following steps will help you practice the flexed arm hang:
pg143_n0011: Use a sturdy bar that allows you to hang freely without touching the ground;
pg143_n0014: Grip the bar using an overhand grip or underhand grip with hands positioned shoulder-width apart.
pg143_n0015: Use a step, box, or have someone to lift you into position if you are not strong enough to pull-up to get your chin above the bar;
pg143_n0018: Keep your chin above the bar without resting it on the bar while engaging your arms, shoulders, and core to maintain the hold, Figure 4.31;
pg143_n0021: Hold on until your muscles fatigue and you can no longer maintain form, aim to increase the hang time as you get used to it.
pg143_n0022: In competitions, the person who can hold the longest is usually the winner.

pg144_n0008: A pike hang is a hanging position on a bar where the gymnast keeps their legs straight and lifted in a pike position, Figure 4.32.
pg144_n0009: This skill helps develop core strength, flexibility, and body control for more advanced bar movements.
pg144_n0010: The following steps will help you practice a pike hang:
pg144_n0014: Grip the bar using an overhand grip or an underhand grip keeping hands shoulder-width apart;
pg144_n0017: Keep your shoulders active and tighten your abs and hip flexors;
pg144_n0020: Keep your legs straight and together, toes pointing while lifting them to hip height, creating an “L” shape with your body; and
pg144_n0023: Hold the pike hang for at least 5-10 seconds at first and aim to increase it.

pg145_n0005: An inverted hang is a position where a gymnast hangs upside down from a bar, rings, or another apparatus with body fully extended in a controlled shape.
pg145_n0006: This skill helps develop core strength, body awareness, and inversion control, which are essential for flips, giants, and other advanced skills.
pg145_n0007: There are various forms of the inverted hangs including straight body, tuck, pike inverted hangs and an inverted hang on rings.
pg145_n0008: The following are general steps that will help you practice the inverted hangs:
pg145_n0012: Hold the apparatus using an overhand grip (on a bar) or a neutral grip (on rings);
pg145_n0015: Pull yourself upside down with legs tucked or straddled using your core and shoulders to control the motion.
pg145_n0016: Keep your arms slightly bent or straight, depending on the apparatus;
pg145_n0019: Hold the position by engaging your core, back, and shoulders keeping your legs together and pointed for proper form, Figure 4.33; and
pg145_n0022: Lower yourself in a controlled manner to exit avoiding swinging too much.
pg145_n0023: If on rings, return to a normal hang before dismounting.

pg146_n0005: A tucked pullover is a fundamental bar skill where a gymnast starts from a hanging position, pulls their legs up in a tuck, and rotates around the bar to end in a front support position on top of the bar.
pg146_n0006: This skill is commonly taught to beginners on uneven bars as it helps develop strength and body control for more advanced bar skills.
pg146_n0007: The following steps will help you practice a tucked pull over:
pg146_n0011: Stand under the low bar and grab it with an overhand grip with hands shoulder width apart;
pg146_n0014: Hang with arms straight and feet slightly off the ground while engaging your core and arms;
pg146_n0017: Pull your knees toward your chest in a tight tuck position keeping your chin tucked and eyes looking toward the bar;
pg146_n0020: Push with your arms as the hips get closer to the bar to help rotate your body over keeping legs tucked and letting your back roll over the bar smoothly, Figure 4.34; and
pg146_n0023: Finish by extending your arms as you press your hips onto the bar, straighten the legs ending in a front support position.

pg147_n0005: Swings are a fundamental movement in gymnastics that involves a controlled, rhythmic motion of the body around a bar or set of rings.
pg147_n0006: It includes forward and back swings, and tap swing on bars.
pg147_n0007: Other swings on bars include straight-body swings, pike swings, straddle swings and giant swings.

pg147_n0011: The forward and back swing on rings is a swinging movement where a gymnast swings the body forward and backward while hanging from the rings, Figure 4.35.
pg147_n0012: They are typically part of the basic swing technique on rings.
pg147_n0013: The following steps will help you practice the forward and backward swing on rings:
pg147_n0017: Hang from the rings with your arms fully extended and feet off the ground.
pg147_n0018: Keep your body straight, grip the rings firmly, engage your core, and maintain a slight bend in your knees;
pg147_n0021: Lean your upper body slightly backward and push your legs behind you.
pg147_n0022: Use your arms and shoulders to help create momentum, applying a gentle pull as you lean back;
pg147_n0025: Let the momentum carry your body forward.
pg147_n0026: As your legs swing ahead, kick your hips upward toward the rings while allowing your upper body to follow naturally; and
pg147_n0029: When you reach the peak of the forward swing, let your legs extend in front of you.
pg147_n0030: Then begin leaning backward again to smoothly transition into the backward phase of the swing.

pg148_n0009: A tap swing on bars is a gymnastics skill in which the gymnast swings back and forth on the bars in a controlled and rhythmic motion.
pg148_n0010: The skill builds momentum for more advanced skills such as releases, dismounts, or transitions between bars.
pg148_n0011: It is often one of the first swinging techniques learned in developing bar routines.
pg148_n0012: The following steps will help you practice tap swing:
pg148_n0016: Grip a bar with arms straight and legs hanging down, engage the shoulders and activate the core to maintain a stable body position;
pg148_n0019: Swing your legs behind you, slightly bending at the hips and knees.
pg148_n0020: Keep your body tight and controlled to prevent swinging wildly;
pg148_n0023: Push your hips to create momentum and allow your hips to tap the bar just as your legs come forward, giving the swing more power; and
pg148_n0026: Move your body in an arch, bringing your feet above the bar, and use your arms and core to control the motion and prepare for the next swing, Figure 4.36.

pg149_n0013: In gymnastics, holding refers to the action of maintaining a position on an apparatus for a specific amount of time.
pg149_n0014: This is often done to demonstrate strength, coordination, stability, agility, and control in a routine.
pg149_n0015: Holding can be done in various positions, whether on the rings, bars, beam, or floor, and is commonly used to showcase the gymnast’s ability to maintain balance and body control.

pg149_n0020: Hold on the rings refers to the action of gripping the gymnastic rings tightly with hands and keeping body steady, either by hanging below or holding one-self up above the rings without moving.

pg150_n0026: Hold your legs together and stay upright with your core (stomach muscles) tight;

pg007_n0011_easy_read:
Netball is a team sport.
Players use their hands to pass the ball and shoot it into the other team's goal to score.
pg007_n0012_easy_read:
Male and female players play netball.
They play it in competitions and for fun.
pg007_n0013_easy_read:
Playing netball can:
- provide job opportunities
- improve physical health
- help players develop important life skills
pg007_n0014_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn about:
- the concept of netball
- safety measures in netball
- netball skills
- netball rules
pg007_n0015_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you analyse netball and play it well and with confidence.
pg007_n0019_easy_read: Netball is a game with set positions and skills.
pg007_n0023_easy_read:
Netball is a team sport.
Players use their hands to play on a rectangular court with clearly marked areas.
pg007_n0024_easy_read:
A team has 7 players.
Each player has a specific role and position.
These positions limit where players can move.
pg007_n0025_easy_read:
Players must pass the ball to a teammate within 3 seconds after receiving it.
They do this to move the ball and score in their attacking goal.
pg007_n0026_easy_read:
The game has 4 quarters.
Each quarter lasts 15 minutes.
There is a 4-minute break between the 1st and 2nd quarters.
There is a 12-minute break at half time.
There is a 4-minute break between the 3rd and 4th quarters.
pg007_n0028_easy_read: A team scores when the Goal Shooter (GS) or Goal Attack (GA) shoots the ball through the other team's hoop.
pg007_n0029_easy_read: At the end of the match, the team with the most goals wins.
pg007_n0030_easy_read:
If the game ends in a tie, extra time or other tie-breaking rules may be used.
This depends on the competition rules.
pg007_n0031_easy_read:
Netball helps players build:
- teamwork
- discipline
- strategic thinking
- physical fitness
- hand-eye coordination
- spatial awareness
pg007_n0032_easy_read:
Netball is inclusive.
People can take part whatever their skill level, gender, or ability.
This makes netball a valuable activity for fun and competition.
pg008_n0005_easy_read:
Basic netball facilities are:
- a court with goal posts

People can play netball outdoors or indoors.
pg008_n0006_easy_read:
The equipment changes with the level of play.
It can be for recreation or for professional play.
pg008_n0007_easy_read:
However, these items are basic requirements:
- netballs
- shoes
- bibs
pg008_n0011_easy_read:
People play netball on a flat, firm, rectangular court.
The court has specific markings for smooth play.
pg008_n0012_easy_read:
A standard netball court is 30.5 metres long and 15.25 metres wide.
The court has 3 sections:
- the attacking third
- the centre third
- the defensive third
pg008_n0013_easy_read:
The court features are:
- a centre circle
- 2 goal circles, each with a radius of 4.9 metres
- the sidelines
- the goal lines

Figure 1.1 shows these features.
pg009_n0005_easy_read:
Look at a netball court at your school.
Identify all the markings.
Measure the playing area.
Then decide if the court is standard or not.
pg009_n0009_easy_read: Netball goalposts are necessary for scoring.
pg009_n0010_easy_read:
Each court has 2 goalposts.
1 goalpost is at each end.
They are at the centre of the goal line, inside the goal circle.
pg009_n0011_easy_read:
The goalposts are 65 mm to 100 mm in diameter.
They are 3.05 m high.
They go into the ground.
A ring is fixed at the top of each goalpost.
pg009_n0012_easy_read:
The ring is 15 mm thick.
It has a 150 mm long connection to the post.
pg009_n0013_easy_read:
The ring has an internal diameter of 380 mm.
A net is fitted to the ring.
pg009_n0014_easy_read:
The net is open at both ends.
It is 380 mm to 457 mm long, as shown in Figure 1.2.
pg009_n0033_easy_read:
The netball is round, as shown in Figure 1.3.
It is made of leather, rubber, or another suitable synthetic material.
pg009_n0034_easy_read: The netball measures 690 mm to 710 mm in circumference.
pg010_n0004_easy_read:
The standard netball is size 4 for players below 10 years old.
The standard netball is size 5 for players above 10 years old.
pg010_n0010_easy_read:
Netball shoes are non-slip sports shoes.
They are made for the strong side-to-side movements that players make on the netball court.
Figure 14.
pg010_n0011_easy_read:
The netball shoes have rubber soles.
The rubber soles give stability, a better grip, and easy pivots.
They keep the foot on the sole and help protect players from slipping.
pg010_n0017_easy_read: In netball, player bibs are used to show each player's position on the court.
pg010_n0018_easy_read:
Player bibs are sleeveless vests.
They have large letters on the front and back to show the player's role, as shown in Figure 1.5.
pg010_n0019_easy_read:
Players wear bibs over the uniform.
This helps teammates, opponents, and officials recognise the players and their positions easily during the game.
pg011_n0008_easy_read:
Watch netball training and matches.
Identify other equipment used in netball that this book does not mention.
pg011_n0012_easy_read:
To play netball safely, players must take care.
This helps protect themselves and other people from injuries such as dislocations, fractures, or wounds.
pg011_n0013_easy_read:
Netball has quick movements, jumping, and sudden stops.
So, it is important to follow these safety measures before, during, and after the game:
pg011_n0019_easy_read:
Warm-up:
Do stretching and light exercises.
This prepares the muscles, lowers the risk of injury, and improves performance.
pg011_n0022_easy_read:
First aid kit:
Make sure a first aid kit is at the playing area for emergencies.
pg011_n0025_easy_read:
Inspect the playing area and the equipment:
Check the netball's pressure and quality.
Remove debris, wet spots, and unsafe objects from the court.
pg011_n0028_easy_read:
Wear proper gear:
Use suitable netball shoes, uniforms, and protective gear if needed.
pg011_n0034_easy_read:
Observe the rules:
Follow netball rules to avoid fouls and make sure the game is fair.
pg011_n0037_easy_read:
Communicate with teammates:
Use verbal and non-verbal signals to prevent collisions.
pg011_n0040_easy_read:
Be aware of your movements:
Avoid sudden stops or dangerous landings that may cause injury.
pg012_n0005_easy_read:
Respect opponents and officials.
Do not use trash talk or aggressive and disrespectful behaviour.
pg012_n0011_easy_read:
Cool down.
Do light stretching to relax your muscles, reduce stiffness, and slowly return to your pre-exercise level.
pg012_n0014_easy_read:
Report injuries.
Get medical help for any discomfort or injury during the game.
pg012_n0017_easy_read:
Rehydrate and rest.
Drink enough water and let your body recover after physical activity.

pg012_n0028_easy_read: The main aim of netball is to score goals by shooting the ball through the other team’s goal ring and stopping the other team from scoring.
pg012_n0029_easy_read: To play netball well, players need to develop key skills and techniques that improve their performance on the court.
pg012_n0030_easy_read: Techniques are the parts that make up a skill.
pg012_n0031_easy_read:
The skills include:
- passing
- movement
- shooting
- positioning
- defending

These skills help the player perform well.
They also help the team succeed.
pg012_n0035_easy_read: Passing is one of the most important skills in netball because players cannot run with the ball.
pg012_n0036_easy_read: Good passing keeps the ball moving smoothly, helps the team keep possession, and supports teamwork.
pg012_n0037_easy_read:
Players can use several types of passes to move the ball around the court.
Each pass has a different purpose for different situations.
pg012_n0038_easy_read:
Common types of passes are:
- chest pass
- bounce pass
- overhead pass
- shoulder pass
pg012_n0042_easy_read:
A chest pass is a 2-handed pass from the chest.
It is fast and accurate over short distances.
pg012_n0043_easy_read:
The chest pass works best when defender pressure is low.
It is good for quick passes between teammates.
pg012_n0044_easy_read:
The player pushes the ball forward with both hands.
The ball goes straight from the player’s chest to the teammate’s chest.
pg013_n0003_easy_read: This gives speed and precision, so it is good for short-range passes.
pg013_n0004_easy_read: Follow these steps to practise a chest pass:
pg013_n0008_easy_read:
Stand with your legs shoulder-width apart.
Bend your knees a little.
pg013_n0011_easy_read:
Hold the ball with 2 hands at chest height, as shown in Figure 1.6 (a).
This helps you keep a strong and stable grip.
pg013_n0014_easy_read:
Spread your fingers around the side of the ball.
Point your thumbs towards the back.
Keep your elbows bent and get ready to push the ball.
pg013_n0017_easy_read:
Push the ball forward.
Straighten your elbows, fingers, and thumbs.
Follow through after you release the ball.
This helps with accuracy and power, as shown in Figure 1.6 (b).
pg013_n0020_easy_read:
Step forward after you pass the ball.
Move your weight onto your front foot.
This helps move the ball forward and helps you keep your balance.
pg013_n0028_easy_read: Figure 1.6: How to do a chest pass
pg013_n0033_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practise the chest pass many times to master the skill.
pg013_n0037_easy_read:
A bounce pass is a way of passing the ball.
You throw the ball down towards the ground.
The ball bounces 1 time before it reaches the other player.
pg013_n0038_easy_read:
This pass helps you avoid defenders.
It travels low to the ground, so it is harder to intercept.
pg013_n0039_easy_read:
The ball should bounce about 2-thirds of the way to the target player.
Keep the bounce controlled so the pass is accurate.
pg013_n0040_easy_read: This pass is ideal for passing through tight spaces where
pg014_n0003_easy_read: The defenders stay close together. This helps the ball move more smoothly and lowers the chance of interception.
pg014_n0004_easy_read:
You can do a bounce pass with 1 hand or 2 hands.
You can pass from the front of the body or the side of the body.
pg014_n0005_easy_read: To practice a bounce pass, follow these steps:
pg014_n0009_easy_read:
Stand with your legs shoulder-width apart.
Bend your knees a little.
pg014_n0012_easy_read:
Hold the ball at chest height with 1 hand or 2 hands.
Keep your elbows out in front.
pg014_n0015_easy_read:
Spread your fingers on both sides of the ball.
Keep your thumbs behind the ball.
Point your fingers downward.
pg014_n0018_easy_read:
Step forward with your dominant foot.
Release the ball at wrist height.
Push the ball forward toward the ground, as shown in Figure 1.7.
pg014_n0021_easy_read: Aim for the ball to bounce a little over halfway between you and the receiver.

After you release the ball, extend your arms.

This pass is good for sending the ball over an opponent's head to teammates who are farther away on the court.
pg015_n0007_easy_read:
This pass is very useful when a player is under pressure.
It helps the player send the ball farther in an efficient way.
pg015_n0008_easy_read: To practice the overhead pass, follow these steps:

pg015_n0024_easy_read:
Follow through with your arms, wrists, and fingers.
This helps with accuracy and control of the ball.
pg015_n0033_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practice the overhead pass many times to master the skill.
pg016_n0005_easy_read: A shoulder pass is a strong pass with 1 hand from the shoulder.
pg016_n0006_easy_read:
This pass is best for long passes.
Use it when you need a quick, strong throw to reach a teammate who is far away.
pg016_n0007_easy_read:
Hold the ball with 1 hand near your shoulder.
Push it forward with force.
This pass is best for longer, faster passes.
pg016_n0008_easy_read:
This pass needs good hand-eye coordination.
This helps you pass accurately and move the ball well across the court.
pg016_n0009_easy_read: To practise the shoulder pass, follow these steps:

pg016_n0016_easy_read:
Bend your elbow to a 90-degree angle.
Use your other hand to support the ball.
pg016_n0019_easy_read:
Place your feet shoulder-width apart.
Put 1 foot in front of the other.
pg016_n0022_easy_read:
Take away your supporting hand.
Use your dominant arm to push the ball towards your target, as shown in Figure 1.9.
pg016_n0025_easy_read:
Use your fingers to guide the ball.
Move your arm through the pass for accuracy and control.
pg016_n0033_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practise the shoulder pass many times to master the skill.
pg016_n0037_easy_read: Catching the ball means stopping a ball that is moving through the air and taking hold of it.
pg016_n0038_easy_read:
Catching is very important.
It helps you:
- keep possession
- keep the game moving
- set up attacking plays
pg016_n0039_easy_read: A good catch lets players pass or shoot quickly and accurately.
pg016_n0040_easy_read: Effective ways to catch the ball include:
pg017_n0005_easy_read: This is the safest and most used catching technique.
pg017_n0006_easy_read: A player uses both hands to catch the ball. This gives a firmer grip and better control.
pg017_n0007_easy_read: Players often use a 2-handed catch when the ball comes fast or rebounds.
pg017_n0008_easy_read: Players stretch their arms toward the ball. They spread their fingers wide. They take the force of the ball by pulling it toward their chest.
pg017_n0009_easy_read: This method gives better control. It lowers the risk of fumbling. It helps the player pass or shoot more accurately.
pg017_n0010_easy_read: To practise the 2-handed catch, follow these steps:
pg017_n0014_easy_read: Keep your body balanced. Keep your eyes on the ball. This helps you follow its flight and see where it will go.
pg017_n0017_easy_read: Stretch your arms toward the ball. Spread your fingers to make a shape like the round shape of the ball.
pg017_n0020_easy_read: Catch the ball firmly. Bring your palms and fingers together. This gives you a secure grip.
pg017_n0023_easy_read: After you catch the ball, pull it back toward your chest. This helps you keep control and get ready for the next move, as shown in Figure 1.10.
pg017_n0029_easy_read: Players use this technique when the ball is out of reach, for example during a high pass or a deflection.
pg017_n0030_easy_read: This technique needs quick reflexes, strong hand-eye coordination, and grip strength. These skills help the player control the ball before holding it with both hands.
pg017_n0031_easy_read: This technique is riskier than a 2-handed catch. It is useful in fast situations when a player needs to react quickly.
pg017_n0032_easy_read: To practise the 1-handed catch, follow these steps:
pg017_n0036_easy_read: Keep your body balanced. Keep your eyes on the ball. This helps you follow its flight path.
pg018_n0005_easy_read:
Stretch your arm toward the ball.
Place your fingers so they match the shape of the ball.
pg018_n0008_easy_read:
Catch the ball firmly with the palm and fingers of 1 hand.
Keep a strong grip when the ball touches your hand, as shown in Figure 1.11.
pg018_n0011_easy_read:
Pull the ball back toward your body to hold it safely.
Use your other hand to help.
pg018_n0018_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practice the 2-handed catch and the 1-handed catch many times to master the skills.
pg018_n0022_easy_read:
Good movement and footwork are very important.
They help players create space, keep possession of the ball, and stay quick on the court.
pg018_n0023_easy_read:
Players must follow the footwork rules.
This helps them avoid violations and play well.
pg018_n0024_easy_read:
The main footwork techniques are:
- pivoting
- dodging
- landing
pg018_n0028_easy_read:
Pivoting means keeping 1 foot on the ground.
At the same time, the player turns on that foot to pass or shoot.
pg018_n0029_easy_read:
Pivoting creates space on the court.
It does this by changing the direction of play.
pg018_n0030_easy_read:
After receiving the ball, a player can pivot on 1 foot.
This lets the player change direction quickly without losing possession of the ball.
pg018_n0031_easy_read: This technique helps the player stay in control while getting ready to pass or shoot.
pg018_n0032_easy_read: To practice pivoting, follow these steps:
pg019_n0005_easy_read:
Receive the ball.
Then stop completely with 1 or 2 feet firmly on the ground.
pg019_n0008_easy_read:
Choose your pivot foot.
The pivot foot stays still.
Put your weight on that foot.
pg019_n0011_easy_read:
Turn on your pivot foot.
Turn your body in the direction you want to move.
Keep control of the ball with your other hand.
pg019_n0014_easy_read:
Keep your body low and balanced.
Bend your knees a little to stay stable during the pivot.
pg019_n0017_easy_read:
After you pivot, step with your free foot in the direction you want to go.
Make the change of direction smooth and controlled, as shown in Figure 1.12.
pg019_n0020_easy_read:
Pay attention to what is around you.
After the pivot, get ready for the next pass or play.
pg019_n0030_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practice pivoting many times to learn the skill well.
pg019_n0034_easy_read:
Dodging is a quick sideways movement.
Players use it to get away from defenders and make space for a pass or shot.
pg019_n0035_easy_read: It needs agility and quick decisions to get away from the
pg020_n0004_easy_read: To practice dodging, follow these steps:
pg020_n0008_easy_read:
Keep low.
Bend your knees.
Keep your body balanced.
pg020_n0011_easy_read: Push off quickly with your non-dominant foot to start the dodge.
pg020_n0014_easy_read: Move quickly to 1 side to get away from the defender, as shown in Figure 1.13.
pg020_n0017_easy_read: Sprint away to make space for a pass or a shot.
pg020_n0020_easy_read:
Be ready to change direction again if needed.
Stay hard to predict.
pg020_n0025_easy_read: Practice dodging again and again with different drills to master the skill.
pg020_n0029_easy_read: Landing is when a player stops after receiving the ball, either from a jump or from moving across the court.
pg020_n0030_easy_read: The player lands on 1 foot or on both feet.
pg020_n0031_easy_read: Proper landing techniques are very important for balance and for preventing injury.
pg020_n0032_easy_read:
Bend your knees and land softly.
This gives you a stable position and lowers the risk of injury or falls.
pg020_n0033_easy_read:
There are 2 landing techniques:
- 1-foot landing
- 2-foot landing
pg021_n0005_easy_read: A 1-foot landing happens when a player catches the ball while moving and lands on 1 foot.
pg021_n0006_easy_read:
The 1st foot that touches the ground is the landing foot.
The 2nd foot is the pivot foot.
The player can use the pivot foot to step in any direction before passing or shooting.
This helps the player make quick decisions on the court.
pg021_n0007_easy_read: To practise 1-foot landing, follow these steps:
pg021_n0011_easy_read:
Look at the ball.
Get ready for the landing while you are moving.
pg021_n0014_easy_read:
Land on 1 foot first.
This helps absorb impact and keep control, as shown in Figure 1.14.
pg021_n0017_easy_read:
Keep your knees slightly bent.
This helps you stay stable and balanced.
pg021_n0020_easy_read: Use the 2nd foot as a pivot to change direction before passing or shooting.
pg021_n0023_easy_read: Move the ball quickly to keep the game flowing well.
pg021_n0034_easy_read: A 2-foot landing happens when a player catches the ball and lands on both feet at the same time.
pg021_n0035_easy_read:
This technique gives the player more balance and stability.
The player can then choose which foot to use as the pivot foot before passing or shooting.
pg021_n0036_easy_read: This is especially useful when a player receives the ball under defensive pressure.
pg021_n0037_easy_read: To practise 2-foot landing, follow these steps:
pg021_n0041_easy_read:
Keep your eyes on the ball.
Get ready for the landing while you are moving.
pg021_n0044_easy_read:
Land on both feet at the same time.
This spreads your weight evenly and helps you keep control.
pg021_n0047_easy_read:
Keep your knees slightly bent.
This helps absorb impact and keep you stable, as shown in Figure 1.15.
pg022_n0005_easy_read:
Choose 1 foot as the pivot.
Use it to adjust your position for passing or shooting.
pg022_n0008_easy_read:
Stay balanced.
Decide quickly if you will pass, pivot, or shoot.
pg022_n0017_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practice 1-foot and 2-foot landing many times to master the skills.
pg022_n0021_easy_read:
Shooting means trying to score a goal.
A player throws the ball through the other team's hoop from inside the goal circle.
pg022_n0022_easy_read:
This is how a team scores goals.
It uses a 1-handed shot.
The player needs a strong shooting arm and a supporting non-shooting hand.
pg022_n0023_easy_read:
Shooting uses leg power and upper-body strength.
This helps players release the ball with a high arm and finish with a wrist action.
pg022_n0024_easy_read:
Only a Goal Shooter (GS) and a Goal Attack (GA) can shoot.
They can shoot only from inside the goal circle.
pg022_n0025_easy_read: Shooting technique directly affects a team's ability to score.
pg022_n0026_easy_read:
Learning proper shooting techniques improves accuracy.
It also increases the chance of successful shots.
pg023_n0005_easy_read: A steady, controlled shot for accuracy. Players usually take it with both hands.
pg023_n0006_easy_read: In this technique, the player stands still. The player looks at the target. Then the player shoots with a smooth, controlled movement for accuracy and consistency.
pg023_n0007_easy_read: To practise the set shot, follow these steps:
pg023_n0011_easy_read: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Keep your knees slightly bent for balance and stability.
pg023_n0014_easy_read: Hold the ball in front of you with both hands. Keep your shooting hand under the ball. Keep your non-shooting hand on the side.
pg023_n0017_easy_read: Look at the target. Aim for the centre of the goal or the highest point of the net.
pg023_n0020_easy_read: Push the ball upwards with a smooth movement. Use your legs for power. Stretch your arms fully, as shown in Figure 1.16.
pg023_n0023_easy_read: Finish the shot by flicking your wrist towards the target. Keep your shooting hand relaxed at the end. Point it towards the hoop.
pg023_n0031_easy_read: A jump shot is taken while the player is jumping. This helps the player avoid defenders and increases the shooting angle.
pg023_n0032_easy_read: When players jump as they shoot, they can create space between themselves and the defenders. This makes the shot harder to block. It also gives the shot a higher path.
pg023_n0033_easy_read: To practise the jump shot, follow these steps:
pg024_n0005_easy_read:
Stand with your feet as wide as your shoulders.
Bend your knees a little.
Get ready to jump up.
pg024_n0008_easy_read:
Hold the ball in front of you with both hands.
Put your shooting hand under the ball.
Put your other hand on the side to support it.
pg024_n0011_easy_read:
Look at the target.
Get ready to jump.
Aim at the centre of the goal ring.
pg024_n0014_easy_read:
Jump up and use your legs for power.
At the same time, stretch your arms.
Release the ball at the highest point of your jump, as shown in Figure 1.17.
pg024_n0017_easy_read:
Finish with a flick of your wrist.
Keep your shooting hand relaxed.
Point your shooting hand towards the hoop for accuracy.

pg024_n0025_easy_read:
In netball, a lay-up shot is a shooting technique from close range.
Players usually use it when moving towards the hoop and when they need to score quickly.
pg024_n0026_easy_read:
A lay-up shot is very useful when the player is close to the goalpost.
The player can do it by jumping off 1 foot.
Aim for a smooth and accurate shot.
pg024_n0027_easy_read: To practise the lay-up shot in netball, follow these steps:
pg024_n0031_easy_read:
Move towards the goalpost at a controlled pace.
Hold the ball in your hand.
Keep the defender behind you or at your side.
pg025_n0005_easy_read:
Step with your dominant foot.
Then jump from your non-dominant foot.
Bring the ball towards the goalpost, as shown in Figure 1.18.
pg025_n0008_easy_read:
Use your shooting hand to gently push the ball straight into the hoop.
Aim for a soft and accurate shot.
pg025_n0011_easy_read:
Keep your body in line.
Use your non-shooting hand for balance.
pg025_n0014_easy_read: Continue the movement of your arms and fingers in the direction of the ball.
pg025_n0020_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practice these shots again and again to master the skills:
- set shot
- jump shot
- lay-up shot
pg025_n0024_easy_read: Defending means stopping the other team from scoring and making them lose the ball.
pg025_n0025_easy_read:
Defenders must use:
- good position
- quick reflexes
- strong anticipation skills

This helps them challenge opponents and stop their attacking plays.
pg025_n0026_easy_read:
Good defensive play needs:
- focus
- discipline
- teamwork

This helps the team win back the ball and create chances to attack quickly.
pg025_n0027_easy_read:
The key defense techniques are:
- marking
- intercepting
- blocking
pg026_n0005_easy_read:
Marking is a defensive strategy.
A player follows an opponent and limits the opponent's movement.
This helps stop the opponent from getting the ball or making a pass.
pg026_n0006_easy_read: Marking helps limit an opponent's movement and passing options, as shown in Figure 1.19.
pg026_n0007_easy_read:
To mark well, a defender must stay close to the opponent.
The defender must keep about an arm's length away.
This lets the defender apply pressure without making a foul.
pg026_n0008_easy_read: Following the attacker's movements and taking a good position can limit the attacker's chance to receive passes or take a shot.
pg026_n0009_easy_read:
Good body position also pushes the opponent into less dangerous areas of the court.
This makes it harder for the opponent to help in the attack.
pg026_n0019_easy_read: Interception means getting the ball from the other team during a pass.
pg026_n0020_easy_read:
To intercept, a player needs to predict what will happen and react quickly.
This helps the player stop passes before they reach the intended player, as shown in Figure 1.20.
pg026_n0021_easy_read:
A defender must read the game by watching the opponent's eyes and body movement.
This helps the defender predict where the ball will go.
pg026_n0022_easy_read: Moving into passing lanes at the right time or jumping at the right time increases the chance of a successful interception.
pg026_n0023_easy_read:
After a player intercepts the ball, the player must keep balance.
This is important to move quickly into an attacking play.
pg027_n0007_easy_read:
Blocking shots is a defensive technique.
Players use it to stop an opposing player from scoring.
They do this by intercepting or blocking shots that go toward the goal.
pg027_n0008_easy_read:
Blocking shots is an important defensive skill.
It makes shooting harder.
It also lowers how often shooters score.
pg027_n0009_easy_read:
A defender should stand with arms fully stretched out and hands open.
This makes it harder for the shooter to score, as shown in Figure 1.21 (a and b).
pg027_n0010_easy_read:
The defender must jump at the right time.
This helps the defender challenge the shot without making a foul or giving away a penalty.
pg027_n0011_easy_read:
After blocking, the defender should keep a strong stance.
This helps the defender react quickly to rebounds or loose balls.
pg028_n0005_easy_read:
Use different drills.
Practice marking, interception, and blocking shots many times to learn these skills well.

pg028_n0017_easy_read:
In netball, each player has a specific position.
Each position has clear roles and rules about where the player can move on the court.
pg028_n0018_easy_read: Understanding positions is very important for good teamwork, strategy, and play.
pg028_n0019_easy_read:
The 7 playing positions in a netball team are divided into 3 groups:
- attacking roles
- defending roles
- midcourt roles
pg028_n0020_easy_read:
Each position has an important role.
It helps the team keep its structure, move the ball smoothly, and defend against the other team.
pg028_n0023_easy_read: These positions are in the area from the centre circle to the attacking team's goal third, including the goal circle.
pg028_n0024_easy_read:
This area is for these positions:
- Goal Shooter (GS)
- Goal Attack (GA)
- Wing Attack (WA)
pg028_n0028_easy_read: Goal Shooter (GS): The main job is to score goals.
pg028_n0029_easy_read:
The Goal Shooter stays inside the goal circle.
The Goal Shooter works closely with the Goal Attack (GA) to create chances to shoot.
pg028_n0032_easy_read: Goal Attack (GA): The Goal Attack helps the Goal Shooter (GS) by passing the ball into the goal circle and shooting when needed.
pg028_n0033_easy_read: The Goal Attack (GA) plays in the centre third and the attacking goal third, including the goal circle.
pg028_n0036_easy_read: Wing Attack (WA): The Wing Attack helps deliver the ball to the shooters (GS and GA).
pg028_n0037_easy_read:
The Wing Attack focuses on:
- accurate passing
- good positioning
- creating space in the attacking third
pg028_n0040_easy_read: Centre (C): This position is between defence and attack.
pg028_n0041_easy_read: The Centre controls the speed of play, stops the other team's attacks, and keeps the ball.
pg028_n0042_easy_read:
The Centre also links play from defenders to attackers.
The Centre often creates chances for forward players.
pg028_n0043_easy_read: The Centre moves in all 3 thirds, except the goal circles of both teams.
pg028_n0044_easy_read: The Centre starts and restarts play each time a goal is scored.
pg029_n0005_easy_read: This position is between the centre circle and the defending team's goal third, including the goal circle.
pg029_n0006_easy_read:
This area is where these players play:
- Wing Defense (WD)
- Goal Defense (GD)
- Goal Keeper (GK)
pg029_n0007_easy_read: Players in defensive positions must stop the other team from scoring.
pg029_n0011_easy_read: Wing Defense (WD): This player marks the other team's Wing Attack and stops them from passing the ball into the shooting circle.
pg029_n0014_easy_read: Goal Defense (GD): This player marks the Goal Attack, stops them from shooting, and intercepts passes into the goal circle.
pg029_n0015_easy_read: Goal Defense (GD) also helps move the ball into attack; and
pg029_n0018_easy_read: Goal Keeper (GK): This player is the last line of defense. The Goal Keeper marks the Goal Shooter and stops goals.
pg029_n0019_easy_read: The Goal Keeper stays in the defensive third and inside the goal circle.

pg030_n0055_easy_read: Rules and regulations for playing netball
pg030_n0057_easy_read: Netball rules help make play fair, safe, and consistent at all levels of competition.
pg030_n0058_easy_read:
The rules are updated from time to time.
However, they still follow key values:
- equal opportunity
- fair play
- respect for opponents
pg030_n0059_easy_read: These are the main rules of the game:
pg030_n0063_easy_read:
A netball team has 7 players on the court.
Each player has a specific position.
This position decides where the player can move on the court.
pg030_n0064_easy_read:
Players must stay in their designated areas.
This keeps the game structure and stops unfair advantages.
pg030_n0065_easy_read:
The player positions are:
- Goal Shooter (GS)
- Goal Attack (GA)
- Wing Attack (WA)
- Centre (C)
- Wing Defense (WD)
- Goal Defense (GD)
- Goal Keeper (GK)
pg030_n0069_easy_read:
A standard netball match has 4 quarters.
Each quarter lasts 15 minutes.
pg030_n0070_easy_read: There are short breaks of no more than 4 minutes after the 1st and 3rd quarters.
pg031_n0003_easy_read: There is also a longer halftime break of 12 minutes.
pg031_n0004_easy_read: Teams change ends after each quarter.
pg031_n0005_easy_read: If the game ends in a draw in knockout rounds or finals, extra time or a 2-goal lead rule may decide the winner.
pg031_n0009_easy_read: Before the game starts, the umpire tosses a coin. The captains of both teams take part.
pg031_n0010_easy_read: The game starts with a centre pass. The Centre (C) player of the team that won the toss takes it from the centre circle.
pg031_n0011_easy_read: The centre pass changes between teams after each goal. This gives both teams a fair chance to restart play.
pg031_n0012_easy_read: Players must stay in their starting positions before the whistle blows.
pg031_n0016_easy_read: Netball players cannot run with the ball or dribble the ball.
pg031_n0017_easy_read: After a player receives a pass, the player must pass the ball within 3 seconds.
pg031_n0018_easy_read: Players can pivot on 1 foot to change position before passing. But they cannot take extra steps.
pg031_n0019_easy_read: This rule helps players make quick decisions and keeps the ball moving.
pg031_n0023_easy_read: A team scores a goal when the Goal Shooter (GS) or Goal Attack (GA) shoots the ball through the other team's hoop.
pg031_n0024_easy_read:
There are 2 ways to score goals:
- through open play
- through free shots after a technical foul in a goal circle
pg031_n0025_easy_read: A goal counts only if the shot comes from inside the shooting circle.
pg031_n0026_easy_read: If a player shoots from outside the goal circle, the goal does not count.
pg031_n0027_easy_read: The team with the most goals at the end of the game wins.
pg031_n0031_easy_read:
Physical contact is not allowed, for example:
- pushing an opponent
- hitting an opponent
- holding an opponent
pg031_n0032_easy_read: If contact stops an opponent from moving, the other team gets a penalty pass.
pg031_n0033_easy_read: If the contact happens inside the goal circle, the team that did not commit the contact may get a penalty pass or shot.
pg031_n0035_easy_read: Defenders must stay at least 3 feet (0.9 metres) away from the player with the ball.
pg031_n0036_easy_read: If a defender gets too close, within 3 feet or 0.9 metres, this is obstruction. The attacking team gets a penalty pass.
pg031_n0037_easy_read: If the obstruction happens inside the shooting circle against a shooter, the result is a penalty pass or shot. This gives the shooter a free try at the goal.
pg031_n0041_easy_read: Each player in netball can move only in certain areas of the court.
pg031_n0042_easy_read: If a player steps outside the permitted zone, the player commits an offside violation. This results
pg032_n0003_easy_read: This results in a free pass for the other team.
pg032_n0004_easy_read: This rule helps the team stay disciplined and organised. It also stops unfair advantage.
pg032_n0008_easy_read: A player must not take more than 1 step while holding the ball.
pg032_n0009_easy_read: If a player catches the ball and lands on 1 foot, the player can pivot. The player must release the ball before lifting the landing foot.
pg032_n0010_easy_read: If a player lands on both feet at the same time, the player may choose 1 foot to pivot on. The other foot must stay on the ground.
pg032_n0011_easy_read: If a player takes extra steps, this is a footwork infringement. The other team then gets possession of the ball.
pg032_n0015_easy_read: When the ball goes out of court, the team that did not touch it last gets a throw-in. The throw-in is taken from the place where the ball crossed the boundary line.
pg032_n0016_easy_read: The player taking the throw-in must have at least 1 foot close to the line and touching it. The player must release the ball within 3 seconds.
pg032_n0017_easy_read:
A free pass is given for minor infringements, such as:
- offside
- over-a-third violations
- footwork errors
pg032_n0018_easy_read: The player taking the pass must stand still before throwing the ball to a teammate.
pg032_n0022_easy_read: A penalty in netball is a sanction for a serious rule infringement.
pg032_n0023_easy_read:
For example, a penalty pass is given when a player commits a major foul, such as:
- obstruction
- contact
pg032_n0024_easy_read:
A sanction is the action an umpire takes after an infringement by:
- a player
- a team official
- a bench player
pg032_n0025_easy_read: The penalised player must stay out of play until the pass is taken.
pg032_n0026_easy_read: If a player holds the ball for more than 3 seconds, the other team gets a free pass for a "held ball" violation.
pg032_n0027_easy_read: Umpires may also give warnings or suspensions for repeated rule-breaking or unsporting behaviour.

pg036_n0008_easy_read: Field events is a sport about jumping and throwing.
pg036_n0009_easy_read: Male and female people do field events for fun or for competition.
pg036_n0010_easy_read:
Doing field events can:
- give people job opportunities
- improve physical health
- help players develop important life skills
pg036_n0011_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the concept of field events
- safety measures
- skills
- rules
pg036_n0012_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you:
- analyse different field events
- do different field events with skill and confidence
pg036_n0020_easy_read: Field events is a sport with athletic activities that take place on the field, not on the track.
pg036_n0021_easy_read:
The activities are in 2 categories:
- throwing events
- jumping events
pg036_n0022_easy_read:
Jumping events include:
- long jump
- triple jump
- high jump
- pole vault
Throwing events include:
- shot put
- discus throw
- javelin throw
pg036_n0023_easy_read:
People can organise these events:
- as competitive sport
- as recreational activities
These events are also an important part of major athletic competitions, such as:
- the Olympics
- World Championships
- regional meets
pg036_n0024_easy_read:
When field events are organised as a competition, they test an athlete’s:
- strength
- technique
- coordination
They also show how well the athlete can move themselves or an object across a measured distance.
pg037_n0005_easy_read:
In athletics, throwing events are field events.
Athletes throw an object as far as possible.
pg037_n0006_easy_read:
This sport needs:
- strength
- good technique
- coordination
pg037_n0007_easy_read:
The main throwing events are:
- javelin throw
- discus throw
- shot put
pg037_n0008_easy_read: In organised throwing events, winners get medals and other prizes, including cash.
pg037_n0009_easy_read:
The medals are:
- gold medal for 1st place
- silver medal for 2nd place
- bronze medal for 3rd place
pg037_n0013_easy_read:
Safety measures are very important in throwing events.
They help prevent injuries to athletes and spectators during the event.
pg037_n0014_easy_read:
Athletes and officials must make safety a priority.
They must use correct movements.
They must also keep the facilities and equipment in good condition.
pg037_n0015_easy_read: The main safety precautions before, during, and after throwing events are:
pg037_n0019_easy_read:
Do warm-up exercises before workouts.
Do cool-down exercises after workouts.
pg037_n0022_easy_read:
Keep the throwing area clean.
Remove any objects that could cause injury to athletes and spectators.
pg037_n0025_easy_read:
Make sure protective barriers, such as throwing cages, are in place.
They help control the direction of the throw.
They also help stop the implement from flying into athletes, officials, or spectators and causing injury.
pg037_n0028_easy_read:
Keep all equipment and throwing implements in good condition.
Make sure they have the correct weight and size for the athletes' age and physical maturity.
pg037_n0031_easy_read:
Prepare a complete first aid kit.
It must contain all the medical supplies needed to give first aid during training and competitions.
pg037_n0034_easy_read:
Make sure all athletes use correct movement techniques during training and competitions.
This helps reduce the risk of injury.
pg037_n0037_easy_read:
Keep your body hydrated.
Drink suitable fluids, including water, to prevent dehydration.
pg037_n0043_easy_read: Why is it important to keep the body hydrated in field events?
pg037_n0045_easy_read: How do people maintain the equipment used in field events so it lasts long and stays safe?

pg038_n0005_easy_read:
The javelin throw is a field event.
In this event, athletes throw a javelin as far as possible in a set direction.
pg038_n0006_easy_read:
This section explains the basic techniques, rules, and regulations of the javelin throw.
It helps you develop the skills you need to do the javelin throw.
pg038_n0010_easy_read:
The facilities and equipment for the javelin throw include:
- a throwing area
- a measuring tape
- flags
- a javelin
- markers
- wind indicators
- score and display boards
pg038_n0014_easy_read:
A javelin throwing area has these parts:
- runway
- throwing arc
- foul line
- landing sector
See Figure 2.1.
pg038_n0015_easy_read: The runway is 36.5 m long and 4 m wide.
pg038_n0016_easy_read:
The landing sector has an angle of 29° from the end of the runway.
It is 25 m wide.
pg039_n0005_easy_read:
A javelin is a spear-shaped object.
People make it from:
- metal
- fibreglass
- carbon fibre
- wood
pg039_n0006_easy_read:
The javelin is 2.2 m to 2.7 m long.
It weighs 500 g to 800 g.
The length and weight depend on the athlete's age and sex.
pg039_n0007_easy_read:
Figure 2.2 shows the main parts of a javelin:
- the shaft
- the metal tip
- the grip
pg039_n0013_easy_read:
Use the internet and other relevant sources.
Find the length and weight of a javelin for the athlete's age and sex.
pg039_n0017_easy_read:
Throwing a javelin needs a mix of skills.
These skills are:
- technical skills
- physical skills
- mental skills
This includes gripping and throwing.
pg039_n0021_easy_read: Gripping means holding the javelin during the throw.
pg039_n0022_easy_read:
The grip is very important.
It affects the control, stability, and power of the javelin during the throw.
pg039_n0023_easy_read:
A proper grip helps the javelin leave the hand smoothly.
It also helps the throw use the right force and angle for the maximum distance.
pg039_n0024_easy_read:
There are different types of grip:
- American grip
- Finnish grip
- V-grip
pg039_n0028_easy_read:
In this grip, the index finger goes on top at the edge of the cord.
The thumb goes underneath.
pg039_n0029_easy_read:
The middle finger and ring finger support the javelin.
See Figure 2.3.
pg039_n0030_easy_read:
The thrower holds the javelin above the shoulder.
Then the thrower makes a sharp, whipping motion to throw it.
pg039_n0031_easy_read:
This grip allows a more controlled release.
People often use it to add spin or more distance by rotating the wrist.
pg040_n0007_easy_read:
In this grip, the index finger goes along the top of the javelin.
The thumb goes underneath.
This makes the grip more secure.
pg040_n0008_easy_read:
The other fingers wrap around the shaft.
See Figure 2.4.
pg040_n0009_easy_read: Use this grip when the javelin is raised a little higher and the wrist is bent back.
pg040_n0010_easy_read:
This grip can make the throw more powerful.
It gives more wrist snap and more control during the release.
pg040_n0016_easy_read:
In the V-grip, the thrower holds the javelin between the index finger and the middle finger.
This makes a "V" shape, as shown in Figure 2.5.
pg040_n0017_easy_read:
This grip gives a secure hold.
It gives better control and a balanced release.
This helps the throw go farther.
pg041_n0005_easy_read:
Practice these grips many times:
- American grip
- Finnish grip
- V-grip
Then choose the grip that is best for you.
pg041_n0009_easy_read: In javelin, throwing means sending the javelin through the air to the landing area.
pg041_n0010_easy_read:
A good throw needs:
- speed
- technique
- strength
pg041_n0011_easy_read:
Javelin throwing uses a series of movements.
These movements include:
- a controlled run-up
- a strong impulse step
- a powerful throw
Then the thrower must follow through well.
This helps the javelin go as far as possible and with accuracy.
pg041_n0012_easy_read: The aim is to throw the javelin as far as possible and follow the official rules of the sport.
pg041_n0013_easy_read: These are the steps for throwing a javelin:
pg041_n0017_easy_read:
Hold the javelin at the grip, which is the corded section.
Use 1 of these 3 techniques:
- Finish
- American
- V-grip
pg041_n0020_easy_read:
Stand tall.
Point the javelin slightly upward.
Start running and increase your speed.
Keep the javelin steady.
pg041_n0023_easy_read:
Use crossover strides in the final steps to get ready for the throw.
Make the last 2 steps longer.
pg041_n0026_easy_read:
Plant your front foot firmly.
Keep your back foot slightly bent.
Turn your hips and shoulders forward.
Keep your throwing arm stretched back.
pg041_n0029_easy_read:
Throw the javelin with a fast whipping arm movement.
Snap your wrist when you release the javelin.
This helps the javelin fly smoothly.
Figure 2.6.
pg041_n0032_easy_read:
Keep moving forward after the throw.
Keep your balance.
Stay in the throwing area until the javelin lands.
pg042_n0005_easy_read: Do javelin throwing while walking and while running.
pg042_n0009_easy_read: These are some rules for javelin throw:
pg042_n0013_easy_read: The javelin must have the correct size and weight for the athlete's age and sex.
pg042_n0016_easy_read:
Athletes must hold the javelin by its corded grip.
They must throw it over the shoulder or over the upper part of the throwing arm.
pg042_n0019_easy_read: Athletes must throw from the marked throwing arc at the end of the runway.
pg042_n0022_easy_read:
The metal head of the javelin must hit the ground first.
It must land inside the marked sector lines.
pg042_n0025_easy_read: The javelin must land inside the landing sector for the throw to be valid.
pg042_n0028_easy_read: Athletes have 30 seconds to complete the throw after their name is called.
pg042_n0031_easy_read:
A throw is a foul if:
- the athlete steps over the boundary lines of the runway
- the javelin lands outside the sector lines
- the athlete does not complete the throw in the allowed time
pg042_n0035_easy_read: How does learning javelin throw technique help you throughout your life?
