pg042_n0043_easy_read:
Shot put is a field event.
In this event, a person pushes a heavy, round metal ball.
pg042_n0044_easy_read:
The throw starts close to the chin or neck.
It needs a controlled and strong movement.
pg042_n0045_easy_read: The main goal in shot put is to throw the shot as far as possible and stay inside the marked throwing area.
pg042_n0046_easy_read: The winner is the athlete who throws the shot the furthest from the starting point.
pg043_n0005_easy_read:
Shot put needs specific facilities and equipment.
These help performance and keep athletes safe.
pg043_n0006_easy_read:
This includes:
- the shot put area
- the shot
- carbonate powder, such as magnesium
- specialised gear for the athletes
pg043_n0010_easy_read:
The shot put area includes:
- a throwing circle
- a stop board
- a landing sector

Figure 2.7 shows this.
pg043_n0011_easy_read:
The throwing circle has a diameter of 2.135 m.
The stop board is 10 cm high.
pg043_n0012_easy_read: The landing sector spreads about 35 degrees from the centre of the throwing circle.
pg044_n0003_easy_read:
The equipment used in the shot put event includes:
- the shot
- spike
- recording sheet
- towel
- broom
- flags (white and red)
- stopwatch
- tape measure
- stop board
pg044_n0007_easy_read: The shot is a heavy round object used in the shot put event, Figure 2.8.
pg044_n0008_easy_read: The shot is made of metal, such as iron or brass. Its weight changes depending on the competition category.
pg044_n0009_easy_read: Men’s shots can weigh 7.26 kg. Women’s shots weigh 4 kg.
pg044_n0010_easy_read: Youth and junior weight categories are lighter, depending on age group.
pg044_n0016_easy_read: The main goal in shot put is to push the shot as far as possible.
pg044_n0017_easy_read: To do this, the thrower needs important skills to throw the shot over long distances.
pg044_n0018_easy_read:
These basic skills include:
- gripping the shot
- shot placement
- putting the shot
pg044_n0022_easy_read: Gripping is the action of holding the shot.
pg044_n0023_easy_read: It means holding the shot with the fingers.
pg044_n0024_easy_read: To grip the shot properly, follow these steps:
pg044_n0028_easy_read: Rest the shot on the base of the fingers, as shown in Figure 2.9.
pg044_n0031_easy_read: Place the thumb and little finger opposite the index, middle, and ring fingers. Keep them slightly apart.
pg044_n0034_easy_read: Keep the shot on the base of the fingers. The shot should not touch the palm. This helps with better control and a smooth pushing action.
pg045_n0007_easy_read: Placement means putting the shot near the shot putter's chin.
pg045_n0008_easy_read: The athlete puts the shot under the jaw, close to the neck.
pg045_n0009_easy_read: These steps will help you do shot placement:
pg045_n0013_easy_read: Rest the shot at the base of your fingers.
pg045_n0016_easy_read: Press the shot against the hollow part at the base of your neck, just under the jaw.
pg045_n0019_easy_read: Keep your palm facing up and your thumb pointing down.
pg045_n0022_easy_read: Keep your elbow high, at shoulder level, and parallel to the ground, as shown in Figure 2.10.
pg046_n0005_easy_read: Practice gripping and placing the shot again and again until you master the skills.
pg046_n0009_easy_read: Putting the shot means pushing a heavy metal ball from the shoulder with 1 hand.
pg046_n0010_easy_read: There are 2 main techniques for putting the shot: the linear technique and the rotational technique.
pg046_n0014_easy_read: The linear technique is also called the glide technique. In this technique, the shot putter moves in a straight line from the starting position to the centre of the circle.
pg046_n0015_easy_read: These are the steps for putting the shot by the linear technique:
pg046_n0019_easy_read: Stand at the back of the circle with your back facing the throwing direction.
pg046_n0022_easy_read: Squat slightly. Place the shot against your neck. Support it with your fingers.
pg046_n0025_easy_read: Shift your weight onto the rear leg. Keep your torso relaxed.
pg046_n0028_easy_read: Drive back with your rear leg. Push off the toe. Keep your hips low. Let your rear leg land about in the centre, pointing slightly to the front.
pg046_n0031_easy_read: When your rear leg lands in the centre, place your front leg at the back of the circle, slightly open to the front.
pg046_n0034_easy_read: Turn your hips and shoulders toward the throwing sector when you reach the front of the circle.
pg046_n0037_easy_read: Push the shot strongly forward and upward while tightening your core, as shown in Figure 2.11.
pg046_n0040_easy_read: Quickly bring the rear leg forward to prevent fouling. Stay inside the circle until the shot lands.
pg046_n0047_easy_read: Figure 2.11: Putting the shot by linear technique
pg047_n0006_easy_read: Practice the linear technique for shot put many times until you can do it well.
pg047_n0010_easy_read: The rotational technique, also called spin, is a way to put the shot. The athlete spins inside the circle to get more speed and power. This helps the athlete throw farther.
pg047_n0011_easy_read: These are the steps for putting the shot with the rotational technique.
pg047_n0015_easy_read: Stand facing the back of the circle. Keep your feet shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees a little. Place the shot against your neck with the correct hand position.
pg047_n0018_easy_read: Start to spin by turning on the ball of the non-throwing foot. Rotate your body across the circle.
pg047_n0021_easy_read: Land at the front of the circle. Keep your hips and shoulders square. Use your rear leg to create force for the push.
pg047_n0024_easy_read: Push the shot forward at an upward angle. Use full body rotation to increase the distance.
pg047_n0027_easy_read: Quickly bring the rear leg forward to avoid fouling. Stay inside the circle until the shot lands. See Figure 2.12.
pg047_n0036_easy_read: Figure 2.12: Putting the shot with the rotational technique
pg047_n0041_easy_read: Practice the rotational technique for shot put many times until you can do it well.
pg047_n0045_easy_read: These are some of the rules for shot put:
pg047_n0049_easy_read: The athlete must put the shot from the shoulder with 1 hand.
pg047_n0050_easy_read: When an athlete takes a stance in the circle to start a put, the shot must not touch the neck.
pg048_n0005_easy_read:
The stop board must be white.
It must be made of wood or another suitable material.
It must have an arc shape.
Its inner surface must line up with the inner edge of the rim.
pg048_n0008_easy_read:
The stop board must be 11.2 cm wide.
The arc must have a chord of 123 cm.
The arc must have the same radius as the circle.
The stop board must be 10 cm high from the level of the inside of the circle next to the stop board.
pg048_n0011_easy_read:
The shot must be made of solid iron, brass, or another metal that is not softer than brass.
It can also be a shell of this metal filled with lead or other solid materials.
pg048_n0014_easy_read: The shot must match the weight and diameter rules shown in Table 2.1.
pg048_n0054_easy_read:
Practice shot putting many times to learn the skill well.
Follow the rules and regulations.
pg048_n0061_easy_read: Name any 3 common mistakes that can lead to incorrect shot putting during shot put events.
pg048_n0064_easy_read: State the purpose of the stop board in shot put.
pg048_n0067_easy_read: Describe why the shot put circle has a slightly rough surface.
pg048_n0071_easy_read:
Discus throw is a field event.
In this event, an athlete throws a heavy, flat object called a discus.
The athlete throws it from inside a marked circle.
The aim is to throw it as far as possible.
pg048_n0072_easy_read: The winner is the thrower who throws the discus the longest distance from the throwing circle.
pg048_n0076_easy_read: Discus throwing needs some facilities, such as the throwing area and measuring tools.
pg048_n0077_easy_read:
Discus throwing also needs equipment such as:
- the discus
- shoes
- chalk
- a stopwatch
- flags (white and red)
- a recording sheet
pg049_n0005_easy_read:
The discus throwing area has 3 parts:
- the throwing circle
- the cage
- the landing zone, also called the sector area
pg049_n0006_easy_read: The throwing circle is the area where players start and finish the throw.
pg049_n0007_easy_read: The throwing circle has a diameter of 2.5 m.
pg049_n0008_easy_read: The cage is a U-shaped net or metal fence. It stops wrong throws from hurting officials, spectators, and other athletes.
pg049_n0009_easy_read: The landing zone is the area where the discus lands. It is marked by 2 lines. The 2 lines make an angle of 34.92 degrees from the centre of the circle. Figure 2.13.
pg049_n0015_easy_read: The main equipment for discus throwing is a discus.
pg049_n0016_easy_read:
A discus is a flat throwing object. It can be made from different materials:
- rubber
- wood
- metal
pg049_n0017_easy_read:
For women, the discus has:
- diameter: 18 cm
- weight: 1 kg
For men, the discus has:
- diameter: 22 cm
- weight: 2 kg
pg049_n0018_easy_read: The discus is circular in shape. It often comes with a case that protects it from damage. Figure 2.14.
pg050_n0005_easy_read:
Other equipment includes:
- a tape measure to measure the length of the discus throw
- flags to show a valid or invalid throw
- a recording sheet to keep scores and other details about the thrower
pg050_n0009_easy_read: Discus throwers try to throw the discus well and as far as possible.
pg050_n0010_easy_read: These are the basic skills for discus throw.
pg050_n0014_easy_read: Gripping the discus means holding the discus in the correct position.
pg050_n0015_easy_read: The grip affects how the discus leaves the hand and the direction it goes.
pg050_n0016_easy_read: These are the steps for gripping the discus:
pg050_n0020_easy_read: Hold the discus on your non-throwing hand for support.
pg050_n0023_easy_read: Place your throwing hand on top of the discus.
pg050_n0026_easy_read: Spread your fingers evenly on the rim of the discus.
pg050_n0029_easy_read:
Hold the discus at the first joint of your fingers.
Rest the first knuckle over the rim.
pg050_n0032_easy_read:
Place your fingertips firmly over the discus.
Make sure most of the pressure comes from your fingers, not your palm.
pg050_n0035_easy_read: Keep your wrist straight and relaxed, as shown in Figure 2.15 (a, b and c).
pg051_n0004_easy_read: Practice gripping the discus again and again until you can do it well.
pg051_n0008_easy_read: Throwing the discus means sending the discus in the right direction by using the correct body movements.
pg051_n0009_easy_read: Discus throwing starts with the thrower's standing position and ends when the discus leaves the hand.
pg051_n0010_easy_read: These steps will help you throw the discus:
pg051_n0014_easy_read:
Put the discus in your throwing hand.
Spread your fingers evenly around the rim.
pg051_n0017_easy_read:
Stand at the back of the throwing circle.
Keep your feet shoulder-width apart.
Face away from the direction of the throw.
pg051_n0020_easy_read:
Turn your upper body.
Move your discus arm backwards.
Keep your other arm forward for balance.
pg051_n0023_easy_read:
Turn your body by moving your weight onto your dominant leg.
Use your core to create turning force.
Stay low and balanced.
pg051_n0026_easy_read:
Put your non-dominant foot down first when you get near the front of the circle.
Pull your throwing hand back.
Get ready to release the discus.
pg051_n0029_easy_read:
Move your throwing arm forward.
Turn your wrist for a smooth spin.
Aim for a high, flat path for the longest distance.
See Figure 2.16.
pg051_n0032_easy_read:
Keep moving forward after you release the discus to stay balanced.
Keep your eyes on the discus.
Stay in the circle until the discus lands.
pg051_n0044_easy_read: Practice throwing the discus again and again until you can do it well.
pg052_n0008_easy_read: Here are some rules for discus throw:
pg052_n0012_easy_read:
Men's discus is 2 kg and 22 cm.
Women's discus is 1 kg and 18 cm.
pg052_n0015_easy_read:
The thrower must start the throw from a still position inside the circle.
The thrower may place the discus inside the circle or outside the circle.
pg052_n0018_easy_read: The thrower must stay inside the circle until the discus lands in the sector.
pg052_n0021_easy_read:
The chief judge controls the whole event.
2 judges support the chief judge:
- 1 judge checks if the throws are legal.
- 1 judge records the results and is in charge of the throwers and standards.
pg052_n0024_easy_read: All discus throws must stay inside the cage enclosure for the safety of the participants.
pg052_n0028_easy_read:
Practice discus throws many times until you master the skill.
Follow the rules and regulations.

pg052_n0032_easy_read: 2. How does the release angle affect how far a discus travels?

pg052_n0037_easy_read: In athletics, jumping means athletes push themselves off the ground to reach the greatest distance or height.
pg052_n0038_easy_read:
There are 4 main jumping events in athletics:
- long jump
- triple jump
- high jump
- pole vault
pg052_n0039_easy_read:
These events are in 2 groups:
- horizontal jumps, which focus on distance
- vertical jumps, which focus on height
pg052_n0043_easy_read: In jumping events, athletes and officials must follow important safety rules before and during competitions.
pg052_n0048_easy_read: Make sure all equipment is suitable and in good condition.
pg053_n0005_easy_read: Wear clean clothes and shoes that fit well.
pg053_n0008_easy_read: Check the landing area and the run-up area before the event. Remove any objects that could injure the jumpers.
pg053_n0011_easy_read: Do warm-up exercises before the event. Do cool-down exercises after the event.
pg053_n0014_easy_read: Prepare a first aid kit with all the medical supplies you need.
pg053_n0018_easy_read: In horizontal jumps, the athlete jumps as far as possible from a take-off board into a sandpit.
pg053_n0019_easy_read:
Horizontal jumping events are:
- long jump
- triple jump
pg053_n0023_easy_read: A long jump is a horizontal jumping event. In this event, the athlete tries to jump as far as possible from the take-off board to the landing point.
pg053_n0027_easy_read:
The long jump needs a long jump facility, also called a long jump area. It also needs equipment such as:
- measuring tapes
- marking devices
- maintenance tools
pg053_n0028_easy_read:
A proper facility setup and the right equipment help with:
- accurate measurements
- the athlete's consistency
- the event running well
pg053_n0032_easy_read:
The long jump area has 3 main parts:
- the runway
- the take-off board
- the landing area
Figure 2.17 shows these parts.
pg053_n0038_easy_read: The runway must be at least 40 metres long and 1.22 m wide.
pg053_n0039_easy_read:
The runway is measured from the start of the runway to the take-off board. It is marked with white lines or broken lines. The lines are:
- 0.05 m wide
- 0.10 m long
- 0.50 m apart
pg054_n0005_easy_read:
The take-off board is a white rectangle.
It measures 1.22 m long, 0.20 m wide, and at most 0.10 m deep.
pg054_n0006_easy_read:
The take-off board must be level with the runway surface.
This gives athletes a smooth transition.
pg054_n0010_easy_read:
The landing area is about 7 m to 9 m long.
This depends on the distance from the take-off board.
pg054_n0011_easy_read:
The landing area is 2.75 m wide.
The best setup is 8 m long and 1 m from the take-off board.
pg054_n0012_easy_read: The centre of the runway must line up with the centre of the landing area.
pg054_n0016_easy_read: Different equipment is needed for the long jump, as shown in Table 2.2.
pg054_n0030_easy_read: This board shows foul jumps in major competitions.
pg054_n0036_easy_read: Tape measures show the distance jumped.
pg054_n0042_easy_read: Use a rake to level the sand in the landing area after each attempt.
pg055_n0014_easy_read: Helps keep the sand in good condition and move it in the landing area.
pg055_n0020_easy_read: Used to mark the different points in the long jump area.
pg055_n0026_easy_read:
Red and white flags show if a jump is valid.
Yellow flags are used as a warning.
pg056_n0003_easy_read:
Other equipment includes:
- a stopwatch
- a wind gauge
- a wind sock
- a spike
- a hand-brush
- a recording sheet
- a bucket
- a hose
- a watering cane
pg056_n0005_easy_read: Basic skills in the long jump
pg056_n0007_easy_read: To jump as far as possible, an athlete must have the basic skills of the long jump.
pg056_n0008_easy_read:
The long jump is a speed event.
Jumpers must be good at 4 basic skills:
- approach run
- take-off
- flight
- landing
pg056_n0012_easy_read:
The approach run is very important.
It helps the athlete build momentum and place the foot correctly on the take-off board.
pg056_n0013_easy_read:
A good approach run helps jumpers gain speed.
It also helps them keep control and accuracy for take-off.
pg056_n0014_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the approach run:
pg056_n0018_easy_read:
Start from the long jump starting position.
Start your run with your take-off foot forward.
Build up speed gradually, as shown in Figure 2.18.
pg056_n0021_easy_read: Keep your head in a natural position.
pg056_n0024_easy_read:
Look forward all the time.
Keep your back flat.
pg056_n0027_easy_read:
Extend your take-off leg.
Place the thigh of the other foot in a good position.
pg056_n0030_easy_read: Make sure the last 2 strides are long enough to prepare you for take-off.
pg056_n0036_easy_read: The take-off starts in the later part of the approach run.
pg056_n0037_easy_read: During the last 2 strides of the approach run, the athlete lowers and raises the hips at the take-off point.
pg056_n0038_easy_read: These steps will help you do a take-off:
pg057_n0005_easy_read:
Push strongly through these parts to move up and forward:
- the ankle
- the knee
- the hip
pg057_n0008_easy_read: Make sure the take-off foot lands on the middle line of the take-off board during take-off, Figure 2.19.
pg057_n0011_easy_read:
Make sure the heel of the take-off foot touches first.
Then roll onto the ball of the foot.
Then use the toes.
This gives the greatest upward lift.
pg057_n0014_easy_read: Push the take-off foot strongly with your toes.
pg057_n0017_easy_read: Use your arms and the non-take-off leg to increase upward acceleration.
pg057_n0024_easy_read:
Flight is the movement of the body from the take-off point to the landing point.
During flight, keep balance, try to get the greatest distance, and prepare for a smooth landing.
pg057_n0025_easy_read:
The athlete cannot create more momentum in the air.
So the goal is to control body position and reduce forward rotation.
This helps the athlete reach the best landing position.
pg057_n0026_easy_read: These steps will help you do the flight:
pg057_n0030_easy_read: Raise the non-take-off leg to a horizontal position during take-off.
pg057_n0033_easy_read: Keep your hands above shoulder level, Figure 2.20.
pg057_n0036_easy_read:
Keep your trunk upright.
This helps your leg move up during landing.
pg057_n0039_easy_read: Keep your head, back, and hips in a straight line.
pg058_n0007_easy_read: Flight is essential to keep control and get the greatest distance.
pg058_n0008_easy_read: Athletes use 3 main techniques to stay balanced in the air and get ready to land.
pg058_n0009_easy_read:
These techniques are:
- the stride
- the hang
- the hitch-kick
pg058_n0013_easy_read: In the stride technique, the athlete keeps the take-off position until landing. Then the take-off leg joins the free leg to make a good landing position, as shown in Figure 2.21.
pg058_n0014_easy_read: The athlete lifts the take-off leg and stays in the air until the non-take-off leg joins it. This helps the athlete land with control and in an effective way.
pg058_n0028_easy_read: In this flight technique, the athlete stays hanging in the air before landing.
pg058_n0029_easy_read: The following steps will help you do an efficient flight:
pg059_n0005_easy_read: Push off hard from the take-off board.
pg059_n0008_easy_read: Straighten the front leg. Then bring it back to join the take-off leg. This front leg was bent first and pushed upward.
pg059_n0011_easy_read: Push both legs back behind the body. Keep the legs straight.
pg059_n0014_easy_read:
Move the arm in a circle:
- down
- back
- up
- forward
Figure 2.22.
pg059_n0017_easy_read: Bend your leg and push it forward. As your legs straighten for landing, move your arms in a forward circle.
pg059_n0020_easy_read: When you land in the sand, bend your knees. Move your upper body forward over your feet.
pg059_n0035_easy_read: The hitch-kick technique is a way of moving in the air. It helps you keep balance, stop too much forward rotation, and jump farther.
pg059_n0036_easy_read: In this technique, the legs move in a repeated cycle in the air. This gives better control and makes the flight phase more effective. See Figure 2.23.
pg059_n0037_easy_read: These steps will help you do the hitch-kick technique:
pg059_n0041_easy_read: After a fast run-up, drive up strongly at take-off.
pg059_n0044_easy_read: Stretch the front leg forward as if you are running in the air.
pg059_n0047_easy_read: Swing the straight leg backward. Keep it straight.
pg059_n0050_easy_read: Bend both legs and bring them forward for landing.
pg059_n0053_easy_read: Rotate your arms forward and then backward. This balances the leg movement and helps push forward during landing.
pg060_n0018_easy_read: In landing, the athlete takes the heels as far away as possible from the take-off board.
pg060_n0019_easy_read:
A proper landing helps the athlete get the greatest distance.
It also makes the finish safe and controlled.
pg060_n0020_easy_read:
A good landing helps athletes avoid losing distance.
They should not fall backwards.
They should not put their hands behind them in the sand, as shown in Figure 2.24.
pg060_n0021_easy_read: These steps will help you practise landing:
pg060_n0025_easy_read:
Keep the body upright.
Keep the head looking forward.
pg060_n0028_easy_read:
Move the arms down and back.
This helps the legs move up.
pg060_n0031_easy_read: Keep the arms forward until the landing is complete.
pg060_n0041_easy_read:
The long jump has specific rules and regulations.
These rules help make the competition fair.
pg060_n0046_easy_read:
Athletes must take off from the take-off board.
They must not step beyond its front edge.
pg061_n0005_easy_read: Measure the jump from the front edge of the take-off board to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the athlete's body.
pg061_n0008_easy_read: If the athlete takes off before the take-off board, measure the jump from the break in the sand to the front edge of the take-off board.
pg061_n0011_easy_read: The athlete must land inside the marked landing pit.
pg061_n0014_easy_read: A valid attempt must be finished within 30 seconds after the athlete is called to jump.
pg061_n0017_easy_read: In standard competitions, each athlete gets 3 to 6 attempts, depending on the level of the competition.
pg061_n0020_easy_read: If there is a tie, the athlete with the second-best jump gets the higher rank.
pg061_n0023_easy_read: After landing, the jumper must leave the pit from the front or the sides. This helps avoid making the measured distance shorter.
pg061_n0029_easy_read:
Build a long jump area.
Mark the key parts.
pg061_n0032_easy_read: Practice the different flight techniques used in the long jump.
pg061_n0036_easy_read: How does taking off at too low or too high an angle affect an athlete's jump distance?
pg061_n0038_easy_read: What changes can an athlete make to improve their take-off if they are having trouble keeping speed and rhythm in the approach run?
pg061_n0040_easy_read: Why is it important for athletes to bend their knees slightly when landing?
pg061_n0044_easy_read:
The triple jump is a jumping event. In this event, athletes try to jump as far as possible from the take-off point after 3 jumps called:
- hop
- step
- jump
pg061_n0045_easy_read:
The 3 jump rhythms are:
- right-right-left
- left-left-right
pg061_n0049_easy_read: The equipment for the triple jump is the same as the equipment used in the long jump.
pg061_n0050_easy_read:
The triple jump needs a jumping area and different equipment, such as:
- tape measures
- marking devices
- maintenance tools
pg061_n0051_easy_read:
A proper facility setup and the right equipment help with:
- accurate measurements
- athlete consistency
- overall event efficiency
pg062_n0005_easy_read:
The triple jump area has 3 parts:
- the runway
- the take-off board
- the landing area
See Figure 2.26.
pg062_n0009_easy_read: This is the space where an athlete gets ready to jump.
pg062_n0010_easy_read:
The runway is 40 m long and 1.22 m wide.
White lines mark it.
The lines are 5 cm wide.
pg062_n0014_easy_read: The take-off board is 13 m from the landing area.
pg062_n0015_easy_read:
The distance from the take-off board to the landing area is 9 m to 13 m.
This distance depends on the athlete's age and gender.
pg062_n0019_easy_read:
The landing area is 10 m long.
It is 2.74 m to 3.0 m wide.
pg062_n0020_easy_read: The landing area is filled with soft, damp sand.
pg062_n0022_easy_read: Figure 2.25: Jumping area in the triple jump
pg062_n0026_easy_read: When athletes master triple jump skills, they can jump the greatest distance possible.
pg062_n0027_easy_read:
The fundamental skills in the triple jump are:
- the approach run
- take-off
- 3 successive jumps
- flight
- landing
pg062_n0028_easy_read: People usually call these skills the phases of the triple jump.
pg062_n0032_easy_read: The main purpose of the approach run is to build as much speed as possible for a successful jump.
pg062_n0033_easy_read: The best run-up distance and speed depend on the athlete's strength and technique.
pg062_n0034_easy_read: Use these steps to do the approach run:
pg062_n0038_easy_read:
Start in the starting position.
Run fast with the take-off foot forward.
See Figure 2.26.
pg063_n0005_easy_read:
Keep your head upright in a natural position.
Look forward all the time.
pg063_n0008_easy_read:
Stretch your take-off leg forward.
Raise the other knee slightly to get ready for the hop.
pg063_n0011_easy_read:
Land your take-off leg on the ground.
Be ready for the take-off.
pg063_n0013_easy_read: Figure 2.26: The approach run in triple jump
pg063_n0017_easy_read: The take-off happens in the final phase of the approach run.
pg063_n0018_easy_read: Follow these steps for a successful take-off:
pg063_n0022_easy_read:
Bend your take-off leg slightly.
Strike the board with a quick, firm motion.
pg063_n0025_easy_read: Move your body forward by extending your free leg.
pg063_n0028_easy_read: Place your take-off foot flat on the take-off board.
pg063_n0031_easy_read: Swing your free leg’s thigh horizontally.
pg063_n0034_easy_read:
Bend the knee at a sharp angle.
See Figure 2.27.
pg064_n0005_easy_read: The 3 jumps in order are hop, step, and jump.
pg064_n0006_easy_read: These jumps happen in a set order after the athlete takes off from the take-off board.
pg064_n0010_easy_read: In the 1st jump, the athlete takes off from 1 foot at the take-off board and lands on the same foot on the runway.
pg064_n0011_easy_read: Follow these steps to do the hop well:
pg064_n0015_easy_read: Place the take-off foot firmly on the ground before take-off.
pg064_n0018_easy_read: Move the take-off leg forward and upward.
pg064_n0021_easy_read: Swing the thigh of the free leg so it is parallel to the ground.
pg064_n0024_easy_read: Stretch the free leg fully. As you land, reach forward and make a pawing action.
pg064_n0027_easy_read: Bring the take-off leg up toward your buttock. Then move it forward and downward.
pg064_n0030_easy_read: Keep your trunk upright. Keep your head still. Look forward.
pg064_n0033_easy_read: Push slightly backward with your foot as you land. This helps you stay stable and get ready for the next jump, Figure 2.28.
pg064_n0045_easy_read: At this stage, the athlete lands on the opposite foot on the runway.
pg064_n0046_easy_read: Follow these steps to do the step well:
pg064_n0050_easy_read: Stretch your ankle, knee, and hip to make a quick take-off.
pg064_n0053_easy_read: Keep the take-off position to get ready for the jump.
pg064_n0056_easy_read: Keep the thigh of the free leg parallel to the ground. Then stretch the foot forward until it is almost fully stretched from the hip.
pg065_n0004_easy_read: (iv) Land with the free leg about in front of your centre of gravity;
pg065_n0006_easy_read: (v) Swing both arms backwards. Keep them close to the body during the second half of the flight;
pg065_n0008_easy_read: (vi) Keep your upper body upright. Keep your eyes looking forward. Figure 2.29.
pg065_n0022_easy_read: The jump is the last stage of the triple jump. It comes after the hop and the step.
pg065_n0023_easy_read: Follow these steps to do the jump well:
pg065_n0026_easy_read: (i) Swing the take-off foot up quickly to a horizontal position;
pg065_n0028_easy_read: (ii) Stretch the body with the arms above the shoulders;
pg065_n0030_easy_read: (iii) Bring the arms forward and down. Bring the legs forward and up to prepare for landing. Figure 2.30.
pg065_n0043_easy_read: The flight is the stage in the air that takes the athlete from the jump stage to landing.
pg065_n0044_easy_read: The main aim is to take a position in the air that allows an efficient transfer
pg066_n0004_easy_read:
While in the air, the athlete can use these jumping styles:
- stride
- hang
- hitch-kick
pg066_n0005_easy_read: Follow these steps to do the flight well:
pg066_n0009_easy_read: Stretch both legs forward fully as you jump.
pg066_n0012_easy_read:
Lift your arms high above your head.
Let them swing down before you land in the sandpit.
pg066_n0018_easy_read: Keep your trunk upright to help your legs move upward, Figure 2.31.
pg066_n0024_easy_read:
Landing in the triple jump is very important.
It helps you get the longest distance and finish smoothly.
pg066_n0025_easy_read: Follow these steps to land well:
pg066_n0029_easy_read: Swing your arms down and back to help an upward movement.
pg066_n0032_easy_read: Then keep your arms forward until the landing is complete, Figure 2.32.
pg066_n0035_easy_read: Bend your knees a little to absorb the impact of landing.
pg066_n0038_easy_read: Keep your body leaning slightly forward during the landing.
pg067_n0014_easy_read:
Athletes must follow specific rules in triple jump competitions.
This helps make the competition fair and safe.
pg067_n0015_easy_read: Some rules for triple jump events are:
pg067_n0018_easy_read:
1. The triple jump has 3 parts:
- hop
- step
- jump
They happen in this order.
pg067_n0020_easy_read:
2. In the hop, the athlete lands on the same foot used for take-off.
In the step, the athlete lands on the other foot.
Then the athlete jumps into the sandpit.
pg067_n0024_easy_read: 4. The take-off foot must be on the take-off board or before it.
pg067_n0026_easy_read:
5. Markers are allowed beside the runway.
Markers are not allowed on the runway or in the landing area.
pg067_n0028_easy_read: 6. An attempt is invalid if the athlete:
pg067_n0033_easy_read: (b) Takes off outside the edges of the board.
pg067_n0035_easy_read: (c) Does a somersault during the jump.
pg067_n0037_easy_read: (d) Touches the runway or the ground outside the landing area before landing.
pg067_n0039_easy_read: (e) Loses control and lands outside the sandpit or too close to the take-off line.
pg067_n0041_easy_read: 7. Officials measure the jump distance from the nearest mark in the sand to the take-off board.
pg067_n0043_easy_read: 8. If the athlete takes off before the board, officials measure from the front edge of the board.
pg067_n0045_easy_read: 9. The winner is the athlete with the longest valid jump.
pg067_n0047_easy_read: 10. If there is a tie, officials use the next best jump to decide the winner.
pg068_n0004_easy_read: Practice the triple jump many times until you learn the skills well.
pg068_n0009_easy_read:
Name 1 common mistake that athletes often make in the hop phase.
Then explain how this mistake affects their overall performance.

pg068_n0015_easy_read: How can an athlete balance speed and control during the approach run to make the best jump possible?
pg068_n0019_easy_read: Vertical jumps include the high jump and the pole vault.
pg068_n0020_easy_read:
In these jumps, the athlete must jump as high as possible from the ground to a landing surface.
The landing surface is usually cushioned with:
- sawdust
- rice hull
- mattresses
pg068_n0024_easy_read:
The high jump is a field event.
In this event, athletes try to jump as high as possible to clear the bar.
pg068_n0025_easy_read: Each jumper has 3 tries to clear the bar.
pg068_n0026_easy_read:
Depending on the event, the bar goes up by 3.8 cm or 5.1 cm for the next height.
This happens after all jumpers have tried to clear the previous height.
pg068_n0027_easy_read: Only jumpers who cleared the previous height can move to the new height.
pg068_n0028_easy_read: This process continues until the last jumper fails to clear the bar after 3 tries.
pg068_n0032_easy_read:
High jump needs facilities and equipment.
These include:
- the jumping area
- tape measures
- marking devices
- maintenance tools
pg068_n0036_easy_read:
The jumping area has:
- a semi-circular runway with a radius of 15 m or 20 m
- a landing area
Figure 2.33 shows this area.
pg068_n0037_easy_read: The runway allows a 15 m approach run from any angle within a 180-degree arc.
pg068_n0038_easy_read: The runway should be at a similar level to the court.
pg069_n0003_easy_read: Figure 2.33: Jumping area in high jump
pg069_n0005_easy_read: Also, the landing area is about 5 m long and 3 m wide.
pg069_n0006_easy_read:
The landing area can have:
- landing mats
- other suitable materials
- a pit with mattresses
- a pit with sawdust
- a pit with rice hull
pg069_n0007_easy_read: The landing area is rectangular, as Figure 2.34 shows.
pg069_n0009_easy_read: Figure 2.34: Landing area in high jump
pg069_n0013_easy_read:
Common equipment for the high jump includes:
- stands
- a crossbar
- landing bags
- a measuring stick or tape
- markers
- flags
- bloom
- restraining straps
pg069_n0017_easy_read:
A stand has 2 vertical bars and an adjustable bracket to hold the crossbar.
See Figure 2.35.
pg069_n0018_easy_read: The distance between the 2 stands is from 4.00 m to 4.04 m.
pg070_n0005_easy_read: Table 2.3 shows the other equipment for the high jump.
pg070_n0021_easy_read:
It is circular in shape.
Its diameter length is 3.98 m - 4.02 m.
pg070_n0024_easy_read: It marks the height that athletes try to clear.
pg070_n0032_easy_read: It helps the athlete land safely.
pg070_n0038_easy_read: It ranges from 1.00 metres to over 2.50 metres.
pg070_n0040_easy_read: It measures the legal jumping height.
pg071_n0005_easy_read: The high jump needs physical, technical, and mental skills.
pg071_n0006_easy_read:
The skills are:
- the approach run
- the take-off
- flight
- bar clearance
- landing
pg071_n0010_easy_read:
In the high jump, the approach run follows a J-shaped runway, as shown in Figure 2.36.
It has:
- a straight path for acceleration
- a curved path to prepare for take-off
pg071_n0011_easy_read: The goal is to build momentum and get the correct take-off position.
pg071_n0012_easy_read: The key steps for an effective approach run are:
pg071_n0016_easy_read:
Put the take-off foot forward.
Shift your body weight slightly forward for a powerful start.
pg071_n0019_easy_read:
Take strong strides.
Swing your arms alternately with your legs to build momentum.
pg071_n0022_easy_read:
Keep your head up.
Keep your eyes on the turning point as you go toward the curve.
pg071_n0025_easy_read:
As you move into the curve, lean your body slightly inward.
This helps you turn smoothly.
pg071_n0028_easy_read:
In the last 3 strides, lower your hips.
Make the second-last stride a little longer.
pg071_n0031_easy_read: Make sure you have a quick, explosive push-off for take-off.
pg071_n0037_easy_read: Take-off is the change from the approach run into the flight.
pg071_n0038_easy_read: For a safe landing, the athlete must do the take-off point correctly to create the ideal flight.
pg072_n0003_easy_read:
Keep the path clear.
Make sure the landing is safe.
pg072_n0004_easy_read:
It should be near the middle of the crossbar.
This gives the right height and space.
pg072_n0005_easy_read: Follow these steps for a successful take-off:
pg072_n0009_easy_read:
Place the take-off foot in the correct position on the take-off mark.
Point the foot towards the landing area, as shown in Figure 2.37.
pg072_n0012_easy_read:
Place the foot correctly at first contact:
The take-off foot should land 2-3 foot lengths in front of the hips and trunk.
It should make a 20-40 degree angle with the crossbar.
pg072_n0015_easy_read:
Lean away from the crossbar:
Push the free leg strongly upward.
Keep your body in a "six o’clock" position.
This means the legs are down and the upper body is upright.
pg072_n0018_easy_read:
Stretch your arms upward:
Keep your head upright.
Fully extend the take-off leg and foot.
pg072_n0021_easy_read:
Lift the non-take-off leg high:
Raise the thigh until it is horizontal.
Swing the arms upward to head level.
pg072_n0024_easy_read:
Extend the body into a vertical line:
Let the lower body follow naturally into a fully extended take-off position.
This gives maximum height and stability.
pg073_n0005_easy_read:
Flight happens after take-off.
At this time, the body is in the air and tries to go over the bar.
pg073_n0006_easy_read: Good body position and body control are very important for a successful jump.
pg073_n0007_easy_read: Follow these steps for a good flight:
pg073_n0011_easy_read:
Lift your hips.
Keep your head up.
This helps you keep balance and height.
pg073_n0014_easy_read:
Stretch your arms out.
This helps you control your body and clear the bar.
pg073_n0017_easy_read: Fully stretch the take-off leg as it goes over the bar.
pg073_n0020_easy_read:
Lower your shoulders and lift your hips.
This makes an arch shape and helps you clear the bar smoothly.
See Figure 2.38.
pg073_n0030_easy_read: In this phase, the athlete jumps up and tries to go over the crossbar, as shown in Figure 2.39, without knocking it down.
pg073_n0031_easy_read: These steps will help you practise clearing the bar successfully:
pg073_n0035_easy_read: Drive the knee up until the shoulder reaches the bar.
pg073_n0038_easy_read:
Stretch the hips.
Lay the body back towards the bar.
pg073_n0041_easy_read: Bend the knee and drop below the bar.
pg073_n0044_easy_read: Lift the hips while you clear the bar.
pg073_n0047_easy_read:
When the hips go over the bar, pull the chin towards the chest.
Then stretch the legs to stop the heels from touching the bar.
pg074_n0007_easy_read: Figure 2.39: Bar clearance in high jump
pg074_n0009_easy_read: Bar clearance technique in high jump
pg074_n0011_easy_read: There are 5 techniques that jumpers use to clear the bar in the high jump.
pg074_n0012_easy_read:
The techniques are:
- straddle
- western roll
- eastern cut-off with or without trunk layout
- scissors
- Fosbury flop
pg074_n0013_easy_read: However, this section will cover scissors and Fosbury flop.
pg074_n0017_easy_read: In this technique, the athlete clears the bar in a scissors shape.
pg074_n0018_easy_read: When the jumper uses this style to clear the bar, the jumper lands on the feet first.
pg074_n0019_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the scissor bar clearance technique:
pg074_n0026_easy_read: Speed up in the last few strides.
pg074_n0029_easy_read: Drive the leg near the bar up and over the bar first.
pg074_n0032_easy_read: Keep your hips up and run tall.

Rules are important.
They help keep standards, fairness, and athlete safety before and during events.
pg076_n0013_easy_read: These are some rules for jumping events:
pg076_n0017_easy_read:
The jump:
The athlete must take off using only 1 leg.
The chief judge decides the jumping height.
pg076_n0020_easy_read:
Jumping area:
The runway must be 15 m long and 16 m wide.
A level take-off area must be between the uprights.
The uprights must be 4 m apart in the middle of the runway.
pg076_n0021_easy_read:
The crossbar must be cylindrical and hollow.
It must have tapered ends.
It is placed on the uprights.
pg076_n0022_easy_read: The landing area must be at least 6 m x 4 m wide and 0.7 m high.
pg076_n0025_easy_read:
Officials:
There will be:
- the chief judge
- the landing judge
- the crossbar judge
- the recorder judge
- the scoreboard judge
- the clock judge
- the judge in charge of the athlete
pg076_n0028_easy_read:
Athlete’s trial:
The athlete has 3 trials to clear the bar.
pg076_n0031_easy_read:
A foul:
An attempt fails if:
pg076_n0035_easy_read: The jumper knocks the bar off its support.
pg076_n0038_easy_read: The jumper does not take off on 1 foot.
pg076_n0041_easy_read: The jumper steps outside the take-off area before or after the jump.
pg076_n0044_easy_read: The athlete goes over the time limit for the attempt.
pg076_n0047_easy_read: The jumper misses all 3 attempts at a given height.
pg077_n0006_easy_read:
Jump-off:
The athlete must jump at every height until the decision is made.
Each athlete has 1 jump at each height.
The jump-off starts at the next height.

pg080_n0007_easy_read:
Swimming is a sport.
A person moves through water using different strokes, like aquatic animals.
pg080_n0008_easy_read:
People swim for different reasons:
- for fun
- for fitness
- for competition

Swimming is an important skill for survival and sport.
It helps people of all genders and ages.
pg080_n0009_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the concept of swimming
- safety measures
- basic skills
- the rules of swimming
pg080_n0010_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you swim well and with confidence.
pg080_n0014_easy_read: Swimming is more than just being in water.
pg080_n0018_easy_read:
Swimming is a competitive water sport.
It can involve 1 swimmer or a team.
Swimmers race against each other in water.
They use different strokes and swim different distances.
pg080_n0019_easy_read:
Swimmers compete in:
- freestyle
- backstroke
- breaststroke
- butterfly
- medley
pg080_n0020_easy_read:
Competitive swimming takes place in:
- pools
- open water

It needs:
- endurance
- speed
- technique
- strategic planning
pg080_n0021_easy_read:
Competitive swimming is part of events such as:
- the Olympics
- World Championships
- collegiate competitions
pg080_n0022_easy_read:
As a leisure activity, swimming is a skill for life.
It improves physical fitness, heart health, and endurance.
pg080_n0023_easy_read:
Swimming is also important for safety in water.
It gives people the skills they need to survive and respond well in water emergencies.
pg080_n0024_easy_read:
Therapeutic swimming can give people a supportive environment.
It can help them:
- strengthen muscles
- improve mobility
- manage pain
pg081_n0005_easy_read: Swimming needs special facilities and equipment for training and competition.
pg081_n0006_easy_read: These facilities and equipment help make swimming smooth and enjoyable for swimmers at all levels.
pg081_n0010_easy_read: The main swimming facilities are swimming pools and open water areas.
pg081_n0014_easy_read:
A swimming pool is a man-made place that holds water for swimming, diving, and other water activities for fun or competition.
See Figure 3.1.
pg081_n0015_easy_read:
A swimming pool gives swimmers a planned and controlled place.
This helps make swimming safe, easy to use, and efficient for swimmers at all levels.
pg081_n0016_easy_read: Swimming pools are grouped by their main use.
pg081_n0017_easy_read:
Recreational pools are for leisure.
People usually find them in:
- homes
- hotels
- resorts
pg081_n0018_easy_read:
Training pools are in schools and sports facilities.
People use them to develop swimming skills.
pg081_n0019_easy_read:
Competitive pools are built to meet national and international standards.
People use them for professional swimming competitions.
pg081_n0021_easy_read:
Competitive pools have 2 types:
- short course pools (25 m), for national and club-level competitions
- long course pools (Olympic-size) pools (50 m), for international tournaments such as the Olympics and World Championships
pg081_n0022_easy_read:
A swimming pool has features for different needs:
- different depths for different skill levels
- lane markings to guide swimmers
- starting blocks for race starts
- filtration and chlorination systems to keep the water clean and hygienic
pg081_n0023_easy_read:
Together, these features create the best swimming environment.
They help swimmers develop skills and perform at a professional level.
pg082_n0005_easy_read:
Open waters are natural water places, such as:
- lakes
- rivers
- seas
- oceans

People use them for:
- swimming for fun
- endurance training
- competitions

Figure 3.2.
pg082_n0006_easy_read:
Open waters are different from swimming pools.
Open waters do not have artificial edges.
This makes them harder to use.
Water conditions can change, such as:
- currents
- tides
- changes in temperature
pg082_n0007_easy_read:
People often use open water swimming in:
- triathlons
- long-distance races
- lifesaving training

Swimmers need advanced skills for:
- navigation
- endurance
- safety awareness
pg082_n0013_easy_read:
Swimming equipment means the tools people use for:
- training
- recreation
- competitions

These tools help to:
- keep people safe
- improve performance
- improve technique
pg082_n0014_easy_read:
The equipment includes:
- swimsuits
- goggles
- swim caps
- kickboards
- pull buoys
- fins
- hand paddles
- earplugs
pg082_n0018_easy_read: A swimsuit is clothing for swimming or for other water activities.
pg082_n0019_easy_read:
A proper swimsuit should be comfortable.
It should be flexible.
It should help the swimmer move easily in the water.
pg082_n0020_easy_read:
A swimsuit is usually made from materials like polyester.
Polyester gives a close fit.
It also reduces drag in the water.
pg082_n0021_easy_read:
Streamlined swimsuits reduce water resistance.
They help the swimmer move faster and better in the water.
Figure 3.3.
pg083_n0009_easy_read:
Goggles protect the eyes during swimming.
They protect the eyes from water, chlorine, salt, and other things that can irritate them.
pg083_n0010_easy_read:
Goggles also help swimmers see clearly.
This helps swimmers stay focused, especially during long swims or races.
pg083_n0011_easy_read:
Goggles are usually made from soft and adjustable materials, such as rubber seals.
This helps them fit tightly around the eyes and keep water out.
Figure 3.4.
pg083_n0016_easy_read:
A swim cap is a close-fitting and flexible cover for the head.
People wear it while swimming.
Figure 3.5.
pg083_n0017_easy_read:
The swim cap helps protect the hair.
It also reduces drag, which can slow down performance.
pg083_n0018_easy_read:
The swim cap is made of materials that fit closely.
This helps protect the hair from chlorine damage.
pg083_n0019_easy_read:
In competitive swimming, the swim cap also makes the swimmer’s head smoother in the water.
It also reduces drag.
This helps the swimmer move faster in the water.
pg084_n0007_easy_read:
The kickboard is a floating tool for training.
It supports the swimmer's upper body.
This helps the swimmer focus on improving leg movements.
Figure 3.6.
pg084_n0008_easy_read: People often use kickboards to practise kicking techniques.
pg084_n0009_easy_read:
Kickboards help swimmers use only their leg movements.
Kickboards also help swimmers make their lower body stronger.
Swimmers do not need to worry about balance in the water.
pg084_n0015_easy_read:
A pull buoy is a floating device.
Swimmers place it between their legs, usually at the thighs or ankles.
It helps swimmers stay afloat and stable while they focus on arm movements.
Figure 3.7.
pg084_n0016_easy_read:
The pull buoy isolates the upper body.
This helps swimmers focus on improving:
- stroke technique
- strength
- endurance
Swimmers can do this without the extra effort of kicking.
pg085_n0007_easy_read:
Fins are devices you wear on your feet.
They help you move faster and improve your kicking technique.
See Figure 3.8.
pg085_n0008_easy_read:
Fins help swimmers move forward better in the water.
They help swimmers make stronger kicks.
They also reduce tiredness.
pg085_n0009_easy_read:
Fins also help improve leg strength and flexibility.
This makes fins an important tool for training kicking technique.
pg085_n0015_easy_read:
Hand paddles are flat, hard plastic devices.
Swimmers wear them on their hands while swimming.
Hand paddles increase resistance and make arm strokes stronger.
See Figure 3.9.
pg085_n0016_easy_read:
Hand paddles increase surface area.
So, they create more resistance.
This helps swimmers build arm strength and improve stroke technique.
pg085_n0017_easy_read: Hand paddles are very useful for swimmers who work on speed and endurance in swimming strokes.
pg086_n0007_easy_read:
Earplugs are devices that go into the ears.
They stop water from entering the ear canal during swimming.
See Figure 3.10.
pg086_n0008_easy_read:
Swimmers commonly use earplugs.
Earplugs reduce the risk of ear infections, such as ear fungus.
Earplugs also make swimming more comfortable.
pg086_n0009_easy_read:
There are different types of earplugs.
The type depends on the swimmer's preference and need.
pg086_n0010_easy_read:
Earplugs are especially useful during long training sessions.
They are also useful for people with sensitive ears.
pg087_n0005_easy_read:
Watch a swimming session.
It can be:
- training
- recreation
- competition
pg087_n0006_easy_read:
While you watch, look at the other equipment used in swimming.
Identify what each piece of equipment is used for.
pg087_n0010_easy_read:
Swimming is enjoyable and good for you.
But you must follow safety rules.
This helps prevent:
- accidents
- injuries
- drowning
pg087_n0011_easy_read:
Follow these safety measures.
They help make swimming safe and enjoyable.
pg087_n0015_easy_read:
Do light stretching and warm-up exercises before you enter the water.
This helps:
- prevent muscle cramps
- improve flexibility
- reduce the risk of injuries while swimming
pg087_n0019_easy_read:
Always swim in places where lifeguards are watching.
For example:
- designated swimming pools
- marked parts of open water
pg087_n0020_easy_read:
Do not swim in unknown or restricted areas.
For example:
- areas with strong currents
- deep water
pg087_n0024_easy_read: Swimmers should know their skill level before they swim.
pg087_n0028_easy_read: Children and inexperienced swimmers should always have supervision.
pg087_n0032_easy_read: Follow all signs and safety rules at swimming facilities.
pg087_n0033_easy_read:
For example, do not:
- run on slippery surfaces
- dive into shallow water
- play roughly, because this may cause injuries
pg087_n0037_easy_read:
Wear suitable swimming gear.
For example:
- swimsuits
- goggles
- swim caps
This helps keep you comfortable and safe while swimming.
pg087_n0038_easy_read:
Beginners should use flotation devices for extra safety.
For example:
- kickboards
- life jackets
pg088_n0005_easy_read:
Be careful of these things when you swim in open water:
- tides
- waves
- water animals
- underwater currents
These can be dangerous, even for experienced swimmers.
pg088_n0006_easy_read: Always check the weather forecast and the water temperature before you swim in natural waters.
pg088_n0010_easy_read:
Always swim with another person or with a group.
This helps keep you safe in an emergency.
Never swim alone.
pg088_n0014_easy_read:
Swimming needs a lot of physical effort.
If your body does not have enough water, you can feel very tired.
pg088_n0015_easy_read:
Swimmers should drink enough water before and after swimming.
Swimmers should also take breaks when they feel very tired.
pg088_n0019_easy_read:
Swimmers should know basic water rescue techniques.
Swimmers should also know CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) for emergencies.
pg088_n0020_easy_read: Learning to notice the signs of drowning and to help a swimmer who is struggling can save lives.

pg088_n0029_easy_read:
Swimming is a basic life skill.
It improves physical fitness, safety, and enjoyment during free time.
pg088_n0030_easy_read: To become a good swimmer, a person must learn essential swimming skills and proper techniques.
pg088_n0031_easy_read:
These swimming skills help swimmers:
- move well in the water
- save energy
- stay safe while swimming
pg088_n0035_easy_read:
Before learners master swimming strokes, they must first learn basic swimming skills.
These basic skills are the foundation for moving well in water.
pg088_n0036_easy_read:
These swimming skills help swimmers:
- build confidence
- keep control
- stay safe while swimming
pg088_n0037_easy_read: The main essential swimming skills are:
pg089_n0005_easy_read: Floating means staying partly on the surface of the water without sinking.
pg089_n0006_easy_read: Floating is a basic swimming skill. It helps swimmers save energy, rest, and stay calm in the water.
pg089_n0007_easy_read: Learning to float well improves confidence and safety in the water, especially in deep water or emergencies.
pg089_n0008_easy_read: There are 2 main types of floating:
pg089_n0012_easy_read: The back float is an important skill. It lets swimmers stay on the surface of the water and breathe freely.
pg089_n0013_easy_read: To do a back float, follow these steps:
pg089_n0017_easy_read: Lie on your back. Keep your body straight and relaxed. See Figure 3.11.
pg089_n0020_easy_read: Move your arms a little away from your body, or stretch them out for better balance.
pg089_n0023_easy_read: Keep your legs straight and slightly apart. You can also bend your knees if that feels more comfortable.
pg089_n0026_easy_read: Tilt your head slightly back. Keep your ears under the water. Keep your face above the water.
pg089_n0029_easy_read: Breathe normally. Stay as still as possible to keep floating.
pg089_n0039_easy_read: The front float is a skill that helps swimmers get ready for different strokes and learn to balance in the water.
pg089_n0040_easy_read: To do a front float, follow these steps:
pg089_n0044_easy_read: Stretch your body face-down in the water. Keep your arms and legs stretched out.
pg089_n0047_easy_read: Take a deep breath before going under the water. This helps your body stay buoyant.
pg090_n0005_easy_read:
Put your arms forward or keep them at your sides for balance.
See Figure 3.12.
pg090_n0008_easy_read:
Keep your legs straight and relaxed.
This helps avoid extra movement.
pg090_n0011_easy_read:
When you are ready to stand up or change position, lift your head.
Bend your knees.
Push down with your hands to return to an upright position.
pg090_n0017_easy_read: Figure 3.12: How to do a front float
pg090_n0021_easy_read: Good breathing control is very important for efficient swimming, endurance, and relaxation in the water.
pg090_n0022_easy_read: Good breathing control helps swimmers keep a steady rhythm, feel less tired, and improve their overall performance.
pg090_n0023_easy_read: Without good breathing techniques, swimmers may find coordination difficult and get tired quickly.
pg090_n0024_easy_read: To develop good breathing control, swimmers must focus on 3 key parts:
pg090_n0030_easy_read:
Before entering the water, swimmers should take a deep breath.
They should fill their lungs with enough air to improve buoyancy and oxygen supply.
pg090_n0033_easy_read: Swimmers should breathe in deeply through the nose or mouth.
pg090_n0036_easy_read: Holding the breath for a short moment before breathing out helps swimmers stay stable and avoid panic underwater.
pg090_n0042_easy_read: Breathe out slowly through the nose or mouth while the face is under the water.
pg090_n0045_easy_read: Controlled breathing out stops water from entering the airway and makes the breathing cycle smooth.
pg090_n0048_easy_read: In front crawl and backstroke, swimmers usually breathe out through the nose to stop water from entering it.
pg090_n0049_easy_read: In breaststroke and butterfly, swimmers breathe out through both the nose and mouth.
pg091_n0005_easy_read: A steady and full exhalation makes it easier to take the next breath well.
pg091_n0010_easy_read:
Each swimming stroke has its own breathing pattern.
This breathing pattern must match the arm movements to keep the swimmer moving well.
pg091_n0013_easy_read:
In front crawl, swimmers turn their head to the side during the arm recovery phase to breathe in.
Then they breathe out underwater.
pg091_n0016_easy_read:
In breaststroke and butterfly, swimmers lift their head above the water at the right time to take a quick breath.
Then they go under the water again.
pg091_n0019_easy_read: Good timing makes sure breathing does not interrupt the swimming stroke or slow movement.
pg091_n0022_easy_read: Practice the following breathing control with different drills:
pg091_n0025_easy_read: Breathe in deeply before going under the water.
pg091_n0031_easy_read: Time your breathing with your arm movements.
pg091_n0034_easy_read: Treading water is the ability to stay upright in deep water without sinking.
pg091_n0035_easy_read:
This skill is important for:
- resting
- survival
- staying stable when a swimmer needs to stay in 1 place, such as while waiting for rescue or watching the surroundings
pg091_n0036_easy_read: Unlike swimming strokes that focus on moving forward, treading water lets the swimmer stay in 1 place and keep the head above water.
pg091_n0038_easy_read:
To tread water well, swimmers must use sculling arm movements to create lift.
See Figure 3.13.
pg091_n0039_easy_read:
The arms should move in a continuous circular motion.
They should push the water down and outward to create buoyancy.
pg091_n0040_easy_read: This movement helps keep the swimmer afloat without using too much energy.
pg091_n0041_easy_read:
The hands should stay relaxed.
Small, controlled movements are better than strong splashes.
pg091_n0042_easy_read: Swimmers also need to use effective kicking techniques to keep balance.
pg091_n0043_easy_read: There are 3 common kicks used for treading water:
pg091_n0048_easy_read: Rapid leg movements up and down, one after the other, like in front crawl.
pg091_n0052_easy_read: A wide sweeping kick like the one used in breaststroke.
pg092_n0003_easy_read: (iii) Eggbeater kick: The legs make a continuous circular movement, one after the other. People often use this kick in water polo for stability and efficiency.
pg092_n0012_easy_read: Watch a video that shows treading water.
pg092_n0013_easy_read:
Then choose 1 of these kicking techniques.
Practice it with drills until you can do it confidently:
pg092_n0023_easy_read: Kicking is a basic swimming skill. It moves the swimmer forward and helps keep the body in position in the water.
pg092_n0024_easy_read: Good kicking improves speed, balance, and efficiency in different swimming strokes.
pg092_n0025_easy_read: Each swimming stroke needs a specific kicking technique. This helps the swimmer move as much as possible and stay coordinated with the arms and breathing.
pg092_n0029_easy_read: The flutter kick is 1 of the most common kicking techniques in swimming.
pg092_n0030_easy_read: The flutter kick uses small, fast, alternating leg movements.
pg092_n0031_easy_read: Swimmers use this kick in front crawl and backstroke. It moves the swimmer forward and keeps the body aligned. Figure 3.14.
pg092_n0032_easy_read: The movement starts from the hips, not the knees. The legs stay straight but slightly flexible.
pg092_n0033_easy_read: To do an efficient flutter kick, swimmers
pg093_n0003_easy_read:
Swimmers should keep their feet close together.
They should make quick, continuous movements.
This helps reduce drag and keep speed.
pg093_n0009_easy_read: Figure 3.14: How to do the flutter kick
pg093_n0014_easy_read:
Use a kickboard.
Practice flutter kicks many times.
Keep your body straight.
Keep your legs relaxed.
Practice until you master the skill.
pg093_n0018_easy_read:
The frog kick is a wide leg movement.
It gives power to the breaststroke.
pg093_n0019_easy_read:
In this kick, the swimmer bends the knees outward.
At the same time, the swimmer brings the feet toward the body.
Then the swimmer pushes the legs outward and backward in a circular movement.
After that, the swimmer brings the legs back together.
See Figure 3.15.
pg093_n0020_easy_read:
The frog kick gives strong forward movement in each cycle.
It works best when the swimmer moves the arms in time with the breaststroke.
pg093_n0021_easy_read:
To do this well, use a controlled and smooth movement.
Do not make forceful splashes.
pg093_n0023_easy_read: Figure 3.15: How to do the frog kick
pg094_n0005_easy_read:
Use kickboards to practise frog kicks again and again.
This helps you master the skill.
pg094_n0009_easy_read:
The dolphin kick is a strong, wave-like movement.
Swimmers use it in the butterfly stroke and when swimming underwater.
pg094_n0010_easy_read:
In the dolphin kick, keep your legs together.
Make the movement start from your hips.
This creates a smooth wave-like movement, like a dolphin's tail.
See Figure 3.16.
pg094_n0011_easy_read:
This kick needs strong core muscles and flexibility.
They help you make a continuous wave through your body.
pg094_n0012_easy_read: The dolphin kick is useful for fast starts and turns in competitive swimming.
pg094_n0018_easy_read:
Use kickboards to practise dolphin kicks again and again.
This helps you master the skill.
pg094_n0022_easy_read:
Arm movements are very important.
They affect the swimmer's speed, direction, and how well the swimmer moves in the water.
pg094_n0023_easy_read:
Good arm technique helps the swimmer move forward.
It reduces resistance and helps the swimmer keep balance.
pg094_n0024_easy_read:
Each stroke needs its own arm movements.
The swimmer must synchronise them with breathing and kicking.
This helps the swimmer move smoothly and effectively.
pg094_n0025_easy_read: The principles for arm movements include:
pg094_n0028_easy_read:
If the fingers are slightly apart, water can pass through the gaps.
This makes the movement less efficient.
pg094_n0029_easy_read:
If swimmers keep their fingers close together and slightly cupped, they make a larger surface to push against the water.
This creates more force with each stroke.
See Figure 3.17.
pg094_n0030_easy_read:
This technique is important in these strokes:
- front crawl
- breaststroke
- backstroke
- butterfly
In these strokes, continuous propulsion is necessary.
pg095_n0007_easy_read:
In strokes like front crawl and butterfly, a high elbow catch helps swimmers pull more water.
This helps swimmers move forward with little resistance.
pg095_n0008_easy_read:
When swimmers do swimming strokes, they should keep the elbow high during the recovery phase.
This helps the movement stay smooth and circular.
pg095_n0009_easy_read:
A correct elbow position makes the stroke stronger and reduces drag.
This helps the swimmer move through the water more efficiently.
Figure 3.18.
pg095_n0015_easy_read:
Each swimming stroke has its own timing pattern.
This timing matches:
- arm strokes
- leg kicks
- breathing cycles
pg095_n0016_easy_read:
In front crawl and backstroke, 1 arm enters the water while the other arm recovers.
At the same time, the legs do a continuous flutter kick.
pg096_n0003_easy_read:
In butterfly, both arms move together in a circular motion.
This movement needs exact timing with kicks and breathing.
pg096_n0004_easy_read:
Good technique helps the swimmer move smoothly.
It reduces tiredness.
It also improves overall swimming performance.
pg096_n0009_easy_read:
Use different drills to practise arm movements many times.
Follow the 3 principles until you master the skill.
