pg096_n0026_easy_read: Swimming strokes are different techniques that move the body through water.
pg096_n0027_easy_read:
Each stroke has its own arm movements, leg kicks, and breathing patterns.
These movements need coordination for efficient swimming.
pg096_n0028_easy_read: When swimmers master these strokes, they can swim well and save energy.
pg096_n0029_easy_read:
The 4 main competitive swimming strokes are:
- front crawl
- backstroke
- breaststroke
- butterfly
pg096_n0033_easy_read:
Front crawl is a swimming stroke.
It uses flutter kicks and alternating arm movements in a face-down position.
One arm pulls through the water from above the head to the hip.
At the same time, the other arm recovers above the water.
pg096_n0034_easy_read: This stroke is the fastest and the most commonly used stroke in freestyle swimming races.
pg096_n0035_easy_read:
People favour this stroke for its efficiency and speed.
It is the preferred stroke for long-distance swimming and racing.
pg096_n0036_easy_read: The following steps will help you practise front crawl:
pg096_n0040_easy_read:
Lie in the water face-down.
Keep your body straight to reduce resistance.
pg096_n0043_easy_read: Move your arms in an alternating windmill motion.
pg096_n0044_easy_read:
One arm stretches forward and enters the water.
The other arm pulls back under the body to move the body forward.
pg096_n0047_easy_read:
Move your legs continuously in a flutter kick.
This helps you keep balance, stability, and forward movement.
It also reduces drag.
pg096_n0050_easy_read:
Turn your head to the side after a set number of strokes and breathe in.
Usually, this is after every 2 or 3 strokes.
Breathe in quickly through the mouth while one arm
pg097_n0003_easy_read:
The arm recovers above the water.
Breathe out while your face is under the water.
See Figure 3.19.
pg097_n0008_easy_read: Practice front crawl many times to learn the skill well.
pg097_n0012_easy_read:
Backstroke is a swimming style done on the back.
The swimmer uses a flutter kick.
The arms move one after the other.
1 arm pulls through the water from above the head to the hip.
The other arm recovers above the water.
pg097_n0013_easy_read:
This stroke lets you breathe freely because your face stays above the water.
This makes it a good stroke for beginners.
It is also an important technique in competitive swimming.
pg097_n0014_easy_read: Good coordination of the arms, legs, and body position helps you swim smoothly and well.
pg097_n0015_easy_read: The following steps will help you practise backstroke:
pg097_n0019_easy_read:
Lie in the water on your back.
Keep your body straight to reduce resistance.
pg097_n0022_easy_read: Move your arms in an alternating windmill motion.
pg097_n0023_easy_read:
1 arm reaches forward and enters the water.
The other arm pulls back under the body to move you forward.
pg097_n0026_easy_read:
Move your legs all the time in a flutter kick.
This helps you keep:
- balance
- stability
- forward movement
It also reduces drag.
pg097_n0029_easy_read:
Breathe naturally because your face is up.
Keep your head in the correct position.
This helps you avoid too much movement that could slow you down.
pg097_n0030_easy_read: Keeping your head still and looking up helps you keep balance and direction.
pg097_n0033_easy_read: Use lane markers or ceiling patterns to help you keep direction without turning.
pg097_n0034_easy_read:
A straight body position, with the hips and legs near the water surface, reduces drag and improves speed.
See Figure 3.20.
pg098_n0006_easy_read: Practice backstroke many times to learn the skill well.
pg098_n0010_easy_read: This swimming stroke is done face down in the water. You move your legs forward with your knees together. You turn your feet outward and push them back. You also glide and sweep your arms backward.
pg098_n0011_easy_read: Breaststroke is 1 of the oldest and most widely used swimming strokes.
pg098_n0012_easy_read: It uses controlled and strong movements. These movements focus more on saving energy than on speed.
pg098_n0013_easy_read: This stroke needs careful coordination of the arms, legs, and breathing. This helps you keep a smooth and steady movement.
pg098_n0014_easy_read: These steps will help you practise breaststroke:
pg098_n0018_easy_read: Push off the wall with your feet. Keep your face down. Keep your body straight. Stretch your arms forward. Keep your hands together. Keep your head in line with your body.
pg098_n0021_easy_read: Move your arms in a circular scooping motion in front of your body. First, stretch your arms forward. Then pull them outward and back toward your chest in a sweeping motion. This creates propulsion.
pg098_n0022_easy_read: Keep your hands close together at the start of the stroke to reduce drag.
pg098_n0025_easy_read: Do a frog kick. Bend your knees. Push your feet outward in a circular motion. Then bring them back together.
pg098_n0028_easy_read: Breathe during each stroke cycle. Lift your head above the water when you pull your arms back.
pg098_n0029_easy_read: After you breathe in, breathe out as you go under the water again. This helps you move smoothly from 1 stroke to the next.
pg098_n0030_easy_read: Good breathing timing helps you keep momentum and avoid fatigue. See Figure 3.21.
pg099_n0006_easy_read: Practice breaststroke many times until you can do it well.
pg099_n0010_easy_read: Butterfly stroke is a swimming style. Both arms move together in the same way, like a windmill. Both legs kick together in a smooth wave-like motion.
pg099_n0011_easy_read: In this movement, the swimmer's body moves in a wave-like way to help the swimmer move forward. The swimmer breathes during arm recovery, when the head lifts.
pg099_n0012_easy_read: Butterfly stroke is one of the strongest and hardest swimming strokes. It needs a high level of strength, endurance, and coordination.
pg099_n0013_easy_read: People know butterfly stroke by its special wave-like motion and the way both arms move together. It is the 2-fastest stroke after the front crawl.
pg099_n0014_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the butterfly stroke:
pg099_n0018_easy_read: Dive or push away from the wall with your face down. Keep your body moving in a wave-like motion.
pg099_n0021_easy_read: Move both arms together in a wide motion over the water. Then pull them down to move forward.
pg099_n0022_easy_read: Start the stroke with both arms straight in front. Then push your arms out and down through the water. After that, bring them back over the surface in a smooth, circular motion.
pg099_n0023_easy_read: In butterfly stroke, the arms create most of the forward movement.
pg099_n0026_easy_read: Do a dolphin kick. Move both feet together in a wave-like motion.
pg099_n0027_easy_read: This kick starts from the hips. Then the legs and feet follow in a smooth wave-like movement.
pg099_n0028_easy_read: The dolphin kick gives continuous forward movement. It also helps you keep the right body position.
pg099_n0031_easy_read: Breathe as you lift your head forward during the arm recovery phase.
pg099_n0032_easy_read: Breathe in quickly before your face goes back into the water. Then breathe out under the water.
pg100_n0003_easy_read:
Good timing is very important.
It helps keep the stroke rhythm steady.
pg100_n0004_easy_read:
Many swimmers breathe every stroke cycle or every 2 cycles.
This depends on their endurance.
pg100_n0006_easy_read:
The butterfly stroke uses a continuous wave-like movement.
This movement goes through the whole body.
pg100_n0007_easy_read:
Swimmers must coordinate:
- arm movements
- leg kicks
- breathing
This helps them keep speed and efficiency.
See Figure 3.22.
pg100_n0008_easy_read:
A streamlined body position helps reduce drag.
It also improves momentum.
pg100_n0013_easy_read: Practice the butterfly stroke many times to master the skill.
pg100_n0017_easy_read:
Swimming competitions are organised by:
- distance
- stroke
- format
pg100_n0018_easy_read:
By stroke, the races include:
- freestyle
- backstroke
- breaststroke
- butterfly
- medley
pg100_n0022_easy_read:
Freestyle is a swimming race.
Swimmers can use any stroke they prefer.
pg100_n0023_easy_read:
However, in most freestyle races, swimmers use front crawl.
So, some people wrongly think front crawl is the freestyle stroke.
pg100_n0024_easy_read: Below are the key rules for a freestyle swimming race:
pg100_n0032_easy_read: Swimmers must start the race by diving into the pool from the starting block.
pg100_n0035_easy_read: The race starts when there is a whistle sound or another starting signal.
pg100_n0038_easy_read: To complete the race, a swimmer must touch the wall at the end of the final lap with any part of the body.
pg101_n0009_easy_read:
Swimmers may use any stroke.
The front crawl is the stroke swimmers use most often.
pg101_n0012_easy_read: Any movement forward is allowed if it does not break other competition rules.
pg101_n0019_easy_read: In races with more than 1 lap, swimmers must touch the wall before they turn.
pg101_n0022_easy_read: Swimmers often use flip turns (tumble turns) to turn faster.
pg101_n0029_easy_read:
Swimmers can breathe as often as they want.
They usually turn their heads to the side.
pg101_n0032_easy_read:
The head can go under the water.
But swimmers must come up within 15 m after the start and after each turn.
pg101_n0039_easy_read: A swimmer may be disqualified for a false start if the swimmer moves before the starting signal.
pg101_n0042_easy_read: Swimmers are disqualified if they do not stay in their own lanes and they interfere with other swimmers.
pg101_n0045_easy_read: A swimmer is also disqualified if the swimmer does not touch the wall at the end of a lap or at the finish.
pg101_n0048_easy_read: A swimmer must not stay underwater for more than 15 metres after the start or a turn.
pg101_n0051_easy_read: Practise competing in freestyle swimming while following its rules.
pg101_n0055_easy_read: In backstroke swimming, the swimmer must use the backstroke during the whole race.
pg101_n0056_easy_read: These are the main rules for a backstroke swimming race:
pg101_n0064_easy_read:
Swimmers start in the water.
They hold onto the wall or the starting block grips.
pg101_n0067_easy_read: After the start signal, swimmers push off the wall and stay on their back.
pg102_n0004_easy_read:
After the start, swimmers can stay underwater for up to 15 metres.
They must come to the surface before they pass 15 metres.
pg102_n0010_easy_read:
Swimmers must stay on their back during the whole race.
They can turn only when they do a turn.
pg102_n0012_easy_read:
Swimmers can move their arms in any way.
Most swimmers use alternating arm strokes and a continuous flutter kick.
pg102_n0014_easy_read:
The swimmer's body must stay flat on the back.
A small body rotation is allowed.
pg102_n0020_easy_read: When swimmers turn, they must touch the wall with any part of the body.
pg102_n0022_easy_read:
During the turn, a swimmer can turn onto the stomach.
The swimmer must finish the turn quickly.
pg102_n0024_easy_read:
After pushing off from the wall, swimmers can stay underwater for up to 15 metres.
Then they must come to the surface.
pg102_n0030_easy_read: The race ends when a swimmer touches the wall while still on their back.
pg102_n0032_easy_read: Swimmers cannot turn onto their front before they touch the wall.
pg102_n0036_easy_read: A swimmer may be disqualified for:
pg102_n0039_easy_read: - not staying on their back, except during the turn
pg102_n0041_easy_read:
- doing an illegal turn
- not touching the wall
pg102_n0043_easy_read: - staying underwater for more than 15 metres after the start or a turn
pg102_n0045_easy_read: - false starting, which means leaving before the start signal
pg102_n0048_easy_read:
Practice a backstroke swimming race.
Follow the rules.
pg102_n0052_easy_read: In breaststroke swimming, the swimmer must use breaststroke during the whole race.
pg102_n0053_easy_read: Here are the main rules for a breaststroke swimming race:
pg102_n0060_easy_read: The race starts with a dive from the starting block.
pg102_n0062_easy_read: After the dive, swimmers can do 1 arm pull and 1 leg kick underwater before they come to the surface.
pg103_n0003_easy_read: The swimmer's head must come above the water before the swimmer finishes the 2nd arm stroke.
pg103_n0008_easy_read:
Swimmers must stay on their stomachs at all times.
They must not turn onto their backs.
pg103_n0010_easy_read:
Both arms must move at the same time.
They must move in a circular, scooping motion.
pg103_n0012_easy_read:
The legs must do a frog kick, also called a breaststroke kick.
The feet turn outward and then sweep back together.
pg103_n0014_easy_read:
Swimmers must not use alternating kicks or flutter kicks.
If they do, they can be disqualified.
pg103_n0016_easy_read: After each stroke, the swimmer's head must come above the water surface.
pg103_n0021_easy_read: At each turn, both hands must touch the wall at the same time.
pg103_n0023_easy_read:
After pushing off the wall, a swimmer can go underwater for a short time.
The swimmer must come back to the surface before starting the 2nd arm stroke.
pg103_n0025_easy_read: After pushing off the wall, 1 pull and 1 kick are allowed before normal strokes start again.
pg103_n0030_easy_read: At the finish, swimmers must touch the wall with both hands at the same time.
pg103_n0032_easy_read: When finishing the race, the body must stay face-down.
pg103_n0036_easy_read: A swimmer may be disqualified for:
pg103_n0039_easy_read: Using the wrong kick, such as a flutter kick or dolphin kick.
pg103_n0041_easy_read: Not touching the wall with both hands at the same time at turns and at the finish.
pg103_n0043_easy_read:
Moving the arms at different times.
The arms must move together.
pg103_n0045_easy_read: Not coming above the surface of the water after the 2nd stroke.
pg103_n0047_easy_read: Turning onto the back at any time during the race.
pg103_n0051_easy_read: Practice a breaststroke swimming race and follow its rules.
pg104_n0005_easy_read: In butterfly swimming, the swimmer must use the butterfly stroke for the whole race.
pg104_n0006_easy_read: These are the main rules for a butterfly swimming race:
pg104_n0014_easy_read: The race starts with a dive from the starting block.
pg104_n0017_easy_read: After entering the water, swimmers can do 1 arm pull and up to 2 dolphin kicks underwater before they come up to the surface.
pg104_n0020_easy_read: Swimmers must come up to the surface before they finish the 2nd arm stroke.
pg104_n0027_easy_read: Swimmers must stay on their stomach, in a face-down position, during the whole race.
pg104_n0028_easy_read: Swimmers must not turn onto their back.
pg104_n0031_easy_read: The arms must move together and in the same way, with recovery over the water.
pg104_n0034_easy_read: The legs must do a dolphin kick. Both feet move together in a wave-like motion.
pg104_n0037_easy_read: Swimmers must not use flutter kicks or breaststroke kicks.
pg104_n0044_easy_read: Swimmers can breathe at any time. They must lift their head forward and keep their body streamlined.
pg104_n0047_easy_read: When swimmers are not breathing, the head must face forward or downward.
pg104_n0054_easy_read: At each turn, both hands must touch the wall at the same time.
pg104_n0057_easy_read: After turning, swimmers can do 1 arm pull and up to 2 dolphin kicks underwater before they come up to the surface.
pg104_n0060_easy_read: The swimmer must return to a regular stroke pattern before reaching 15 m from the wall.
pg104_n0067_easy_read: The race ends when a swimmer touches the wall with both hands at the same time.
pg104_n0070_easy_read: When finishing, the body must stay in a prone, face-down position.
pg104_n0075_easy_read: A swimmer may be disqualified for:
pg104_n0079_easy_read: Not touching the wall with both hands at the same time at turns and at the finish.
pg104_n0082_easy_read: Using arm movements or leg kicks that are different from butterfly.
pg105_n0004_easy_read: (iii) Not breaking the surface of the water within 15 metres after the start or after a turn; and
pg105_n0006_easy_read: (iv) Turning onto the back at any time during the race.
pg105_n0009_easy_read:
Practice a butterfly swimming race.
Follow its rules.
pg105_n0013_easy_read:
Medley is a race with more than 1 stroke.
1 swimmer can do it. This is an individual medley.
A team can also do it. This is a medley relay.
pg105_n0014_easy_read: The rules for medley are the same as the rules for each stroke used in the race.
pg105_n0015_easy_read:
In these races, the swimmer starts with:
- butterfly
- backstroke
- breaststroke
- front crawl
pg105_n0016_easy_read:
In a medley relay, 4 swimmers each swim 1 stroke in this order:
- backstroke
- breaststroke
- butterfly
- front crawl
pg105_n0019_easy_read:

Follow the rules for each stroke used in the race.

pg109_n0008_easy_read:
Gymnastics is a sport.
It includes many physical exercises and routines on different apparatuses.
pg109_n0009_easy_read:
Both males and females do gymnastics.
They do it for competition and for recreation.
pg109_n0010_easy_read:
Taking part in gymnastics:
- improves physical health
- creates job opportunities
- helps people develop important life skills
pg109_n0011_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the meaning of gymnastics
- safety measures in gymnastics
- skills in gymnastics
- rules in gymnastics
pg109_n0012_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you:
- analyse different gymnastics activities
- do different gymnastics activities with confidence and skill
pg109_n0016_easy_read: Gymnastics is more than physical skills
pg109_n0020_easy_read:
Gymnastics is a competitive sport and a developmental sport.
It includes many movements on apparatuses such as:
- floor
- balance beam
- vault
- rings
- parallel bars
- pommel horse
pg109_n0021_easy_read:
The main goal of gymnastics is to develop and show:
- good motor skills
- physical control
- graceful movement
pg109_n0022_easy_read:
The sport has several categories:
- artistic gymnastics
- rhythmic gymnastics
- trampoline
- acrobatic gymnastics
- aerobic gymnastics

Each category has its own technical requirements and performance standards.
pg109_n0023_easy_read: Gymnastics is very important for a person's full development, especially in early childhood and adolescence.
pg109_n0024_easy_read:
Gymnastics helps improve:
- basic movement patterns
- awareness of space
- muscle development
- self-discipline
pg109_n0025_easy_read:
Gymnastics also supports thinking and emotional growth.
It does this through:
- setting goals
- perseverance
- trying to do your best
pg109_n0026_easy_read: Gymnastics is an important part of physical
pg110_n0003_easy_read: It also gives a full plan for lifelong fitness and motor skill development.
pg110_n0007_easy_read: To stay safe in practice and competition, gymnasts must take safety measures to protect themselves and other people from injuries.
pg110_n0008_easy_read: The measures are in 3 main groups: safety gear, safe practices and competition, and healthy gymnastics.
pg110_n0012_easy_read: Using the right equipment is very important to prevent injuries and to perform well.
pg110_n0017_easy_read:
Apparel: This includes clothes that fit well, such as:
- leotards
- grips
- wrist guards
These clothes allow free movement and help reduce risk.
pg110_n0020_easy_read:
Protective equipment: This includes:
- gymnastics shoes
- knee supports
- elbow supports
- ankle supports
- mouth guards
This equipment helps reduce the impact of falls and repeated strain.
pg110_n0023_easy_read:
Safety equipment: This includes:
- mats
- padding
- spring floors
- spotting blocks
- other training aids
These items give cushioning and support during practice.
pg110_n0026_easy_read:
Gymnast-specific gear: These are personal items that improve comfort and performance, such as:
- headbands
- hair ties
- compression wear
pg110_n0030_easy_read: Safety in gymnastic training and competition depends on following guidelines, doing techniques and skills correctly, and taking action to prevent injuries.
pg110_n0031_easy_read: For safe gymnastic practice and competition, follow these key safety practices:
pg110_n0035_easy_read:
Start with a proper warm-up.
End with cool-down exercises.
pg110_n0038_easy_read:
Move from simple skills to more complex skills.
This builds confidence and reduces the risk of injury.
pg110_n0041_easy_read:
Train under qualified supervision.
Use spotting techniques.
pg110_n0044_easy_read:
Stay hydrated.
Follow a nutritious diet.
Make sure you get enough rest and recovery.
pg110_n0047_easy_read:
Follow rules and regulations.
Be medically prepared.
Show sportsmanship.
Stay mentally ready.
pg110_n0051_easy_read: Healthy gymnastics focuses on keeping the body and mind well while also developing skills.
pg110_n0052_easy_read: Healthy gymnastics includes practices that promote safety, including:
pg111_n0005_easy_read:
Keep your whole body fit.
Avoid too much training.
pg111_n0008_easy_read: Practice techniques that help prevent injuries.
pg111_n0011_easy_read:
Support mental health.
Keep a balanced training schedule.
pg111_n0014_easy_read:
Help people enjoy the sport.
This supports long-term participation and performance.
pg111_n0017_easy_read:

pg111_n0022_easy_read: Basic gymnastics facilities and equipment are the main spaces and tools for training and doing gymnastics.
pg111_n0023_easy_read: These usually include a gymnasium with padded flooring or spring floors.
pg111_n0024_easy_read:
Common equipment includes:
- landing mats
- gripping powder
- balance beams
- uneven bars
- parallel bars
- horizontal bars
- vaults
- gloves
- pommel horse
- rings
- personal kit
pg111_n0027_easy_read: Description of some basic gymnastics facilities and equipment
pg111_n0041_easy_read:
Mats absorb impact.
They give gymnasts a safe place to land when they do activities.
pg111_n0047_easy_read:
Gymnasts use gripping powder (magnesium carbonate) to absorb sweat.
This helps them hold apparatuses better, such as the horizontal bar, rings, and parallel bars.
pg111_n0053_easy_read:
The horizontal bar is also called the high bar.
It is a single metal bar above the ground.
Men use it in gymnastics for swinging, release moves, and dismounts.
pg112_n0010_easy_read:
A narrow wooden beam is used in women’s gymnastics.
It is covered with suede or a similar material.
pg112_n0019_easy_read: 2 suspended rings are used in men’s gymnastics for strength-based routines.
pg112_n0020_easy_read:
The gymnast must control movements during:
- holds
- swings
- dismounts
pg112_n0028_easy_read:
2 bars are set at the same height and are parallel to each other.
They are used in men’s gymnastics for:
- swinging
- vaulting
- strength-based movements
pg112_n0037_easy_read:
Wrist guards help keep the wrist joints stable.
Gymnasts use them especially during:
- handstands
- tumbling
- bar routines
pg112_n0045_easy_read:
A gymnast needs equipment for training and competition, such as:
- grips
- wristbands
- tape
- chalk powder

pg113_n0038_easy_read:
Gymnastics routines need good control of different skills.
These skills help gymnasts perform well and with confidence.
pg113_n0039_easy_read:
The basic skills in gymnastics include:
- handstand
- splits
- bridge
- cartwheel
- back rolls
- forward rolls
pg113_n0040_easy_read: The following text explains the basic skills in gymnastics:
pg113_n0043_easy_read:
A forward roll is a gymnastics skill.
The gymnast rolls forward on the floor.
The gymnast bends the body into a rounded shape.
The gymnast uses momentum to move smoothly.
pg114_n0003_easy_read: roll over the back and return to a standing position.
pg114_n0004_easy_read:
This helps you develop body awareness, coordination, and confidence in rolling movements.
It is a foundation for more gymnastic skills.
pg114_n0005_easy_read: To do a forward roll, follow these steps:
pg114_n0009_easy_read: Stand up straight with your arms raised.
pg114_n0012_easy_read:
Bend your knees.
Place your hands on the floor in front of you.
pg114_n0015_easy_read:
Bend your head forward.
Bring your chin to your chest.
pg114_n0018_easy_read: Roll forward over your back smoothly, as shown in Figure 4.1.
pg114_n0021_easy_read: Finish by landing on your feet and standing up.
pg114_n0031_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a forward roll.
Practice it many times until you master the skill.
pg114_n0035_easy_read:
A backward roll is a gymnastic skill.
The gymnast rolls backward over the shoulders and returns to a standing or seated position.
pg114_n0036_easy_read:
It helps develop core strength, coordination, and body control.
This makes it an important skill for advanced moves like back handsprings and back tucks.
pg114_n0037_easy_read: The following steps will help you practice backward rolls:
pg114_n0041_easy_read:
Stand, then squat with your feet together.
Keep your arms raised.
Keep your chin toward your chest to protect your neck.
pg114_n0044_easy_read:
Sit down and roll onto your back.
Bend your knees toward your chest.
pg114_n0047_easy_read:
Place your hands by your ears.
Keep your palms facing upward.
Push your hands against the floor to lift your back over your head.
pg114_n0050_easy_read:
Roll onto your feet and stand up smoothly.
Keep your arms raised for balance.
See Figure 4.2.
pg114_n0053_easy_read: Repeat the practice several times to perfect the skill.
pg115_n0013_easy_read:
Search on the internet and other sources for how to do a backward roll.
Then practise it many times until you master the skill.
pg115_n0017_easy_read: Handstand gymnastics is the skill of balancing your body upside down on your hands.
pg115_n0018_easy_read:
A handstand is a basic movement in gymnastics.
It needs:
- strength
- balance
- flexibility
- agility
- coordination
- control
pg115_n0019_easy_read:
People use handstands in different types of gymnastics, including:
- artistic gymnastics
- acrobatics
- tumbling
pg115_n0020_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the handstand:
pg115_n0024_easy_read:
Start by kicking up against a wall for support.
Stay there for a short time.
Repeat this many times.
pg115_n0027_easy_read: Balance your body on your hands as you lift your feet away from the wall.
pg115_n0028_easy_read: At first, you may ask someone to help you stay stable.
pg115_n0031_easy_read: Repeat it to improve your balance.
pg115_n0034_easy_read: When you are stable, start with your feet together, your arms raised over your head, and your core engaged.
pg115_n0037_easy_read:
Step 1 foot forward and lean.
Place your hands on the ground at shoulder width.
pg115_n0040_easy_read:
Swing your back leg up first.
Then swing the other leg up.
Use momentum, but stay in control.
pg115_n0043_easy_read:
When your legs are high up, keep your body tight and straight.
Squeeze your core, glutes, and legs to stay balanced.
See Figure 4.3.
pg115_n0046_easy_read:
If you feel that you are falling forward, tuck and roll out.
If you are falling back, bring 1 leg down first to land safely.
pg116_n0010_easy_read:
Search on the internet to find how a handstand is used in gymnastics.
Then practise it.
pg116_n0016_easy_read: Why is it important to tuck the knees in a backward roll?
pg116_n0019_easy_read:
Why is it important for a gymnast to keep the body straight during a handstand?
How does this improve performance?
pg116_n0022_easy_read: How can gymnasts improve their handstand technique for better alignment and control?
pg116_n0025_easy_read:
A cartwheel is a basic gymnastics skill.
The gymnast moves sideways in this order:
- hand
- hand
- foot
- foot
This movement looks like the spokes of a turning wheel.
pg116_n0026_easy_read:
A cartwheel helps to develop:
- coordination
- balance
- flexibility
- agility
- strength
- body control
It is also a foundation for more advanced tumbling skills.
pg116_n0027_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the cartwheel:
pg116_n0031_easy_read:
Start with 1 foot in front and the other foot behind.
Bend the front knee.
pg116_n0034_easy_read:
Step forward with your stronger foot.
Lift your arms straight up by your ears.
pg116_n0035_easy_read: Keep your back leg straight and extended.
pg116_n0038_easy_read:
As you lean forward, place your 1st hand on the floor.
Then quickly place your 2nd hand in line with the 1st hand.
pg117_n0005_easy_read:
Kick your back leg up.
Then kick your front leg up.
Let your body pass briefly through a handstand position.
pg117_n0008_easy_read:
Land one foot at a time.
Finish in a lunge facing the opposite direction.
See Figure 4.4.
pg117_n0011_easy_read: Repeat the movement to improve it.
pg117_n0021_easy_read:
Search on the internet and other sources for how to do a 2-hand cartwheel and a 1-hand cartwheel.
Practice them many times until you master the skills.
pg117_n0025_easy_read: A split in gymnastics is any movement, skill, or position where the legs move apart in opposite directions.
pg117_n0026_easy_read:
Splits are important for flexibility.
Gymnasts use splits in different routines, including:
- floor exercises
- balance beams
- bars
pg117_n0027_easy_read:
Types of splits include:
- front splits, right or left
- middle splits, also called straddle splits
- over splits
- standing splits
- split leaps or jumps
pg117_n0028_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the basic front split:
pg117_n0032_easy_read:
Step 1 leg forward into a deep lunge.
Keep the back leg straight.
Keep your chest upright.
Hold for 20 – 30 seconds on each side.
pg117_n0035_easy_read:
From the lunge position, straighten the front leg.
Try to reach your toes.
Keep your back straight.
Hold for 20 – 30 seconds.
pg117_n0038_easy_read:
Sit down and press the soles of your feet together.
Gently push your knees toward the floor.
Hold for a while.
pg118_n0005_easy_read:
Sit with your legs straight in front of you.
Reach for your toes.
Keep your back flat.
Hold this position for a while.
pg118_n0008_easy_read:
Start in a lunge position.
Slowly straighten your front leg.
Keep your back knee on the ground.
Hold for 20–30 seconds.
Then change legs.
See Figure 4.5.
pg118_n0011_easy_read:
Start in a deep lunge.
Slowly slide your front foot forward.
Keep your hands on the ground.
Hold for 20–30 seconds.
pg118_n0014_easy_read: Repeat this practice regularly to improve the basic cast skill.
pg118_n0023_easy_read:
Use the internet and other sources to find the steps for practising different cast skills.
Then practise them.
pg118_n0027_easy_read:
A split leap is a gymnastics skill.
The gymnast jumps into the air and stretches both legs into a split position.
The gymnast keeps height, flexibility, and control.
pg118_n0028_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the split leap:
pg118_n0032_easy_read:
Start in a lunge position with 1 foot forward.
Lift your arms.
Keep your chest up.
pg118_n0035_easy_read:
Push off with the back leg strongly.
At the same time, swing the front leg upward to start the split.
pg118_n0038_easy_read:
Extend both legs into a full split.
Keep your toes pointed.
Keep your back upright.
See Figure 4.6.
pg119_n0003_easy_read: (iv) Land softly on the opposite foot. Keep your knees bent and your arms controlled.
pg119_n0015_easy_read: Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a split leap. Then practise it.
pg119_n0019_easy_read: The bridge is a gymnastics skill. In this skill, you arch your back and support your body with your hands and feet on the ground.
pg119_n0020_easy_read: The bridge helps you build flexibility, strength, and control. It especially helps the spine, shoulders, and wrists.
pg119_n0021_easy_read: To learn the bridge step by step, start with the basic bridge position. Then do the wall bridge. After that, do the full bridge.
pg119_n0022_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the bridge:
pg119_n0028_easy_read: Lie on your back. Bend your knees. Keep your feet flat and hip-width apart.
pg119_n0031_easy_read: Place your hands flat on the ground near your ears. Point your fingers toward your shoulders.
pg119_n0034_easy_read: Push with your hands and feet to lift your body off the ground.
pg119_n0037_easy_read: Hold the position for a few seconds. Then lower your body slowly.
pg119_n0040_easy_read: Repeat it until the position feels comfortable.
pg120_n0007_easy_read:
Stand close to a wall.
Reach back with your hands.
pg120_n0010_easy_read: Slowly walk your hands down the wall until you are in a deep backbend.
pg120_n0013_easy_read:
Hold for a few seconds.
Then carefully walk back up.
pg120_n0019_easy_read:
Lie on your back.
Bend your knees.
Place your hands near your shoulders.
pg120_n0022_easy_read:
Push up with your arms and legs.
Lift your body into an arch.
See Figure 4.7.
pg120_n0025_easy_read:
Try to straighten your arms.
Keep your shoulders over your wrists.
pg120_n0028_easy_read:
Hold for 5–10 seconds.
Then lower down with control.
pg120_n0034_easy_read:
A round-off is a gymnastics skill.
It has a strong landing on 2 feet.
It builds momentum for tumbling moves.
pg120_n0035_easy_read:
People often use a round-off to prepare for:
- back handsprings
- flips
- other advanced skills
pg120_n0036_easy_read: These steps will help you practice a round-off:
pg120_n0040_easy_read:
Stand with 1 foot forward.
Keep your arms straight up by your ears.
Keep your body upright.
pg120_n0043_easy_read:
Reach forward and place your first hand on the ground.
Turn your second hand inward to help square your body.
pg120_n0046_easy_read:
Kick your legs over and keep them straight.
Start turning your hips to face forward as your legs pass over.
See Figure 4.8.
pg120_n0049_easy_read:
Pull your legs together in the air so both feet land at the same time.
Push off your hands to create power for the next move.
pg121_n0012_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a round-off.
Practice it many times until you master the skill.
pg121_n0016_easy_read:
In gymnastics, a turn on 1 foot is a skill.
The gymnast turns on 1 foot and keeps balance and control.
pg121_n0017_easy_read:
Gymnasts often do turns on the floor and on the balance beam.
These turns are important in artistic and rhythmic gymnastics.
pg121_n0018_easy_read: These steps will help you practise turns on 1 foot:
pg121_n0022_easy_read:
Stand tall.
Keep your arms in a controlled position.
Shift your weight onto the supporting foot.
pg121_n0025_easy_read:
Lift the free foot to the knee of the standing leg.
Keep your toes pointed.
Keep your body tight.
pg121_n0028_easy_read:
Push up onto the ball of the foot.
Turn smoothly.
Use core control and spotting technique.
See Figure 4.9.
pg121_n0031_easy_read:
Lower the foot gently.
Finish with your arms stretched out in a balanced position.
pg122_n0006_easy_read: Search on the internet and in other sources to learn how to do a turn on 1 foot. Practice it many times until you can do the skill well.

pg122_n0016_easy_read: Gymnastics routines are planned series of movements that a gymnast performs on the apparatus.
pg122_n0017_easy_read:
Each routine is made to develop the gymnast's:
- strength
- flexibility
- coordination
- control
- balance
- artistic expression
pg122_n0018_easy_read:
The type of equipment used decides:
- the kind of movements
- the skills performed
- the judging criteria
pg122_n0019_easy_read:
Gymnastics routines include:
- floor routines
- equipment-based routines
pg122_n0023_easy_read: A floor routine is a planned series of acrobatic and dance movements done on the floor in gymnastics.
pg122_n0024_easy_read: Both men and women compete in the floor exercise, but their routines are slightly different.
pg122_n0029_easy_read: A headstand is a basic upside-down balance skill. In a headstand, a gymnast supports body weight on the head and hands and keeps the body straight and controlled.
pg122_n0030_easy_read: Gymnasts often use a headstand as a beginner skill. It helps them develop balance, strength, and body control before they move to harder upside-down skills like handstands.
pg122_n0031_easy_read: These steps will help you practice a headstand:
pg122_n0034_easy_read: (i) Kneel down. Place your hands on the floor, shoulder-width apart.
pg122_n0036_easy_read: (ii) Make a triangle base with your head and hands for stability.
pg122_n0038_easy_read: (iii) Lift your knees to slowly raise your hips. Bring your legs close to your body.
pg122_n0040_easy_read: (iv) Tighten your core and lift your legs. Extend your legs upward in a straight line and keep control, Figure 4.10; and
pg123_n0002_easy_read:
(v) Keep your body straight.
Balance your weight evenly.
pg123_n0008_easy_read:
Practice these exercises:
- headstand with knees on arms
- headstand on wall
pg123_n0012_easy_read:
A standing scale is a gymnastics balance skill.
The gymnast stands on 1 leg and extends the other leg in a controlled way.
pg123_n0013_easy_read:
A standing scale helps develop:
- flexibility
- balance
- body control
People often use it in artistic gymnastics.
pg123_n0014_easy_read:
Depending on the position, there are:
- front scales
- side scales
- back scales
pg123_n0015_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the standing scale:
pg123_n0019_easy_read:
Stand tall with your feet together.
Tighten your core.
Keep the leg you stand on straight and strong.
pg123_n0022_easy_read:
Lift the other leg.
Extend it forward, to the side, or backward.
Keep control.
See Figure 4.11.
pg123_n0025_easy_read:
Tighten your core and hold the position.
Keep your back straight.
Extend your arms for balance.
pg123_n0028_easy_read:
Lower the leg smoothly.
Return to a standing position with control.
pg124_n0018_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a standing scale.
Then practise it many times until you master the skill.
pg124_n0022_easy_read:
A V-sit is a strength and balance exercise.
In this exercise, a gymnast supports the body on the hands and keeps the legs straight in a "V" shape.
pg124_n0023_easy_read:
A V-sit builds core strength, flexibility, and body control.
People often use it in training, conditioning, and some competitive gymnastics routines.
pg124_n0024_easy_read:
There are different types of V-sit:
- tucked V-sit
- L-sit
- V-sit press
pg124_n0025_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a V-sit:
pg124_n0029_easy_read:
Sit on the floor.
Keep your legs straight in front of you.
pg124_n0032_easy_read:
Place your hands on the floor.
Put them slightly behind your hips for support.
pg124_n0035_easy_read: Tighten your core and abdominal muscles.
pg124_n0038_easy_read:
Lift your legs off the ground.
Keep them straight.
pg125_n0005_easy_read:
Hold the V position.
Lean your back back a little for balance.
See Figure 4.12.
pg125_n0008_easy_read:
Lower your legs slowly.
Then bring your legs down to finish.
pg125_n0015_easy_read:
Search the internet and other sources for how to do a V-sit.
Then practise it.
pg125_n0019_easy_read:
A straddle planche is an advanced strength and balance skill.
In this skill, a gymnast holds the body parallel to the ground.
The hands are the only support.
The legs are spread apart in a straddle position.
pg125_n0020_easy_read:
This skill needs core strength, shoulder stability, and balance.
People often see it in:
- men’s gymnastics
- calisthenics
- breakdancing
pg125_n0021_easy_read: The following steps will help you practise a straddle planche:
pg125_n0025_easy_read:
Place your hands on the floor.
Keep them shoulder-width apart.
pg125_n0028_easy_read:
Lean forward.
Shift your weight onto your arms.
Tighten your core and shoulders.
pg125_n0031_easy_read:
Straighten your arms completely.
Keep your elbows locked to stay stable.
pg125_n0034_easy_read:
Move your legs into a straddle position.
Open your legs wide.
Keep them parallel to the floor.
See Figure 4.13.
pg125_n0037_easy_read:
Hold the position to keep control.
Keep your body straight and strong.
pg126_n0007_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a straddle planche hold.
Then practise it.
pg126_n0011_easy_read:
A split press to handstand is a skill.
In this skill, a gymnast lifts into a handstand from a split position on the floor without using momentum.
pg126_n0012_easy_read:
This skill needs:
- flexibility
- core strength
- controlled balance

Gymnasts often use this skill in floor, beam, and parallel bar routines.
pg126_n0013_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a split press handstand:
pg126_n0017_easy_read:
Sit on the floor in a front split.
Put 1 leg forward and 1 leg back.
pg126_n0020_easy_read: Place your hands on the floor near the front leg for support.
pg126_n0023_easy_read:
Tighten your core.
Push through your arms.
Use your core, shoulders, and arms to start lifting.
pg126_n0026_easy_read:
Lift your hips and back leg first.
Then lift the front leg.
pg126_n0029_easy_read:
Press into a controlled handstand.
Slowly bring both legs together overhead.
Keep your balance.
pg126_n0032_easy_read:
Hold the handstand.
Keep your core tight, your arms straight, and your body aligned.
See Figure 4.14.
pg127_n0015_easy_read:
Search on the internet and other sources for how to do a split press to handstand with 1 leg.
Then practise it.
pg127_n0019_easy_read:
Equipment-based routines are planned movements that gymnasts do with special gym equipment, such as:
- beam
- bars
- rings
- vault
pg127_n0020_easy_read: Each routine shows the gymnast's strength, balance, and skills on that piece of equipment.
pg127_n0021_easy_read:
Equipment-based routines include:
- gripping
- mounts
- dismounts
- cast
- swing
- hangs
- holdings
pg127_n0025_easy_read: Gripping means how a gymnast holds an apparatus.
pg127_n0026_easy_read: Proper gripping is very important for control, safety, and performance in different skills and routines.
pg127_n0027_easy_read:
The different types of grips include:
- neutral grip
- false grip
- above-the-ring grip
pg127_n0031_easy_read: A neutral grip is when the palms face each other while the gymnast holds an apparatus.
pg127_n0032_easy_read:
Gymnasts commonly use the neutral grip on:
- parallel bars
- rings
- rope climbing
- some conditioning exercises

This grip gives a natural wrist position and better stability.
pg127_n0033_easy_read: The following steps will help you practise a neutral grip on rings:
pg128_n0005_easy_read:
Hold the ring with your palms facing each other.
Wrap your thumbs around the ring.
See Figure 4.15.
pg128_n0008_easy_read:
Keep your wrists in a neutral position.
Do not bend them forward or backward.
pg128_n0011_easy_read: Use your shoulder to stay stable.
pg128_n0016_easy_read:
Read reliable sources to find out how to do a neutral grip on parallel bars and uneven bars.
Then practise it.
pg128_n0020_easy_read:
A false grip is a special grip.
Gymnasts use it mainly on rings and sometimes on the high bar.
pg128_n0021_easy_read:
In a false grip, the wrist is above the rings or the bar.
This helps gymnasts move smoothly into strength moves, such as:
- muscle-ups
- iron crosses
- levers
pg128_n0022_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a false grip on a ring:
pg128_n0026_easy_read:
Place your hands on the rings.
Rest the inside of your wrist directly on top.
See Figure 4.16.
pg128_n0029_easy_read:
Grip firmly.
Keep your wrist bent.
Your body weight should be supported by the wrist, not only by the fingers.
pg128_n0032_easy_read: Use your forearms and shoulders to stay in control and avoid slipping.
pg129_n0008_easy_read:
Read reliable sources to learn how to do the false grip on the parallel bars and uneven bars.
Then practise it.
pg129_n0012_easy_read:
In gymnastics, the above-the-ring grip is a hand position.
In this position, the gymnast supports body weight above the rings.
The gymnast does not hang below the rings.
pg129_n0013_easy_read: People commonly use this grip in support positions and advanced strength skills on the still rings.
pg129_n0014_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the above-the-ring grip on a ring:
pg129_n0018_easy_read:
Grip the rings with your palms facing down.
See Figure 4.17.
pg129_n0021_easy_read:
Keep your wrists and forearms above the rings.
This helps give stability.
pg129_n0024_easy_read: Keep your shoulders, wrists, and core engaged to maintain control.
pg130_n0004_easy_read: Search on the internet and in other reliable sources for how to do the above-the-ring grip. Then practice it.
pg130_n0007_easy_read: 1. Describe how the false grip is different from the traditional overhand grip. Also describe when the false grip is most useful in gymnastics.
pg130_n0008_easy_read: 2. How do the different grips affect a gymnast’s ability to hold the apparatus and keep control during gymnastics routines?
pg130_n0012_easy_read: In gymnastics, a mount is the way a gymnast gets onto an apparatus at the start of a routine.
pg130_n0013_easy_read: A mount is the first skill. It sets the tone for the rest of the performance.
pg130_n0014_easy_read: Mounts can be simple or complex. This depends on the gymnast’s skill level and the apparatus they use.
pg130_n0015_easy_read:
There are different types of mounts:
- balance beam mounts
- uneven bar mounts
- parallel bar mounts
- pommel horse mounts
pg130_n0019_easy_read: Balance beam mounts are the techniques or movements gymnasts use to get onto the balance beam at the start of a routine.
pg130_n0020_easy_read: Balance beam mounts need more precision because the beam is narrow.
pg130_n0021_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a balance beam mount step by step:
pg130_n0025_easy_read: Stand at the end of the beam.
pg130_n0028_easy_read: Place your hands on the beam. Lift your body. Land with your stomach on the beam.
pg130_n0031_easy_read: Push up into a sitting position. Or swing your legs into a straddle sit. See Figure 4.18.
pg130_n0033_easy_read: Figure 4.18: Mounting on a balance beam
pg131_n0005_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a jump to beam balance mount.
Then practise it.
pg131_n0009_easy_read: Mounting the uneven bars means how a gymnast gets onto the bars to start their routine.
pg131_n0010_easy_read: These steps will help you practise mounting on uneven bars:
pg131_n0017_easy_read:
Jump up and hold the bar.
See Figure 4.19.
pg131_n0020_easy_read: Stretch your legs into a glide swing.
pg131_n0023_easy_read:
Pull your feet to the bar.
Then push into front support.
pg131_n0026_easy_read:
For the high bar:
- jump
- open your legs to the sides
- catch the bar in the air
pg131_n0035_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a mount on uneven bars.
Then practise it again and again until you master the skill.
pg132_n0005_easy_read: Mounting the parallel bars means getting onto the apparatus to start a routine.
pg132_n0006_easy_read: These steps will help you practise mounting on the parallel bars:
pg132_n0010_easy_read: Jump and hold the bars with both hands.
pg132_n0013_easy_read: Swing your legs forward as you pull yourself up.
pg132_n0016_easy_read:
Land in a straight-arm support position and come off.
Then:
pg132_n0019_easy_read: Put your hands on the bars and jump up.
pg132_n0022_easy_read:
Lean forward as you push into a handstand. See Figure 4.20.
And:
pg132_n0025_easy_read: Hold the handstand for a short time before you move into the routine.
pg132_n0031_easy_read:
Search the internet and other sources for how to do a swing-up mount on the parallel bars.
Then practise it.
pg132_n0035_easy_read: What physical skills does a gymnast need to perform well on the uneven bars?
pg132_n0039_easy_read: Mounting the pommel horse is how a gymnast gets onto the pommel horse to start a routine.
pg132_n0040_easy_read: These steps will help you practise mounting on the pommel horse:
pg133_n0010_easy_read:
Jump up.
Place 1 leg over the pommel horse.
Hold the handles.
pg133_n0013_easy_read:
Swing your legs to start a scissor movement and come off.
Then:
pg133_n0019_easy_read:
Jump and glide onto the pommel horse.
Hold the handles.
pg133_n0022_easy_read:
Start your routine at once with leg swings.
See Figure 4.21.
pg133_n0028_easy_read:
Search on the internet and other sources for how to do a knee mount.
Practice it many times until you master the skill.
pg133_n0034_easy_read: Why is body control important when doing a balance beam mount?
pg133_n0037_easy_read: What are the biggest challenges when doing a pommel horse mount?
pg133_n0041_easy_read:
A dismount is a skill in a gymnastics routine.
The gymnast leaves the apparatus and lands on the floor in a controlled way.
pg133_n0042_easy_read:
It is 1 of the most important parts of a routine because it shows:
- control
- difficulty
- precision
pg133_n0043_easy_read:
There are different types of dismounts.
They are grouped by the apparatus used.
pg133_n0044_easy_read:
It includes:
- balance beam dismounts
- uneven bars dismounts
- parallel bars dismounts
- pommel horse dismounts
pg133_n0045_easy_read:
Other types are:
- ring dismounts
- vault dismounts
pg133_n0046_easy_read: The following steps will help you practise the different dismounts:
pg134_n0005_easy_read: A balance beam dismount is the way a gymnast leaves the balance beam at the end of the routine.
pg134_n0006_easy_read: These steps will help you practise getting off the balance beam:
pg134_n0010_easy_read:
Stand at the end of the beam.
Face forward.
pg134_n0013_easy_read:
Push with your legs.
Jump into the air.
pg134_n0014_easy_read:
Keep your body straight or tucked, depending on the style.
See Figure 4.22.
pg134_n0017_easy_read:
Land on both feet.
Keep your knees slightly bent.
pg134_n0020_easy_read:
Hold the landing position.
Keep your arms up for stability.
pg134_n0026_easy_read:
A cartwheel dismount is a type of balance beam dismount.
The gymnast does a cartwheel at the end of the beam to leave the apparatus.
pg134_n0027_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a cartwheel dismount from a balance beam:
pg134_n0031_easy_read:
Place your hands on the beam.
Get ready to move into the cartwheel or round-off.
pg134_n0034_easy_read:
Do a cartwheel or a round-off.
A round-off helps with more rotation and power.
pg134_n0037_easy_read:
As you finish the cartwheel or round-off, push with your hands.
Land with your feet on the floor.
See Figure 4.23.
pg135_n0007_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a cartwheel dismount.
Then practise it many times until you master the skill.
pg135_n0011_easy_read:
A scissor dismount is a way to finish a pommel horse routine.
You use a scissor movement to leave the apparatus with control and style.
pg135_n0012_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a scissor dismount from a pommel horse:
pg135_n0016_easy_read: Start swinging your legs in a controlled scissor movement.
pg135_n0019_easy_read:
Swing your body and legs into a controlled dismount.
Use 1 final powerful leg swing.
See Figure 4.24.
pg135_n0022_easy_read: Focus on landing cleanly and keeping your balance.
pg136_n0007_easy_read:
A swing-off dismount is a gymnastics dismount.
The gymnast swings to build momentum.
Then the gymnast lets go of the pommel horse and lands on the floor.
pg136_n0008_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a swing-off dismount from a pommel horse:
pg136_n0012_easy_read:
Swing both legs.
Push off the pommel horse with momentum.
See Figure 4.25.
pg136_n0015_easy_read:
As you leave the pommel horse, rotate.
Land cleanly with soft knees.
pg137_n0004_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a pommel horse dismount with a hop.
Then practise it.
pg137_n0008_easy_read: The vault is the dismount from the vaulting table.
pg137_n0009_easy_read: After you complete the vault, land properly to show control.
pg137_n0010_easy_read: These steps will help you practise it:
pg137_n0014_easy_read:
Push off the vaulting table with force.
Use your arms to push yourself into the air.
pg137_n0017_easy_read:
Do any flips or twists that are needed.
This depends on the vault style.
pg137_n0020_easy_read:
Look at your landing area.
Then land with both feet at the same time.
Keep your knees slightly bent to absorb the impact.
See Figure 4.26.
pg137_n0025_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a simple tuck-jump vault dismount.
Then practise it.
pg138_n0005_easy_read: A dismount at the rear end of the swing is a technique. The gymnast does the dismount at the farthest point of the swing, just before the body swings back toward the bar.
pg138_n0006_easy_read: This is a common dismount technique on the uneven bars.
pg138_n0007_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the dismount at the rear end of the swing:
pg138_n0011_easy_read: Start by swinging your body back and forth with control.
pg138_n0014_easy_read: Extend your legs and tighten your core as you move toward the rear end. This helps you prepare for the dismount.
pg138_n0017_easy_read: Make sure you reach the highest point of the swing at the rear end, with your hips above the bar.
pg138_n0020_easy_read: Keep your legs extended and arch your body slightly. Get ready to release the bar.
pg138_n0023_easy_read: At the rear end of the swing, push off the bar with your arms. Tuck your knees or keep them extended, depending on the type of dismount you are doing.
pg138_n0026_easy_read: Release the bar at the highest point of the swing. Start your rotation, such as a backflip or twist. Keep your body tight and controlled. See Figure 4.27.
pg138_n0029_easy_read: Look for the landing early as you finish the rotation. Focus on landing with both feet at the same time and with your knees bent.
pg138_n0034_easy_read: Figure 4.27: Dismount at the rear end of the swing
pg139_n0005_easy_read:
Search the internet and other sources to learn how to do a back tuck dismount at the rear end.
Then practice it.
pg139_n0009_easy_read:
The skin-the-cat dismount is a gymnastics movement.
People often do it on rings or on a horizontal bar.
pg139_n0010_easy_read:
In this movement, you hang and turn your body backwards through your arms.
You pass through an upside-down position.
Then you return to a hang or complete the dismount.
pg139_n0011_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the skin-the-cat dismount:
pg139_n0015_easy_read: Hang from a bar or ring with an overhand grip.
pg139_n0018_easy_read:
Tuck your legs and turn backwards.
Bring your feet through your arms and over your head.
pg139_n0021_easy_read: Pass through a controlled upside-down position.
pg139_n0024_easy_read:
Continue the rotation.
Lower your legs back down towards the ground.
See Figure 4.28.
pg139_n0027_easy_read: You can let go and land on your feet instead of returning to a hang.
pg140_n0004_easy_read: Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a skin-the-cat with a straight body. Then practice it.

pg140_n0008_easy_read: 2. Why is it important to bend your knees when landing in gymnastics jumps?
pg140_n0012_easy_read: A cast is a basic skill in gymnastics. Gymnasts do it on the uneven bars, the parallel bars, or the high bar.
pg140_n0013_easy_read: In a cast, the gymnast lifts the body from a front support position to a higher position. This often prepares the gymnast for harder skills.
pg140_n0014_easy_read: There are 4 main types of cast:
pg140_n0018_easy_read: Basic cast: The gymnast pushes away from the bar and lifts the body up from a front support position.
pg140_n0021_easy_read: Cast to handstand: The gymnast continues the movement until they reach a full handstand.
pg140_n0024_easy_read: Straddle cast: The gymnast spreads the legs apart while lifting into a handstand.
pg140_n0027_easy_read: Cast to kip: This movement builds momentum to go into a kip. A kip is a common bar skill used in routines.
pg140_n0029_easy_read: The cast helps build strength in the shoulders, arms, and core. This strength helps with harder bar skills like giants and releases.
pg140_n0030_easy_read: Gymnasts use this skill in transitions and to connect parts of a bar routine.
pg140_n0031_easy_read: To practice a basic cast in gymnastics, especially on uneven bars or parallel bars, you need good technique, strength, and body control.
pg140_n0032_easy_read: These steps will help you practice a cast:
pg140_n0036_easy_read: Start in a front support position on the bar. Keep your arms straight, your body tight, and your hips against the bar.
pg140_n0039_easy_read: Grip the bar firmly with your hands. Keep your arms straight and your shoulders slightly over the bar.
pg140_n0042_easy_read: Lean forward a little and push through your shoulders to create momentum.
pg140_n0045_easy_read: Tighten your core and glutes to keep your body straight.
pg140_n0048_easy_read: Swing your legs slightly backward. Then kick them forward while tightening your core.
pg141_n0005_easy_read: As your legs rise, let your hips move slightly away from the bar.
pg141_n0008_easy_read:
Keep your body tight.
Do not arch your back.
Push down on the bar to make your cast go higher.
See figure 4.29.
pg141_n0011_easy_read:
When your body reaches the highest point of the cast, control the way down.
Keep your muscles engaged.
Land back in the front support position with control.
pg141_n0014_easy_read:
Repeat this many times.
Gradually increase the height of your cast.
pg141_n0020_easy_read:
Search in different sources to find the different ways to do casts.
Then practise them.
pg141_n0025_easy_read:
Explain the advantages of doing a straddle cast instead of a standard cast.
In which routines might this be helpful?
pg141_n0028_easy_read:
What part do timing and body position play in doing a backward cast?
How can a gymnast improve this skill?
pg141_n0032_easy_read: In gymnastics, hangs means a position where a gymnast holds onto the bar or rings while their body hangs in the air.
pg141_n0033_easy_read: Hangs are important for building muscles in
pg142_n0004_easy_read:
There are different types of hangs:
- straight arm hang
- flexed arm hang
- pike arm hang
- inverted hang
pg142_n0008_easy_read: A straight arm hang is a position where a gymnast hangs from a bar with the arms fully extended. The body stays straight or slightly hollow.
pg142_n0009_easy_read: This is a basic position. Gymnasts use it in different swings, releases, and transitions.
pg142_n0010_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the straight arm hang:
pg142_n0014_easy_read:
Find a suitable bar.
Men use a high bar.
Women use an uneven bar.
Make sure the bar is high enough for your height.
pg142_n0017_easy_read:
Grip the bar with an overhand grip.
Keep your hands shoulder-width apart.
Wrap your fingers securely around the bar.
Keep your thumbs under the bar for a better grip.
pg142_n0020_easy_read:
Keep your arms fully extended, but do not lock them.
Use your shoulders and lats.
Keep your body in a slightly hollow position.
pg142_n0023_easy_read:
Keep your legs together.
Keep your legs slightly in front of your body.
Point your fingers.
pg142_n0026_easy_read:
Hold the position for 10-30 seconds.
This helps build grip and shoulder endurance.
Gradually increase the time as you get stronger.
Figure 4.30.
pg143_n0005_easy_read:
A flexed arm hang is an upper-body strength exercise.
You hang from a bar.
Your chin stays above the bar.
Your arms stay bent.
pg143_n0006_easy_read: People often use it in gymnastics to measure upper-body endurance and grip strength.
pg143_n0007_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the flexed arm hang:
pg143_n0011_easy_read:
Use a strong bar.
The bar must let you hang freely.
Your feet must not touch the ground.
pg143_n0014_easy_read:
Hold the bar with an overhand grip or an underhand grip.
Keep your hands shoulder-width apart.
pg143_n0015_easy_read:
Use a step or a box.
Or ask someone to lift you into position.
Do this if you are not strong enough to pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar.
pg143_n0018_easy_read:
Keep your chin above the bar.
Do not rest your chin on the bar.
Use your arms, shoulders, and core to keep holding on.
See Figure 4.31.
pg143_n0021_easy_read:
Hold on until your muscles get tired and you can no longer keep the correct form.
Try to increase the hang time as you get used to it.
pg143_n0022_easy_read: In competitions, the winner is usually the person who can hold on the longest.
pg144_n0004_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a flexed long hang.
Then practise it many times until you master the skill.
pg144_n0008_easy_read:
A pike hang is a hanging position on a bar.
The gymnast keeps the legs straight and lifted in a pike position.
See Figure 4.32.
pg144_n0009_easy_read: This skill helps build core strength, flexibility, and body control for more advanced bar movements.
pg144_n0010_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a pike hang:
pg144_n0014_easy_read:
Grip the bar with an overhand grip or an underhand grip.
Keep your hands shoulder-width apart.
pg144_n0017_easy_read:
Keep your shoulders active.
Tighten your abs and hip flexors.
pg144_n0020_easy_read:
Keep your legs straight and together.
Point your toes.
Lift your legs to hip height.
Your body makes an "L" shape.
pg144_n0023_easy_read:
At first, hold the pike hang for at least 5-10 seconds.
Then try to increase the time.
pg144_n0028_easy_read: Use the internet or other available resources to find information about how to do an extended pike hang.
pg144_n0029_easy_read:
Look for:
- step-by-step instructions
- safety tips
- demonstrations
pg145_n0005_easy_read: An inverted hang is a position where a gymnast hangs upside down from a bar, rings, or another piece of equipment. The body stays fully stretched and controlled.
pg145_n0006_easy_read:
This skill helps build:
- core strength
- body awareness
- control when upside down

These are important for flips, giants, and other advanced skills.
pg145_n0007_easy_read:
There are different types of inverted hangs:
- straight body inverted hang
- tuck inverted hang
- pike inverted hang
- inverted hang on rings
pg145_n0008_easy_read: These are general steps to help you practise inverted hangs:
pg145_n0012_easy_read:
Hold the equipment with:
- an overhand grip on a bar
- a neutral grip on rings
pg145_n0015_easy_read: Pull yourself upside down. Keep your legs tucked or straddled. Use your core and shoulders to control the movement.
pg145_n0016_easy_read: Keep your arms slightly bent or straight, depending on the equipment.
pg145_n0019_easy_read: Hold the position. Use your core, back, and shoulders. Keep your legs together and pointed for proper form. See Figure 4.33.
pg145_n0022_easy_read: Lower yourself in a controlled way to come out of the position. Do not swing too much.
pg145_n0023_easy_read: If you are on rings, return to a normal hang before you dismount.
pg145_n0030_easy_read: Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do an inverted hang. Then practise it many times until you master the skill.
pg146_n0005_easy_read: A tucked pullover is a basic bar skill. The gymnast starts by hanging. Then the gymnast pulls the legs up into a tuck. After that, the gymnast turns around the bar and finishes in a front support position on top of the bar.
pg146_n0006_easy_read: Teachers often teach this skill to beginners on uneven bars. It helps beginners build strength and control of their body for harder bar skills.
pg146_n0007_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a tucked pull over:
pg146_n0011_easy_read: Stand under the low bar. Hold the bar with an overhand grip. Keep your hands shoulder-width apart.
pg146_n0014_easy_read: Hang with your arms straight. Keep your feet slightly off the ground. Keep your core and arms tight.
pg146_n0017_easy_read: Pull your knees toward your chest in a tight tuck position. Keep your chin tucked. Keep your eyes looking at the bar.
pg146_n0020_easy_read: Push with your arms when your hips get closer to the bar. This helps your body turn over the bar. Keep your legs tucked. Let your back roll over the bar smoothly. See Figure 4.34.
pg146_n0023_easy_read: Finish by straightening your arms as you press your hips onto the bar. Straighten your legs. End in a front support position.
pg146_n0030_easy_read: Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a tucked pull over. Practise it many times until you master the skill.
pg147_n0005_easy_read: Swings are a basic movement in gymnastics. The body moves in a controlled and steady way around a bar or rings.
pg147_n0006_easy_read: This movement includes forward swings, back swings, and tap swings on bars.
pg147_n0007_easy_read:
Other swings on bars are:
- straight-body swings
- pike swings
- straddle swings
- giant swings
pg147_n0011_easy_read: The forward and back swing on rings is a movement. A gymnast hangs from the rings and swings the body forward and backward. See Figure 4.35.
pg147_n0012_easy_read: Forward and back swings are usually part of the basic swing technique on rings.
pg147_n0013_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the forward and backward swing on rings:
pg147_n0017_easy_read: Hang from the rings with your arms straight and your feet off the ground.
pg147_n0018_easy_read: Keep your body straight. Hold the rings firmly. Tighten your core. Keep a small bend in your knees;
pg147_n0021_easy_read: Lean your upper body a little backward. Push your legs behind you.
pg147_n0022_easy_read: Use your arms and shoulders to help create momentum. Pull gently as you lean back;
pg147_n0025_easy_read: Let the momentum move your body forward.
pg147_n0026_easy_read: As your legs swing forward, kick your hips up toward the rings. Let your upper body follow naturally; and
pg147_n0029_easy_read: When you reach the highest point of the forward swing, let your legs extend in front of you.
pg147_n0030_easy_read: Then start to lean backward again to move smoothly into the backward part of the swing.
pg147_n0036_easy_read: Figure 4.35: Forward and backward swing on the still rings
pg148_n0005_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do forward and back swings to a hollow hold.
Then practise it.
pg148_n0009_easy_read:
A tap swing on bars is a gymnastics skill.
The gymnast swings back and forth on the bars in a controlled and steady way.
pg148_n0010_easy_read:
This skill helps build momentum for more advanced skills, such as:
- releases
- dismounts
- transitions between bars
pg148_n0011_easy_read: This skill is often one of the first swinging techniques learned when developing bar routines.
pg148_n0012_easy_read: These steps will help you practise a tap swing:
pg148_n0016_easy_read:
Hold the bar with your arms straight and your legs hanging down.
Use your shoulders and your core to keep your body stable.
pg148_n0019_easy_read:
Swing your legs behind you.
Bend your hips and knees a little.
pg148_n0020_easy_read:
Keep your body tight and controlled.
This helps prevent wild swinging.
pg148_n0023_easy_read:
Push your hips to create momentum.
Let your hips tap the bar when your legs come forward.
This gives the swing more power.
pg148_n0026_easy_read:
Move your body in an arch.
Bring your feet above the bar.
Use your arms and your core to control the movement and get ready for the next swing.
See Figure 4.36.
pg148_n0028_easy_read: Figure 4.36: Tap swing on the bar
pg149_n0005_easy_read:
Search on the internet and in other sources for how to do a tape swing on the bar.
Practice it many times until you master the skill.
pg149_n0009_easy_read: What are the common mistakes during bar swings?
pg149_n0013_easy_read: In gymnastics, holding means keeping a position on an apparatus for a set time.
pg149_n0014_easy_read:
Gymnasts often do this to show:
- strength
- coordination
- stability
- agility
- control
pg149_n0015_easy_read:
A gymnast can do holding in different positions on:
- rings
- bars
- beam
- floor

Holding is used to show the gymnast can keep balance and control the body.
pg149_n0016_easy_read:
The main types of holding are:
- hold on the rings
- hold on the bars
- arabesque hold
- split hold

These types are grouped by the apparatus and the type of hold:
pg149_n0020_easy_read:
Hold on the rings means gripping the gymnastic rings tightly with the hands and keeping the body still.
The gymnast can hang below the rings or hold themself above the rings without moving.
pg149_n0021_easy_read:
This routine includes:
- iron cross
- support hold
pg149_n0024_easy_read:
Iron cross: This is a strength skill on the rings.
The gymnast holds the body up with the arms stretched out to the sides in a "T" shape.
pg149_n0025_easy_read: These steps will help you practice the iron cross:
pg149_n0032_easy_read:
Hold each ring with 1 hand.
Keep your palms facing in.
pg149_n0033_easy_read: Wrap your fingers tightly around the rings.
pg149_n0036_easy_read:
Jump or push off a little to lift your feet.
Then hang or hold yourself up.
pg149_n0039_easy_read: Whether you hang below or hold yourself above, keep your arms straight and locked.
pg149_n0042_easy_read:
Keep your legs together.
Keep your body firm to avoid swinging.
pg149_n0045_easy_read:
Stay in this position for a few seconds.
Figure 4.37(a).
pg150_n0003_easy_read: (vii) Repeat the steps above until you can do the iron cross on the ring well.
pg150_n0009_easy_read: Support hold: A gymnastics move where the gymnast supports body weight on the rings with straight arms and keeps the body stable while hanging on the ring.
pg150_n0010_easy_read: These steps will help you practise the support hold on the ring:
pg150_n0014_easy_read:
Stand between the rings.
Adjust the rings to waist height.
pg150_n0017_easy_read:
Hold 1 ring in each hand.
Keep your palms facing inward.
pg150_n0020_easy_read:
Use your legs to jump a little.
Lift your body off the ground.
pg150_n0023_easy_read:
Keep your arms straight by your sides.
See Figure 4.37(b).
pg150_n0026_easy_read:
Keep your legs together.
Stay upright.
Keep your core tight.
Your core means your stomach muscles.
pg150_n0029_easy_read:
Stay still and balanced for a few seconds.
Do not swing.
pg150_n0032_easy_read: Repeat the steps above until you can do the support hold on the ring well.
pg151_n0007_easy_read:
Hold on the bars means gripping the gymnastics bars firmly with your hands.
Keep your body still.
You can hang below the bars or support your body above the bars.
pg151_n0008_easy_read: Some common holds on the bar are front support and back support.
pg151_n0011_easy_read: These steps will help you practise front support hold on the bar:
pg151_n0015_easy_read:
Stand in front of the bar.
For example, use a horizontal bar or parallel bars.
pg151_n0018_easy_read:
Place both hands on the bar with an overhand grip.
Your palms face down.
pg151_n0019_easy_read: Your hands should be shoulder-width apart.
pg151_n0022_easy_read:
Jump up or step from a raised platform.
Bring your chest above the bar.
pg151_n0025_easy_read: Keep your arms straight and extended.
pg151_n0028_easy_read: Place your shoulders directly over your hands or slightly in front of them.
pg151_n0031_easy_read: Tighten your core to keep your body straight and stable.
pg151_n0034_easy_read:
Keep your legs straight.
Keep your feet together.
Point your toes.
See figure 4.38(a).
pg152_n0005_easy_read:
Keep your body tight.
Do not let your back sag or arch.
pg152_n0008_easy_read:
Breathe in a steady way.
Hold the position for the required time, for example 5–10 seconds.
pg152_n0012_easy_read: Repeat the steps above until you can do the hold on the bar well.
pg152_n0018_easy_read: Back support: This is a position on parallel bars. The gymnast faces away from the bars. The body stays straight, and the arms extend behind.
pg152_n0019_easy_read: Follow these steps to practise the back support hold on the bar:
pg152_n0023_easy_read: Stand between the bars at a suitable height.
pg152_n0026_easy_read:
Place your hands on the bar or bars.
Point your fingers forward.
pg152_n0029_easy_read: Use a firm grip to support your body weight.
pg152_n0032_easy_read:
Push through your hands.
Straighten your arms fully.
Lift your hips off the ground.
pg152_n0035_easy_read:
Place your body in a straight position facing upward.
Keep your chest open.
pg152_n0038_easy_read:
Keep your arms straight.
Press your shoulders down and back.
pg152_n0041_easy_read: Keep a straight line from your shoulders to your heels.
pg152_n0044_easy_read:
Look slightly forward or upward.
This helps keep your neck in line.
pg152_n0047_easy_read: Keep your body tight and straight, Figure 4.38(b); and
pg152_n0050_easy_read: Hold the position for the required time, for example 5–15 seconds.
pg153_n0007_easy_read: A position where the gymnast keeps the body in a straight line, balances on 1 leg, and lifts the other leg behind in a horizontal position on the bar.
pg153_n0008_easy_read: Follow these steps to do the back arabesque hold:
pg153_n0012_easy_read:
Stand tall.
Keep your feet together.
Keep your arms at your sides.
pg153_n0015_easy_read: Look forward to help keep your balance.
pg153_n0018_easy_read: Shift your weight onto your supporting leg.
pg153_n0021_easy_read: Tighten your core to help with stability.
pg153_n0024_easy_read:
Slowly lift the opposite leg straight behind you.
See Figure 4.39.
pg153_n0027_easy_read: Point the toes of the raised leg.
pg153_n0030_easy_read: Extend the same arm as the supporting leg forward.
pg153_n0033_easy_read: Extend the opposite arm backward or to the side.
pg153_n0036_easy_read:
Keep your body in a straight line.
Hold the position for 5–10 seconds.
pg153_n0039_easy_read:
Lower your leg gently.
Return to the starting position.
pg154_n0007_easy_read:
This is a balance position on the beam.
The gymnast opens the legs into a split or holds a straddle while balancing on the beam.
pg154_n0008_easy_read: Follow these steps to practise the split hold on the balance beam.
pg154_n0012_easy_read: Warm up well to prepare your muscles;
pg154_n0015_easy_read: Carefully climb onto the balance beam using your preferred technique;
pg154_n0018_easy_read:
Stand upright in the centre of the beam.
Extend your arms to the sides for balance;
pg154_n0021_easy_read:
Take 1 leg forward into a controlled lunge position.
Keep your back leg straight behind you;
pg154_n0024_easy_read:
Slowly slide into a split position.
Keep your legs in line with the beam.
Keep your hips square.
pg154_n0025_easy_read: Use your arms for balance and control;
pg154_n0028_easy_read:
Tighten your core.
Keep a strong upper body posture to hold the position steadily;
pg154_n0031_easy_read:
Keep the split for a few seconds.
Start with 3–5 seconds and build up over time.
Focus on form and control, Figure 4.40; and
pg154_n0034_easy_read:
Gently push back up into a lunge.
Then return to standing and dismount carefully.
pg155_n0008_easy_read:

pg157_n0010_easy_read: (ii) Bend your knees a little. Lean backward. Keep your chest lifted.

pg157_n0016_easy_read: (v) Push your hands off the ground strongly. Your back straightens as your feet move toward the floor.
pg157_n0018_easy_read: (vi) Land with your feet together. Keep your knees slightly bent and your arms high. Figure 4.42.

pg157_n0040_easy_read: A scissors leap in gymnastics is a jump. The gymnast kicks 1 leg forward and moves the other leg backward. This makes a scissor-like movement in the air.
pg157_n0041_easy_read: The gymnast’s body should be fully stretched. Both legs should be in a split position. The arms are usually raised or kept in a controlled position to help balance and grace.
pg157_n0042_easy_read: These steps will help you practice a scissors leap:
pg158_n0005_easy_read:
Stand up straight.
Keep your feet together.
Keep your arms by your sides.
Then bend your knees a little.
Tighten your core and get ready to jump.
pg158_n0008_easy_read:
Push off the floor strongly with both feet.
Move 1 leg forward and the other leg backward in a smooth movement.
pg158_n0011_easy_read:
As you jump, stretch both legs into a split position.
Keep your body upright.
Keep your arms engaged.
Point your toes for elegance.
See Figure 4.43.
pg158_n0014_easy_read:
Land on 1 foot.
Bend your knee a little.
Keep the other leg in front.
Keep your body upright and balanced.

- Goal Shooter (GS)
- Goal Attack (GA)
- Wing Attack (WA)
pg161_n0010_easy_read: Attacking third of a team: The part of the court closest to the other team's goalpost, where the team tries to score.
pg161_n0012_easy_read: Back handspring: A skill where the gymnast jumps backward, lands on their hands, and pushes off to land on their feet.

pg161_n0026_easy_read: Buoyancy: The ability to float or stay afloat in water.
pg161_n0028_easy_read: Cartwheel: A basic skill where the body moves sideways in a hand-hand-foot-foot pattern, like the spokes of a wheel.

pg161_n0032_easy_read: Centre circle: A small circle in the centre of the netball court where play starts and starts again after each goal.
pg161_n0034_easy_read: Centre pass: The way to start or restart play from the centre circle after a goal is scored.
pg161_n0036_easy_read: Centre third: The middle part of the netball court. Teams mainly use it to move the ball from defense to attack.
